Our adapters integrate pretrained all-atom representations through two mechanisms: enriching the diffusion model's molecular block features and incorporating pairwise structural information into the geometric diffusion model's denoiser. Theoretically, we prove that the augmented denoiser preserves geometry and pairwise attention fusion provides additional attention expressivity beyond feature-only fusion. Experimentally, across antibody, peptide, and small molecule binder-design benchmarks, PairFuse achieves stronger performance than the pretrained diffusion model and existing representation-fusion baselines.

AI.tldr: PairFuse is a parameter-efficient method that fuses pretrained all-atom representations into an independently pretrained geometric latent diffusion model through lightweight layerwise adapters, targeting unified binder design. It outperforms the pretrained diffusion model and existing representation-fusion baselines on antibody, peptide and small-molecule binder-design benchmarks.
AI.motivation: All-atom models perform strongly on modality-specific binder design, while geometric latent diffusion models pursue unified binder design in a shared latent space, and the paper seeks to combine these complementary strengths.
AI.method: Lightweight layerwise adapters integrate pretrained all-atom representations through two mechanisms, enriching the diffusion model's molecular block features and incorporating pairwise structural information into the denoiser; the paper proves that the augmented denoiser preserves geometry and that pairwise attention fusion adds expressivity beyond feature-only fusion.
AI.result: Across antibody, peptide and small-molecule binder-design benchmarks, PairFuse achieves stronger performance than the pretrained diffusion model and existing representation-fusion baselines.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained all-atom representations can be generalized to unified binder design through parameter-efficient representation fusion.

title: Preserving Safety During Sequential Fine-Tuning: A Factorial and Geometric Analysis of Replay
summary: Benign fine-tuning can erode safety alignment in large language models, and sequential adaptation substantially compounds this risk. Prior work mitigates this erosion by replaying harmful-prompt refusals and benign-compliance examples, while other work instead matches base-model logits via distillation. However, the individual contributions of supervised exposure and distillation to safety behavior and refusal geometry during sequential adaptation remain unclear. We factor these two strategies apart and study their behavioral and geometric effects during sequential LoRA fine-tuning of Mistral-7B and Llama-3-8B across diverse task sequences (code generation, German-language summarization, and science question-answering). Behaviorally, supervised replay exposure yields the largest reduction in HarmBench attack success rate (ASR) on Mistral, averaging 51.1 points below base, but at a substantial over-refusal cost, averaging 53.4 points above base on OR-Bench-hard. Logit distillation, without any supervised replay loss, largely prevents safety erosion at a fraction of this cost: an average 5.4-point ASR reduction against only a 5.1-point rise in over-refusal. Llama shows the same asymmetry between the two strategies. Combining exposure and distillation moderates exposure's over-refusal while leaving downstream task scores largely unaffected. Geometrically, the two models diverge: on Mistral, distillation preserves the base refusal direction more closely than exposure does, whereas on Llama, refusal behavior after exposure largely survives ablation of the extracted refusal direction. This dissociation between models indicates that preserving the base refusal direction is not a reliable proxy for behavioral safety.

AI.tldr: The paper factors supervised replay and logit distillation apart to study how each preserves safety during sequential LoRA fine-tuning of Mistral-7B and Llama-3-8B. Supervised replay gives the largest HarmBench ASR reduction at a substantial over-refusal cost, while distillation largely prevents safety erosion at a much smaller cost.
AI.motivation: Benign fine-tuning can erode safety alignment and sequential adaptation compounds the risk, but the individual contributions of supervised exposure and distillation to safety behavior and refusal geometry during sequential adaptation remain unclear.
AI.method: Supervised replay exposure and logit distillation are studied separately and in combination during sequential LoRA fine-tuning of Mistral-7B and Llama-3-8B across task sequences of code generation, German-language summarization and science question-answering, with behavioral and refusal-geometry analyses.
AI.result: On Mistral, supervised exposure lowers HarmBench ASR by an average of 51.1 points below base but raises OR-Bench-hard over-refusal by an average of 53.4 points. Distillation alone gives an average 5.4-point ASR reduction against a 5.1-point rise in over-refusal, and Llama shows the same asymmetry. Combining both moderates exposure's over-refusal with little effect on downstream task scores, and the two models diverge geometrically.
AI.conclusion: Preserving the base refusal direction is not a reliable proxy for behavioral safety, so safety after sequential fine-tuning must be assessed behaviorally.

title: Are Seismic Foundation Models More Than Glorified Feature Extractors?
summary: Earthquake sequences are stochastic on two separated timescales: the seismic waves of any individual earthquake propagate over seconds to minutes, while the earthquakes themselves arrive as a sparse, self-exciting occurrence process, with inter-event intervals from seconds to months. Respecting both scales in one training objective is the open challenge. Foundation models (FMs) for seismic waveforms instead import their learning targets from audio and vision, where every target is computed from a single fixed-length window. Such a window holds one realization of the wave propagation (an earthquake trace), never the occurrence process that decides when earthquakes happen. We develop nine model designs sharing one Mamba encoder-decoder, trained on a fixed corpus of 3M windows, varying the self-supervised objective, quantization bottleneck and mixer; the two key comparisons are architecture-matched, varying the objective alone. Each checkpoint is evaluated frozen on three downstream tasks. Varying the target redistributes downstream skill rather than raising it, and no checkpoint wins everywhere. Adding masking pressure to our strongest classifier re-specializes it rather than making it a generalist: it gains 6.9 points of few-shot P-wave picking precision and loses 9.6 points of few-shot classification accuracy. By the standard imported from language and vision, these models are feature extractors rather than FMs. Controls on capacity, architecture, and domain proximity do not explain why skill moves rather than rises. Against task-specific baselines the advantage is regime-dependent: our checkpoints beat them few-shot on classification and ground-motion prediction, and trail them on full data. We argue the binding constraint is the target, and that settling the question requires a learning target defined across events, the timescale that makes seismicity stochastic in the first place.

AI.tldr: The paper trains nine Mamba-based seismic foundation model designs that vary only the self-supervised objective, quantization bottleneck and mixer, and finds that varying the target redistributes downstream skill rather than raising it. The authors argue these checkpoints are feature extractors rather than foundation models under the standard imported from language and vision.
AI.motivation: Seismic waveform foundation models import learning targets from audio and vision, computed from a single fixed-length window, which captures one wave-propagation realization but not the earthquake occurrence process that determines when earthquakes happen.
AI.method: Nine model designs share one Mamba encoder-decoder trained on a fixed corpus of 3M windows, varying the self-supervised objective, quantization bottleneck and mixer; architecture-matched comparisons vary the objective alone, and each checkpoint is evaluated frozen on three downstream tasks.
AI.result: No checkpoint wins everywhere. Adding masking pressure to the strongest classifier gains 6.9 points of few-shot P-wave picking precision and loses 9.6 points of few-shot classification accuracy. Relative to task-specific baselines, the checkpoints beat them few-shot on classification and ground-motion prediction and trail them on full data.
AI.conclusion: The binding constraint is the learning target, and settling the question likely requires a target defined across events, the timescale that makes seismicity stochastic.

title: Measured or Real? When Model-Derived Measurements Can Be Corrected or Compared
summary: Numbers computed from trained models, such as an example's difficulty or a model's benchmark lead, change with seed and prompt. We ask when such measurements can be corrected or compared. Noise shrinks correlations, and the textbook correction divides by the square root of two estimated reliabilities. On two CIFAR-100 difficulty scores, it returned correlations above one in 70 of 100 classes. We prove that its mean squared error is infinite even when the correlation and the reliabilities use separate seeds. Our rule corrects only when both reliabilities pass a significance test, then divides by their upper confidence bounds. Its output is always bounded, and its coverage guarantees assume Gaussian noise. It helps once reliability is well estimated, more than halving the error with 500 simulated units. Prompt settings can reverse rankings. On ARC, Qwen2-1.5B trails Llama-3.2-3B by 3.8 points with no examples in the prompt and leads by 16.6 with two. Across four benchmarks, averaging the two settings names one winner for 15 of 16 such reversals. We compare models within each setting, controlling family-wise error asymptotically in the number of items for a fixed prompt grid. Aligning embedding coordinates across seeds raises held-out per-dimension reliability from 0.003 to 0.813.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the textbook reliability-based correction for model-derived measurements can return correlations above one, and proposes a rule that corrects only when both reliabilities pass a significance test. It also shows that prompt settings can reverse model rankings and proposes comparing models within each setting with family-wise error control.
AI.motivation: Numbers computed from trained models change with seed and prompt, and the textbook correction for noise attenuation can return correlations above one, so the paper asks when such measurements can be corrected or compared.
AI.method: The paper proves that the textbook correction has infinite mean squared error and proposes a rule that divides by upper confidence bounds on the reliabilities, applied only when both pass a significance test; it compares models within each prompt setting, controlling family-wise error asymptotically in the number of items for a fixed prompt grid, and aligns embedding coordinates across seeds.
AI.result: On two CIFAR-100 difficulty scores the textbook correction returned correlations above one in 70 of 100 classes. On ARC, Qwen2-1.5B trails Llama-3.2-3B by 3.8 points with no examples and leads by 16.6 with two. Averaging the two settings names one winner for 15 of 16 such reversals across four benchmarks. Aligning embedding coordinates across seeds raises held-out per-dimension reliability from 0.003 to 0.813.
AI.conclusion: Model-derived measurements need reliability-aware correction, and comparisons should be made within each prompt setting because prompt settings can reverse rankings.

title: Detecting Brain Cancer Progression Through Signatures of Wearable Accelerometry Data
comment: 13 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables. Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 TS-LIMITS Workshop
summary: Glioblastoma and other high-grade gliomas (HGG) have a poor prognosis and are associated with progressive functional decline. The standard of care to assess progressive disease is contrast-enhanced MRI, which is expensive, claustrophobic, and performed only once every 2-3 months. Wearable accelerometers offer a non-invasive alternative for continuously monitoring patient function between clinic visits. However, accelerometry data streams are typically noisy and highly patient-specific, making conventional time series methods and summary statistics poorly suited to detecting clinically meaningful change. This work aims to classify stable versus progressive disease states by applying rough path signatures for feature extraction from wrist-worn accelerometer data. We convert accelerometer recordings from HGG patients enrolled in the BrainWear study into walking-path segments and use signature kernel maximum mean discrepancy (SigMMD) to quantify change in patients' walking behaviour. We overcome the challenge of inter-patient heterogeneity by adjusting for the natural variation in a patient's walking during stable tumour periods. This patient-specific normalisation substantially improves separation, yielding a candidate biomarker of tumour progression. Our results provide proof-of-concept evidence that signature-based analysis of wearable accelerometry can distinguish stable from progressive disease states, motivating larger longitudinal studies of continuous wearable monitoring as a digital biomarker in neuro-oncology.

AI.tldr: The paper applies rough path signatures and signature kernel maximum mean discrepancy to wrist-worn accelerometry from high-grade glioma patients, with patient-specific normalisation, to distinguish stable from progressive disease. The results are proof-of-concept evidence for a candidate digital biomarker of tumour progression.
AI.motivation: Contrast-enhanced MRI, the standard of care, is expensive and performed only every 2-3 months, while continuous accelerometry is noisy and highly patient-specific, making conventional time series methods and summary statistics poorly suited to detecting clinically meaningful change.
AI.method: Accelerometer recordings from high-grade glioma patients in the BrainWear study are converted into walking-path segments, rough path signatures are used for feature extraction, and signature kernel maximum mean discrepancy quantifies change in walking behaviour, with normalisation for the natural variation during stable tumour periods.
AI.result: Patient-specific normalisation substantially improves separation between stable and progressive disease states, yielding a candidate biomarker of tumour progression.
AI.conclusion: Signature-based analysis of wearable accelerometry can distinguish stable from progressive disease, motivating larger longitudinal studies of continuous wearable monitoring as a digital biomarker in neuro-oncology.

title: Learning from Relative Action Credit for Escaping Local Minima
summary: Reinforcement learning holds the promise of robots that learn manipulation skills from interaction alone, without pretrained priors or demonstration data. In practice, on-policy methods such as PPO routinely stall on long-horizon, contact-rich tasks: dense reward shaping carries the policy through stages, yet stitching them together and discovering sparsely rewarded events rarely succeeds. We trace this failure to the missing action discrimination in state-value credit assignment: a state-value critic judges progress only by episode outcomes, so when the policy converges to a partial solution all outcomes coincide, and improvement stops because no action can prove better than another. We therefore extend PPO with an action conditioned value critic which, can compare the executed action with alternatives sampled at the same state and aid the learning signal. Combined with Generalized Advantage Estimation and a bound on exploration noise, we show how the extended algorithm escapes the plateau and completes precise peg insertion within a training budget where PPO with identical exploration fails.

AI.tldr: The paper extends PPO with an action-conditioned value critic that compares the executed action with alternatives sampled at the same state, and shows that together with GAE and a bound on exploration noise it escapes plateaus in contact-rich manipulation. The extended algorithm completes precise peg insertion within a training budget where PPO with identical exploration fails.
AI.motivation: On-policy methods such as PPO stall on long-horizon contact-rich tasks because a state-value critic judges progress only by episode outcomes, so when outcomes coincide at a partial solution, no action can be shown to be better than another.
AI.method: PPO is extended with an action-conditioned value critic that compares the executed action with alternatives sampled at the same state, combined with Generalized Advantage Estimation and a bound on exploration noise.
AI.result: The extended algorithm escapes the plateau and completes precise peg insertion within a training budget where PPO with identical exploration fails.
AI.conclusion: Action discrimination in credit assignment is needed to escape local minima in long-horizon robot manipulation learned from interaction alone.

title: Integral Probability Boundaries
summary: Bounds based on Integral Probability Metrics (IPMs) are ubiquitous in machine learning and statistics, appearing, e.g., in generalization, alignment, fairness, and privacy. IPMs reduce the discrepancy between two distributions to a single worst-case gap between expectations. This compression is costly: for rare events, safety failures, or under-represented groups, IPM-based bounds are loose or vacuous. We introduce a non-linear generalization of IPMs, which we term Integral Probability Boundaries (IPBs). Unlike IPMs, IPBs provide bounds that are tight at the extremes. We derive their basic properties and present algorithms for estimating them in practically relevant settings. We demonstrate the usage of IPBs in both theoretical and practical applications for alignment, judge-free performance estimation, and fairness, where they enable us to obtain sharp bounds on performance and fairness gaps, e.g., 15 p.p. more precise estimates on fairness gaps for rare groups in a realistic generative modeling task, compared to the state of the art.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Integral Probability Boundaries, a non-linear generalization of Integral Probability Metrics that gives bounds tight at the extremes, where IPM-based bounds are loose for rare events, safety failures or under-represented groups. Applied to fairness, IPBs yield estimates of fairness gaps for rare groups that are 15 percentage points more precise than the state of the art in a realistic generative modeling task.
AI.motivation: IPMs reduce the discrepancy between two distributions to a single worst-case gap between expectations, which is costly, so IPM-based bounds are loose or vacuous for rare events, safety failures and under-represented groups.
AI.method: A non-linear generalization of IPMs, termed Integral Probability Boundaries, is introduced; the paper derives its basic properties and presents algorithms for estimating them in practically relevant settings.
AI.result: IPBs yield sharp bounds on performance and fairness gaps, including 15 percentage points more precise fairness-gap estimates for rare groups in a realistic generative modeling task compared to the state of the art.
AI.conclusion: IPBs provide bounds that are tight at the extremes and are useful in theoretical and practical applications to alignment, judge-free performance estimation and fairness.

title: Measuring Deep Learning Performance - An Empirical Study of Performance Distributions Across Architectures and Tasks
summary: Context: Non-determinism in deep learning algorithm design and implementation leads to performance variation, meaning model performance is not a single value, but rather a distribution. These model performance distributions are underexplored despite their impact on robustness. Objective: We investigate the robustness of deep learning performance to sources of non-determinism, specifically focusing on how performance distributions differ across various architectures and tasks. Method: We conducted 186 experiments on image classification and time series forecasting architectures. Each experiment was run 100 times with different random seeds to generate performance distributions, resulting in 18,600 runs. Robustness was quantified using metrics for spread, symmetry, and tail risk. Results: Performance distributions are frequently non-Gaussian, particularly in time series forecasting. Model size does not systematically affect robustness -- larger image classification models show fewer outliers but not lower spread, while smaller time series models show lower spread but more extreme underperformers. Training duration does not scale linearly; early stopping effectively balances performance and robustness. Mean performance does not predict robustness - time series forecasting shows moderate correlation while image classification shows none. Time series models produce nearly three times more underperforming outliers than image classification models, indicating substantially higher tail risk. Conclusions: Tail risk poses serious concerns for Trustworthy AI in high-stakes applications. Models performing well on average may exhibit long tails and extreme outliers revealed only through distributional analysis. Mean performance alone should not guide model selection; assessment of spread, symmetry, and tail risk is essential for reliable model assessment where consistent performance is critical.

AI.tldr: The study runs 18,600 training runs across 186 experiments on image classification and time series forecasting architectures to measure how performance distributions differ across models and tasks. It finds that performance is often non-Gaussian, time series models carry substantially higher tail risk, and mean performance alone should not guide model selection.
AI.motivation: Non-determinism in deep learning makes model performance a distribution rather than a single value, but these distributions are underexplored despite their impact on robustness.
AI.method: 186 experiments on image classification and time series forecasting architectures, each run 100 times with different random seeds, with robustness quantified by metrics for spread, symmetry and tail risk.
AI.result: Performance distributions are frequently non-Gaussian, especially for time series forecasting. Model size does not systematically affect robustness, training duration does not scale linearly with early stopping balancing performance and robustness, and mean performance predicts robustness moderately for time series but not for image classification. Time series models produce nearly three times more underperforming outliers than image classification models.
AI.conclusion: Tail risk is a serious concern for trustworthy AI in high-stakes applications, and assessing spread, symmetry and tail risk is essential where consistent performance is critical.

title: CADENCE: Distributional Next-Transaction Forecasting for Business Cash-Flow Underwriting
summary: Recurring cash flows are the backbone of cash-flow underwriting: they separate durable revenue from one-off deposits, expose standing obligations, and ultimately determine ability to pay. For small businesses, recurrence is both indispensable and hard to estimate, because much of their income arrives as ambiguous transfers, most payment streams are short, and schedules follow calendar conventions that frequency-domain methods treat as noise. We present CADENCE, Calendar-Aware Distributional Event Network for Cash-Flow Estimation, a compact causal Transformer that treats each transaction as a token and predicts the amount and a full, nonparametric timing distribution of every cash flow's next payment. Inheriting transaction semantics from an external labeler and a frozen text encoder keeps CADENCE compact yet general across the long tail of small-business counterparties, while predicting a calibrated distribution rather than an opaque embedding makes its outputs interpretable enough to feed existing underwriting models and power credit decisions. Ablations confirm the role of each design choice, with counterparty semantics driving recall on short histories, calendar inputs driving timing accuracy, and no-event supervision driving precision. Against the production FFT baseline, CADENCE improves one-day timing accuracy by 93.3% and next-event F1 by 6.7%, while producing calibrated distributions that serve directly as a confidence gate for downstream decisions. In an end-to-end credit evaluation on production applications, replacing FFT recurrence features with CADENCE features raises KS by 4.8%, raises the approval rate at a fixed loss rate by 18.2%, and lowers the loss rate at a fixed approval rate by 13.1%.

AI.tldr: CADENCE is a compact causal Transformer that treats each transaction as a token and predicts both the amount and a nonparametric, calibrated timing distribution of each cash flow's next payment for small-business cash-flow underwriting. In an end-to-end credit evaluation on production applications, replacing FFT recurrence features with CADENCE features raises KS by 4.8% and the approval rate at a fixed loss rate by 18.2%.
AI.motivation: Recurring cash flows are central to cash-flow underwriting, but for small businesses recurrence is hard to estimate because income arrives as ambiguous transfers, payment streams are short, and schedules follow calendar conventions that frequency-domain methods treat as noise.
AI.method: A causal Transformer treats each transaction as a token; transaction semantics are inherited from an external labeler and a frozen text encoder, and the model predicts a calibrated nonparametric timing distribution using calendar inputs and no-event supervision.
AI.result: Against the production FFT baseline, CADENCE improves one-day timing accuracy by 93.3% and next-event F1 by 6.7%. In the end-to-end credit evaluation, replacing FFT recurrence features with CADENCE features raises KS by 4.8%, raises the approval rate at a fixed loss rate by 18.2%, and lowers the loss rate at a fixed approval rate by 13.1%.
AI.conclusion: The calibrated distributions make the outputs interpretable enough to feed existing underwriting models and to serve as a confidence gate for downstream credit decisions.

title: Jailbreak Connectivity: Towards Diverse, Transferable, and Universal Multimodal Large Language Model Jailbreak
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are vulnerable to visual jailbreak attacks that bypass safety safeguards. Existing methods typically optimize isolated adversarial examples, limiting attack diversity, transferability, and generalization. We propose Jailbreak Connectivity (JC), a framework based on the observation that effective adversarial inputs can be connected through low-loss regions in image space. JC optimizes continuous adversarial paths: path sampling yields diverse jailbreak images, lightweight surrogate classifiers guide cross-model transfer, and a distribution-level objective enables universal attacks across harmful queries. On MM-SafetyBench, JC achieves average attack success rates of 84.01%, 85.77%, and 97.95% on Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, InternVL3.5-8B, and Gemma-3-12B-IT, respectively, exceeding the strongest baselines by up to 68.36 percentage points. In black-box evaluations, JC improves attack success rates over FigStep by 24.69 and 27.34 percentage points on GPT-5.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro, respectively. These findings reveal structured vulnerabilities in MLLM safety alignment and inform more comprehensive security evaluation.

AI.tldr: Jailbreak Connectivity optimizes continuous adversarial paths through low-loss regions of image space to produce diverse, transferable and universal visual jailbreaks against multimodal large language models. It reaches average attack success rates of 84.01%, 85.77% and 97.95% on Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, InternVL3.5-8B and Gemma-3-12B-IT on MM-SafetyBench.
AI.motivation: Existing visual jailbreak methods optimize isolated adversarial examples, which limits attack diversity, transferability and generalization.
AI.method: The framework rests on the observation that effective adversarial inputs can be connected through low-loss regions in image space; path sampling yields diverse jailbreak images, lightweight surrogate classifiers guide cross-model transfer, and a distribution-level objective enables universal attacks across harmful queries.
AI.result: On MM-SafetyBench, the attack exceeds the strongest baselines by up to 68.36 percentage points in average attack success rate. In black-box evaluations it improves attack success over FigStep by 24.69 and 27.34 percentage points on GPT-5.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro, respectively.
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal structured vulnerabilities in MLLM safety alignment and inform more comprehensive security evaluation.

title: TGTV: An Interpretable Framework for UAV Fault Detection and Traceability via Spatiotemporal Graph Learning and Large Language Models
comment: 21 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to IEEE Sensors Journal
summary: Fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles experience operating-condition transitions, asynchronous sensor sampling, and control-system compensation that can obscure fault signatures. Existing temporal detection methods have limited capacity to represent coupled faults across subsystems, track their evolution, and constrain language-model diagnoses with quantitative evidence. This paper proposes TGTV, an interpretable fault detection and traceability framework that integrates spatiotemporal graph learning with a large language model. A temporal convolutional network and a graph attention network with weighted fused adjacency extract multiscale temporal patterns and spatial dependencies among sensors. A hybrid temporal Transformer and variational autoencoder then evaluates window-level anomalies using prediction errors and reconstruction probabilities. Continuous-time Shapley attribution identifies critical sensors and high-contribution intervals while preserving the temporal continuity of fault evolution. A structured evidence package combines detection results, graph relationships, temporal attribution, sensor attribution, and operating context. An evidence-constrained diagnosis protocol uses this package to generate flight-level conclusions with traceable evidence identifiers. Cross-flight holdout experiments on the public ALFA fixed-wing flight dataset yield a window-level area under the precision-recall curve of 0.976, accuracy of 0.973, recall of 0.902, and F1 score of 0.920. Flight-level fault diagnosis achieves recall of 0.943 and an F1 score of 0.944. These results demonstrate accurate anomaly detection and quantitatively supported fault-tracing cues, providing a basis for interpretable post-flight fault review and analysis.

AI.tldr: TGTV is an interpretable UAV fault detection and traceability framework that combines spatiotemporal graph learning with a large language model constrained by a structured evidence package. Under cross-flight holdout on the public ALFA fixed-wing flight dataset it reaches a window-level PR-AUC of 0.976 and a flight-level fault diagnosis recall of 0.943 with F1 of 0.944.
AI.motivation: Operating-condition transitions, asynchronous sensor sampling and control compensation obscure fault signatures in fixed-wing UAVs, and existing temporal detection methods cannot represent coupled faults across subsystems, track their evolution, or constrain language-model diagnoses with quantitative evidence.
AI.method: A temporal convolutional network and a graph attention network with weighted fused adjacency extract temporal and spatial patterns; a hybrid temporal Transformer and VAE scores window-level anomalies; continuous-time Shapley attribution identifies critical sensors and intervals; and an evidence-constrained diagnosis protocol uses a structured evidence package to generate flight-level conclusions with traceable evidence identifiers.
AI.result: Cross-flight holdout experiments on the ALFA dataset yield a window-level area under the PR curve of 0.976, accuracy of 0.973, recall of 0.902 and F1 of 0.920, and flight-level fault diagnosis achieves recall of 0.943 and F1 of 0.944.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a basis for interpretable post-flight fault review and analysis.

title: A Separation Principle for Adversarial Attacks and Defense of Graph Neural Networks
summary: Adversarial attacks on graph neural networks (GNNs) have been studied as a model-centric optimization problem driven by gradients, learned policies, or meta-learning, with the graph treated as a passive substrate. This view overlooks a defining feature of GNNs: their predictions are produced by structured message passing along the graph, so their adversarial vulnerabilities are encoded as much in the geometry of the graph as in the learned weights. We develop a structure-driven framework for feature attacks in which the attack is derived from the spectral properties of the normalized adjacency operator. Its central result is a separation principle: under a natural relaxation of the attack objective, the optimal feature perturbation is rank one and factorizes into a graph-dependent component (degree-proportional spatial allocation, depending only on the graph) and a weight-dependent component (top singular vector of the composed weights, depending only on the weights). Node degree thus emerges as the fundamental graph quantity governing adversarial vulnerability to feature perturbations. The resulting attack, which we call SepAttack, requires no gradient computation, carries analytical guarantees, achieves competitive or superior performance against established baselines such as Nettack and IG-Attack with up to ${\sim}70\times$ speedup in the targeted setting, and transfers near-perfectly across architectures on continuous-feature graphs because its graph-dependent component is architecture-invariant by construction. We further derive a separation-principle adversarial training procedure (SepAT) directly from the closed-form worst-case attack and report robustness gains on binary-feature benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a structure-driven feature attack on GNNs from the spectral properties of the normalized adjacency operator, showing that the optimal rank-one feature perturbation separates into a graph-dependent and a weight-dependent component. The resulting attack, SepAttack, needs no gradient computation and reaches up to roughly 70 times speedup over baselines in the targeted setting.
AI.motivation: Adversarial attacks on GNNs are typically treated as model-centric gradient, policy or meta-learning problems with the graph treated as a passive substrate, overlooking that GNN predictions are produced by structured message passing along the graph.
AI.method: The attack is derived from the spectral properties of the normalized adjacency operator; under a natural relaxation of the attack objective, the optimal feature perturbation is rank one and factorizes into a degree-proportional spatial allocation that depends only on the graph and the top singular vector of the composed weights that depends only on the weights. A separation-principle adversarial training procedure, SepAT, is derived from the closed-form worst-case attack.
AI.result: SepAttack achieves competitive or superior performance against Nettack and IG-Attack, with up to roughly 70 times speedup in the targeted setting, and transfers near-perfectly across architectures on continuous-feature graphs. SepAT reports robustness gains on binary-feature benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Node degree emerges as the fundamental graph quantity governing adversarial vulnerability to feature perturbations.

title: Estimating Implicit Expected Log Density Ratios
summary: When exact probabilities cannot be computed, \emph{density ratio estimation (DRE)} is a key subroutine in the wide range of applications where density ratios appear, from experimental design to generative modelling and reinforcement learning. In this paper, we introduce the concept of an \emph{expected log density ratio (ELDR)}: log density ratios that are integrated under some third, possibly distinct measure. We show many problems with implicit densities where DRE is naïvely used are actually ELDR estimation tasks, and prove fundamental limitations on finite-sample ELDR estimation. Based on these results, we argue that the typical DRE-based approaches are unsuitable for ELDR estimation, and provide some foundational motivation towards bespoke ELDR estimators. To demonstrate, we propose a simple modification to some DRE methods that allows samples convergent to the integral distribution to appear in training data. We show through benchmarks that this can improve ELDR estimation error.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces expected log density ratios (ELDR), which are log density ratios integrated under a third measure, and argues that many implicit-density problems where density ratio estimation is naively used are actually ELDR estimation tasks. It shows that typical DRE approaches are unsuitable for ELDR estimation and proposes a simple modification to some DRE methods that improves ELDR estimation error on benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Density ratio estimation is a key subroutine across experimental design, generative modelling and reinforcement learning, but with implicit densities it is naively applied to problems that are really ELDR estimation tasks, and finite-sample ELDR estimation has fundamental limitations.
AI.method: The authors introduce ELDR, prove fundamental limitations on finite-sample ELDR estimation, and propose a simple modification to some DRE methods that allows samples convergent to the integral distribution to appear in the training data.
AI.result: Benchmarks show that the modification can improve ELDR estimation error.
AI.conclusion: Typical DRE-based approaches are unsuitable for ELDR estimation, which motivates bespoke ELDR estimators.

title: MASS: Multi-mask Selective Self-Distillation for Leakage-Resilient Reasoning
summary: On-policy self-distillation enables the same model to act as student and teacher, with dense token-level supervision obtained by the teacher being given access to privileged information. However, conditioning the teacher on a single reference can concentrate its predictions on one reasoning trajectory and limit transfer to the student. We propose Multi-Mask Selective Self-Distillation (MASS), which approximates the unavailable marginal over diverse reference realizations using multiple independently masked views of one verified solution. MASS aggregates these complementary teacher predictions, selectively transfers reliable token-level corrections, and adaptively focuses masking on influential reference spans. Across mathematical reasoning benchmarks and model families, MASS consistently outperforms strong self-distillation baselines.

AI.tldr: MASS is a multi-mask selective self-distillation method for on-policy self-distillation in mathematical reasoning. It uses several independently masked views of one verified solution as teacher references and transfers only reliable token-level corrections, and it consistently outperforms strong self-distillation baselines.
AI.motivation: Conditioning the teacher on a single reference concentrates its predictions on one reasoning trajectory, which limits transfer to the student.
AI.method: MASS approximates the marginal over diverse reference realizations by aggregating teacher predictions from multiple independently masked views of one verified solution. It selectively transfers reliable token-level corrections and adaptively focuses masking on influential reference spans.
AI.result: Across mathematical reasoning benchmarks and model families, MASS consistently outperforms strong self-distillation baselines. The abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Diversifying the privileged reference through multiple masked views and selecting reliable corrections is an effective route to better self-distillation for reasoning.

title: Floor It, Then Fill It: Simulating Creator Ecosystems for Fair Video-Content Recommendation Systems at Billion User Scale
summary: Engagement-optimized content recommendation systems exhibit a well-documented rich-get-richer dynamic that structurally disadvantages emerging creators on large-scale platforms. Evaluating debiasing interventions at scale demands faithful simulation of creator-viewer ecosystems, yet the fidelity, diversity, and validity of such simulators remain underexplored. We present a grounded user-simulation framework that models a heterogeneous population of ${\sim}42$K creators and their coupled viewer interactions over 12~weeks, and use it to evaluate equitable view-allocation policies formulated as a budgeted multi-armed bandit (MAB). The simulator captures three behavioral dimensions: (i)~\textbf{creator diversity}, modeled via a clustering approach grounded in real platform creator-level distributions; (ii)~\textbf{behavioral fidelity}, captured through coupled creator-content state machines that represent growth trajectories, engagement accumulation, and graduation dynamics; and (iii)~\textbf{population-level validity}, measured by calibration against observed platform metrics. We evaluate simulative-configurations that vary content-viewership target definitions, reward functions, and a small-creator reserve lever to maximize creator-content recommendation equity. A floor-protected per content-view-target with a view-parity-gap reward guarantees 90\% of view targets being met by creators every week, grows small-creator organic reach ${\sim}{+}33\%$ per week, and achieves high distribution stability (set of creators with funded-views Jaccard $= 0.819$). We analyze the Sim2Real gap and propose validation protocols, contributing evidence for when simulation-derived fairness conclusions can be trusted.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a grounded user-simulation framework for creator-viewer ecosystems and uses it to evaluate equitable view-allocation policies. A floor-protected policy with a view-parity-gap reward meets 90% of view targets each week and raises small-creator organic reach by about 33% per week.
AI.motivation: Engagement-optimized recommendation has a rich-get-richer dynamic that disadvantages emerging creators, and evaluating debiasing interventions requires simulators whose fidelity, diversity and validity remain underexplored.
AI.method: The simulator models about 42K creators and their coupled viewer interactions over 12 weeks. It captures creator diversity through clustering grounded in platform creator-level distributions, behavioral fidelity through coupled creator-content state machines for growth, engagement and graduation, and population-level validity through calibration against observed platform metrics. View allocation is formulated as a budgeted multi-armed bandit, evaluated under different content-view target definitions, reward functions and a small-creator reserve lever.
AI.result: A floor-protected per-content view target with a view-parity-gap reward guarantees that 90% of view targets are met by creators every week, grows small-creator organic reach by about 33% per week, and achieves a funded-views Jaccard stability of 0.819 across creator sets.
AI.conclusion: The paper analyzes the Sim2Real gap and proposes validation protocols, giving evidence on when simulation-derived fairness conclusions can be trusted.

title: Replaying the Same Gradients at a Different $\varepsilon$: A Registered Test of the Fixed-Trajectory Account of Adam's $\varepsilon$ for One Rare Row
summary: Adam divides every update by the square root of a running average of squared gradients plus a small constant, epsilon. For an output-embedding row whose token is rare, which we call the probe row, raising epsilon can be read as shrinking that row's steps by arithmetic alone. We test that reading directly. While a training run proceeds, we also divide the probe row's update by a different epsilon, using the run's own moment estimates; this replay is exact arithmetic on the gradients the run actually saw, so it holds the run's trajectory fixed. A rule for when the replay counts as wrong was written down before the runs. We train a small causal transformer in a standard configuration. When epsilon rises by four orders of magnitude, the replay counts as wrong on each of the three seeds registered for the test: the probe row keeps 8.9--11.4 times more of its displacement than predicted with the main, sampled-negative head, and 5.0--7.7 times more with a full-softmax head scored as a second instrument. At three orders of magnitude, tested with the main head only, it does not, by narrow margins; a further two seeds, registered after this result had been committed and scored on their own, follow the same pattern. In separate real runs, raising epsilon on the probe row alone is enough to reproduce the row's change and raising it on every other parameter alone also moves the row part of the way --- readings about the runs that do not rescue the replay; scaling the row's learning rate instead, with the denominator untouched, is mispredicted by the replay in the same direction. This is one embedding row of one model family on one corpus; we make no claim about rates, about rows in general (other rows were read only as a panel on one trajectory) or about how the effect changes with model size.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether raising Adam's epsilon shrinks a rare output-embedding row's steps, by replaying the run's own gradients under a different epsilon. Under a rule registered before the runs, the replay is judged wrong when epsilon rises by four orders of magnitude, with the probe row keeping 8.9 to 11.4 times more displacement than predicted.
AI.motivation: For a rare token's output-embedding row, raising epsilon can be read as shrinking that row's steps by arithmetic alone, and the authors want to test this fixed-trajectory account directly.
AI.method: While a small causal transformer trains in a standard configuration, the probe row's update is also divided by a different epsilon using the run's own moment estimates, an exact replay that holds the trajectory fixed. Controls raise epsilon on the probe row alone, raise it on all other parameters alone, and scale the row's learning rate with the denominator untouched.
AI.result: At four orders of magnitude, the replay is judged wrong on each of the three registered seeds: the probe row keeps 8.9 to 11.4 times more displacement than predicted with the sampled-negative head, and 5.0 to 7.7 times more with a full-softmax head. At three orders of magnitude, tested with the main head only, the replay is not judged wrong, by narrow margins, and two further seeds follow the same pattern. Raising epsilon on the probe row alone reproduces its change, and raising it on all other parameters moves the row part of the way, which does not rescue the replay.
AI.conclusion: The findings are scoped to one embedding row of one model family on one corpus, with no claims about rates, other rows or the effect of model size.

title: B2P-Corr: Batch-to-Population Gradient Estimators for Non-Decomposable Correlation Losses
summary: Correlation metrics such as the Pearson Correlation Coefficient (PCC) and Concordance Correlation Coefficient (CCC) are standard regression metrics and learning objectives, but their non-decomposable nature poses a challenge for stochastic optimization. Since these metrics depend on dataset-level moments (mean, variance, covariance), naive mini-batch training with local statistics yields biased, high-variance gradients whose expectation does not align with the population gradient. To bridge this ``batch-to-population'' (B2P) gap, we propose \textbf{B2P-Corr}, a novel framework that transforms correlation objectives into decomposable pseudo-losses driven by lightweight global ``moment sketches''. We introduce two efficient variants: \textbf{B2P-EMA}, which utilizes exponential moving averages and stop-gradient operators to ensure asymptotic gradient tracking with $O(B)$ cost ($B$ is batch size); and \textbf{B2P-U}, which uses sampled cross-batch U-statistic estimators and a reservoir-based stabilization with an $O(B)$ implementation. Theoretically, we quantify the $O(B^{-1})$ bias of naive mini-batch optimization, prove a moving-target tracking result for B2P-EMA under a fast-sketch / slow-parameter regime, and provide an idealized control-variate analysis for B2P-U. Experiments on two synthetic and three real-world datasets demonstrate B2P-Corr achieves stable optimization and higher correlation than naive mini-batch optimization with negligible overhead.

AI.tldr: B2P-Corr turns non-decomposable correlation losses such as PCC and CCC into decomposable pseudo-losses driven by global moment sketches, so mini-batch training better tracks the population gradient. Experiments on five datasets show stable optimization and higher correlation than naive mini-batch training at negligible overhead.
AI.motivation: Correlation metrics depend on dataset-level moments, so naive mini-batch training with local statistics gives biased, high-variance gradients whose expectation does not align with the population gradient.
AI.method: The framework replaces these objectives with decomposable pseudo-losses built on lightweight global moment sketches. B2P-EMA uses exponential moving averages and stop-gradient operators for asymptotic gradient tracking at O(B) cost, where B is the batch size. B2P-U uses sampled cross-batch U-statistic estimators with reservoir-based stabilization, also at O(B) cost.
AI.result: The paper quantifies the O(1/B) bias of naive mini-batch optimization and proves a moving-target tracking result for B2P-EMA under a fast-sketch, slow-parameter regime, with an idealized control-variate analysis for B2P-U. Experiments on two synthetic and three real-world datasets show stable optimization and higher correlation than naive mini-batch optimization with negligible overhead.
AI.conclusion: Global moment sketches offer a practical way to narrow the batch-to-population gap for correlation objectives at little extra cost.

title: Data Amount Heterogeneity Improves Performance in Federated Learning for Neuroimaging
summary: Federated Learning (FL) allows for secure analysis of distributed data without data sharing. We and others have successfully applied FL to neuroimaging tasks, such as Alzheimer's disease classification from structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). FL trains a deep learning model locally at each site, encrypts the local model parameters and sends them to a federation controller that aggregates the local models under homomorphic encryption, the resulting community model is sent back to the sites for further training, and the process repeats for a number of rounds. FL often achieves learning performance (e.g., accuracy) close to centralized training, but no data leaves the sites and model parameters are protected through encryption and other measures. In this paper, we show that federations composed of sites with heterogeneous amounts of data (1 large site plus small sites) perform better than homogeneous (same data per site) federations, particularly in low data regimes, while reaching performance close to centralized training. Having a big site often results in faster convergence and higher final accuracy. Heterogeneous federations better exploit sites with small amounts of data, a common situation in large consortia such as ENIGMA.

AI.tldr: In neuroimaging federated learning, federations of sites with unequal data amounts, one large site plus small sites, outperform homogeneous federations, especially in low-data regimes, and approach centralized training. Alzheimer's disease classification from structural MRI is the motivating application.
AI.motivation: Federated learning allows analysis of distributed data without sharing it and often approaches centralized accuracy, but consortia such as ENIGMA often include many small sites, and it is unclear how unequal site sizes affect federated performance.
AI.method: The authors compare heterogeneous federations, with one large site and several small sites, against homogeneous federations where every site holds the same amount of data. Each site trains a model locally, encrypts its parameters, and a federation controller aggregates them under homomorphic encryption, returning a community model for repeated rounds.
AI.result: Heterogeneous federations perform better than homogeneous ones, particularly in low-data regimes, and reach performance close to centralized training. A big site often gives faster convergence and higher final accuracy. The abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Heterogeneous federations make better use of sites with small amounts of data, so unequal site sizes in large consortia can be an advantage rather than an obstacle.

title: A Gradient based Adversarial Augmentation Framework for Mitigating Unlearnable Datasets
summary: Unlearnable data methods (ULD) protect public data from unauthorized model training by adding imperceptible perturbations that create a learning shortcut. A deep neural network can exploit the shortcut learning path to minimize training loss without learning generalizable features. Intuitively, finding adversarial versions of perturbed images that can substantially increase the model's loss can force the model to learn generalizable features. Existing data augmentation based attacks rely on heuristic search strategies/random sampling over a curated augmentation set to identify adversarial augmentation operations, an approach that often does not scale when the number of candidate operations is large. To address the challenge of a large search space, we propose {\techname}, a gradient based adversarial augmentation framework that learns an augmentation policy via stochastic gradient ascent. {\techname} leverages a differentiable data augmentation pipeline to efficiently search a set of up to 18 augmentation techniques, from which a grid search selects a protection-specific subset. The augmentation subset is trained to maximize a surrogate model's classification loss. We introduce a perceptual-plus-pixel regularization to learn operation parameters that preserve image semantics. Under a controlled ablation, {\techname} consistently outperforms an equivalent random sampling baseline (80.0\% vs. 77.29\% clean test accuracy on EMIN-protected CIFAR-10 for ResNet-18 and 83.28\% vs. 66.45\% on NTGA-protected CIFAR-10 for MobileNet-V2), demonstrating that gradient guidance drives the clean test accuracy recoverability rather than the expanded search space. {\techname} offers an effective and scalable adversarial augmentation framework for stress-testing ULD methods, a critical tool for developing robust ULD methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a gradient-based adversarial augmentation framework that learns augmentation policies by stochastic gradient ascent, to stress-test unlearnable dataset (ULD) protection methods. Under controlled ablation it beats a random-sampling baseline on clean test accuracy.
AI.motivation: Unlearnable data methods add perturbations that create learning shortcuts, and existing augmentation-based attacks rely on heuristic search or random sampling, which does not scale when the number of candidate operations is large.
AI.method: The framework uses a differentiable augmentation pipeline to search up to 18 augmentation techniques, and a grid search selects a protection-specific subset. The subset is trained to maximize a surrogate model's classification loss, with a perceptual-plus-pixel regularization that learns operation parameters preserving image semantics.
AI.result: Under controlled ablation, the method beats an equivalent random-sampling baseline on clean test accuracy: 80.0% vs 77.29% on EMIN-protected CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18, and 83.28% vs 66.45% on NTGA-protected CIFAR-10 with MobileNet-V2.
AI.conclusion: Gradient guidance, rather than the expanded search space, drives clean test accuracy recoverability, making the framework a scalable tool for stress-testing and developing robust ULD methods.

title: Convex-SKM-Net: Low-Latency Block Halfspace Corrections for Neural Convex Constraint Satisfaction
summary: Fast inference and strict constraint satisfaction are essential for learning-based decision-making. Existing methods often rely on constraint-specific projections or feasible-set parameterizations, while iterative repair can be costly. We introduce Convex-SKM-Net, a convex constraint-satisfaction layer that forms linearization halfspaces from residual and (sub)gradient oracles without constraint-specific inequality projectors. It applies fixed-depth dual projected-gradient descent (dual PGD) to minimum-displacement block problems using GPU-friendly matrix operations. We jointly learn the predictor and a positive-definite mobility, adapting the correction geometry to improve objective quality. We prove convergence of the outer iterates at fixed dual depth and linear convergence in distance under Slater's condition and bounded subgradients. All our test outputs on three second-order-cone model-predictive control (SOC-MPC) horizons and six power-system convex relaxations satisfy a $10^{-3}$ feasibility tolerance. Comparisons with the latest constraint-satisfaction methods show inference speedups of up to $144.3\times$ on SOC-MPC and $7.7\times$ on a convex quadratically constrained quadratic programming (QCQP) benchmark with joint training. On QCQP, the mean objective gap is $0.012\%$, with full test feasibility at $10^{-4}$. Learning mobility reduces the five-seed affine-task mean gap by $22.4\%$ and improves gaps in matched power-system comparisons.

AI.tldr: Convex-SKM-Net is a convex constraint-satisfaction layer that corrects predictions with fixed-depth dual projected gradient descent, without constraint-specific projectors. It reports inference speedups of up to 144.3 times on SOC-MPC and 7.7 times on a convex QCQP benchmark while keeping test outputs within a 1e-3 feasibility tolerance.
AI.motivation: Learning-based decision making needs both fast inference and strict constraint satisfaction, but constraint-specific projections or feasible-set parameterizations are restrictive, and iterative repair can be costly.
AI.method: The layer forms linearization halfspaces from residual and (sub)gradient oracles and applies fixed-depth dual projected gradient descent to minimum-displacement block problems, using GPU-friendly matrix operations. The predictor and a positive-definite mobility are learned jointly, adapting the correction geometry to improve objective quality.
AI.result: All test outputs on three SOC-MPC horizons and six power-system convex relaxations satisfy a 1e-3 feasibility tolerance. Inference is up to 144.3 times faster than the latest constraint-satisfaction methods on SOC-MPC and 7.7 times faster on a convex QCQP benchmark with joint training. On QCQP the mean objective gap is 0.012%, with full test feasibility at 1e-4. Learning mobility reduces the five-seed affine-task mean gap by 22.4%.
AI.conclusion: The layer combines speed with feasibility and carries convergence guarantees for its outer iterates under Slater's condition and bounded subgradients.

title: Averaged Annealed Markov Chains Achieve the Algorithmic Threshold for Tensor PCA, Part II: Langevin Dynamics
comment: Companion paper to arXiv:2610.16705 (Part I). 71 pages, 1 figure
summary: We consider the tensor principal components analysis (tensor PCA) problem on the sphere, in which we are asked to recover an unknown vector in $\mathcal{S}_N=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^N:\lVert x\rVert^2=N\}$ from a noisy observation of its $k$-th tensor power, for a fixed $k\ge3$. Tensor PCA exhibits a well-studied information-computation gap: global algorithms such as spectral methods and sum-of-squares work above an algorithmic threshold, below which we know matching lower bounds (against these and some other restricted models of computation). In contrast, local algorithms such as Markov chains were only known to succeed from a random initialization at a polynomially larger signal-to-noise ratio, and were believed to be inferior to global algorithms for tensor PCA. Continuing the program initiated in Part I [arXiv:2610.16705], we show that spherical Langevin dynamics, when supplemented with annealing and ergodic averaging, achieves polynomial-time strong recovery above the algorithmic threshold from a uniformly random initialization. Together with Part I, our results demonstrate that local Markov chains can succeed all the way down to the algorithmic threshold from an uninformative cold start.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that spherical Langevin dynamics, with annealing and ergodic averaging, achieves polynomial-time strong recovery for tensor PCA above the algorithmic threshold from a uniformly random initialization. Together with Part I, it shows local Markov chains can succeed down to the threshold from a cold start.
AI.motivation: Tensor PCA has an information-computation gap in which global algorithms work only above an algorithmic threshold, and local Markov chains were believed to need a polynomially larger signal-to-noise ratio and to be inferior to global methods.
AI.method: The authors analyze spherical Langevin dynamics supplemented with annealing and ergodic averaging, started from a uniformly random initialization, for recovering an unknown vector on the sphere from a noisy k-th tensor power with fixed k at least 3. The work continues the program of Part I (arXiv:2610.16705).
AI.result: The method achieves polynomial-time strong recovery above the algorithmic threshold from a uniformly random initialization. The abstract reports no numerical values.
AI.conclusion: Local Markov chains can succeed all the way down to the algorithmic threshold from an uninformative cold start, which challenges the belief that they are inferior to global algorithms for tensor PCA.

title: Progressive Coupling Method for Diffusion Posterior Sampling in Ptychography
summary: Ptychography is a computational imaging method that reconstructs a sample from overlapping diffraction measurements. This technique relies on these overlapping measurements to provide the redundancy information needed for robust reconstruction, but dense scanning increases acquisition time and data volume. Reducing scan overlaps can improve measurement efficiency but weakens the physical constraints available for reconstruction. Diffusion models provide strong learned prior information, offering a promising approach to compensate for the loss of measurement redundancy. However, effectively utilizing this prior information under weak measurement constraints remains a challenge. We propose a progressive coupling posterior sampling (PCPS) method, which allows for a broader exploration of the solution space under high uncertainty while maintaining stronger diffusion-guided consistency as the reconstruction becomes more refined. Experiments on real X-ray ptychographic data at various scan overlaps demonstrate that PCPS consistently improves reconstruction accuracy compared to traditional iterative methods and existing diffusion posterior samplers, especially at low overlaps. These results show that diffusion priors can reduce the measurement redundancy required for accurate ptychography reconstruction.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes progressive coupling posterior sampling (PCPS) for ptychography, using a diffusion prior to reconstruct samples from measurements with reduced scan overlap. On real X-ray ptychographic data, it beats traditional iterative methods and existing diffusion posterior samplers, especially at low overlaps.
AI.motivation: Dense scanning in ptychography lengthens acquisition and increases data volume, but reducing overlap weakens the redundancy that constrains reconstruction, and it is hard to use diffusion priors effectively under such weak measurement constraints.
AI.method: PCPS allows broad exploration of the solution space under high uncertainty and maintains stronger diffusion-guided consistency as the reconstruction is refined, through a progressive coupling of the measurement constraint and the diffusion prior.
AI.result: Experiments on real X-ray ptychographic data at various scan overlaps show that PCPS consistently improves reconstruction accuracy over traditional iterative methods and existing diffusion posterior samplers, especially at low overlaps. The abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion priors can reduce the measurement redundancy needed for accurate ptychographic reconstruction.

title: RainCheck: Harnessing Historical Weather Data with Machine Learning for Rainfall Forecasting in Bangladesh
summary: Machine-learning rainfall forecasts are often evaluated by shuffling station records into random training and test sets. For rainfall, this lets a model see what happened at neighbouring stations on the very day it is asked to forecast, and it hides the fact that a seasonal lookup table already explains most of the variance. We quantify both effects on 618,650 station-days from 35 Bangladesh Meteorological Department stations (1948-2014). We compare random, temporal (train <=1999, test 2005-2014) and spatio-temporal (unseen stations and unseen years) evaluation, calendar-only versus antecedent-rainfall features, and six learners against climatology, persistence and SARIMA. Three findings stand out. First, a station-month climatology alone classifies high-rainfall months with 88.4% accuracy (AUC 0.950), and no learner improved on it by more than 0.8 points under temporal evaluation. Second, a calendar-only random forest reached a next-day wet-day AUC of 0.889 under a random split, higher than any model with real predictors under temporal evaluation, yet fell to 0.835, below climatology (0.859), on future years. Third, models with lagged rainfall add genuine but modest skill for next-day forecasts: a Brier skill score of 0.074 (95% CI 0.064-0.088) over climatology, rising to 0.091 when station and year inputs are removed and to 0.131 when other stations' same-day observations are added. A GRU sequence model matches but does not exceed gradient boosting, and skill disappears beyond a two-day lead. For monthly totals, no learner beat climatology significantly. We release a leakage-aware protocol and code so that future station-based studies report skill against climatology on held-out years.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that random train-test splitting of station rainfall records overstates machine-learning skill for Bangladesh rainfall, because a station-month climatology already classifies high-rainfall months at 88.4% accuracy. It releases a leakage-aware protocol and finds only modest genuine skill for next-day forecasts from lagged rainfall.
AI.motivation: Rainfall forecasts are often evaluated by shuffling station records into random training and test sets, which lets a model see neighbouring stations on the day it forecasts and hides how much a seasonal lookup table already explains.
AI.method: Using 618,650 station-days from 35 Bangladesh Meteorological Department stations (1948 to 2014), the authors compare random, temporal (train on years up to 1999, test on 2005 to 2014) and spatio-temporal evaluation. They compare calendar-only with antecedent-rainfall features and six learners against climatology, persistence and SARIMA.
AI.result: A station-month climatology alone classifies high-rainfall months with 88.4% accuracy (AUC 0.950), and no learner improves on it by more than 0.8 points under temporal evaluation. A calendar-only random forest reaches a next-day wet-day AUC of 0.889 under random splitting but falls to 0.835 on future years, below climatology at 0.859. Lagged rainfall adds modest skill, a Brier skill score of 0.074 over climatology (95% CI 0.064 to 0.088), rising to 0.091 without station and year inputs and to 0.131 with other stations' same-day observations. A GRU matches but does not exceed gradient boosting, skill disappears beyond a two-day lead, and no learner significantly beats climatology for monthly totals.
AI.conclusion: Station-based rainfall studies should report skill against climatology on held-out years, and the released protocol and code are meant to make this routine.

title: HotPOT: Operator Transformer with Heterogeneous Physics Experts for Large-Scale PDE Pre-training
summary: Large-scale PDE pre-training trains a single model on the data from multiple partial differential equations (PDEs). However, adding heterogeneous PDEs with different governing equations, physical variables, and variable interactions does not always improve predictive performance across tasks. Existing PDE mixture-of-experts models mitigate cross-task interference through learned routing, but typically use homogeneous expert architectures, making it difficult to directly reflect differences in state evolution across equations. We introduce HotPOT, an operator transformer with heterogeneous physics experts for large-scale PDE pre-training. HotPOT uses a shared encoder to capture information common across PDEs, while each PDE family uses a neural-numerical expert that pairs a learnable predictor with a fixed numerical update containing no trainable parameters. Each predictor outputs the quantities required by its paired numerical update, which then computes the next state. This design allows different PDEs to share a common encoder while retaining their own learnable predictors and numerical updates. Experiments across five PDE families and six settings show that HotPOT outperforms MoE-POT in all 24 matched-scale comparisons before and after fine-tuning, reducing rollout error by 50.7% on average. Notably, the 17M model also surpasses substantially larger MoE-POT models, and the performance gains extend to zero-shot prediction under unseen physical conditions. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: HotPOT is an operator transformer for large-scale PDE pre-training that pairs a shared encoder with heterogeneous physics experts, each combining a learnable predictor with a fixed, parameter-free numerical update. It outperforms MoE-POT in all 24 matched-scale comparisons and reduces rollout error by 50.7% on average.
AI.motivation: Adding heterogeneous PDEs to large-scale pre-training does not always improve prediction, and existing PDE mixture-of-experts models use homogeneous expert architectures, which cannot directly reflect differences in how states evolve across equations.
AI.method: A shared encoder captures information common to all PDEs. Each PDE family uses a neural-numerical expert that pairs a learnable predictor with a fixed numerical update containing no trainable parameters. The predictor outputs the quantities the numerical update needs to compute the next state.
AI.result: Across five PDE families and six settings, HotPOT outperforms MoE-POT in all 24 matched-scale comparisons, before and after fine-tuning, reducing rollout error by 50.7% on average. The 17M model surpasses substantially larger MoE-POT models, and the gains extend to zero-shot prediction under unseen physical conditions.
AI.conclusion: Physics-structured heterogeneous experts let different PDEs share an encoder while keeping their own learnable predictors and numerical updates, which improves large-scale PDE pre-training.

title: Variational Consequence-Driven Offline Reinforcement Learning
summary: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) typically mitigates distribution shift by imposing divergence constraints on the action distributions of the learned and behavior policies. However, this paradigm cannot ensure the underlying dynamic consistency structure: even minor action deviations can lead to drastically different transitions, inadvertently driving the agent away from the offline dataset. To address this, we explore policy constraints through their induced state-consequence distributions rather than relying on pure action-distribution matching. Nevertheless, directly enforcing such consequence-aware constraints is computationally intractable without access to the true underlying dynamics model. To bypass this issue, we propose Structural Behavior Regularization (StBR), which replaces the intractable objective with a closed-form latent divergence. Structuring this latent space to reflect transition dynamics renders the latent divergence a theoretically bounded surrogate for the true consequence-distribution divergence. By regularizing the learned policy with this latent divergence, StBR adaptively tightens the behavior constraint in dynamics-sensitive regions, effectively preventing deviations outside the offline dataset. Empirically, we demonstrate that StBR achieves superior performance across diverse offline RL benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Structural Behavior Regularization (StBR), an offline RL method that constrains the policy through its induced state-consequence distributions rather than action distributions. It uses a closed-form latent divergence as a bounded surrogate and reports superior performance across diverse offline RL benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Offline RL usually limits distribution shift with divergence constraints on action distributions, but small action deviations can cause very different transitions and drive the agent away from the offline dataset, so the constraint misses the dynamic consistency structure.
AI.method: Policy constraints are imposed on state-consequence distributions. Enforcing these directly requires the true dynamics, so StBR regularizes the policy with a closed-form latent divergence, in a latent space structured to reflect transition dynamics so that the divergence is a theoretically bounded surrogate for the true consequence divergence. The behavior constraint tightens adaptively in dynamics-sensitive regions.
AI.result: StBR achieves superior performance across diverse offline RL benchmarks. The abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Consequence-aware latent behavior regularization is an effective way to keep the learned policy within the offline dataset.

title: Nearly Minimax Optimal Regret for Adversarial Linear Bandits with Strong Corruptions
summary: We study adversarial linear bandits with strong corruption, in which an adaptive adversary chooses the reward vectors and a strong adversary corrupts each observed reward after seeing the learner's action, subject to a known total corruption budget $C$. Strong corruption breaks the importance-weighted reward estimates used by adversarial bandit algorithms: by corrupting only the rounds in which a rarely sampled action is drawn, the adversary amplifies each unit of corruption by the inverse of its sampling probability. The best known bound for this problem, $\tilde O(\sqrt{d^3T} + dC)$ by Liu et al. (2024), is a factor $\sqrt{d}$ above the corruption-free rate in its leading term, and whether $\tilde O(d\sqrt{T} + dC)$ regret is achievable was left open. We propose CRW-FTRL, which runs follow-the-regularized-leader with a radius-weighted entropy regularizer and estimates rewards with a normalized kernel estimator whose sensitivity to corruption is governed by per-action radii instead of inverse sampling probabilities. The radii are nondecreasing and are chosen jointly with the sampling distribution through a monotone log-determinant barrier problem, so that a negative linear term in the regularizer cancels both the corruption bias and the estimation error of every comparator. For $K$ actions in $\mathbb{R}^d$, CRW-FTRL achieves $\tilde O(\sqrt{dT\log K} + dC)$ regret with high probability against an adaptive adversary, which matches the best known corruption-free rate and the $\Omega(dC)$ lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Applied to a discretization of a general compact action set, it yields $\tilde O(d\sqrt{T} + dC)$ regret, which settles the statistical rate of corrupted adversarial linear bandits under strong corruption.

AI.tldr: The paper gives CRW-FTRL, an algorithm for adversarial linear bandits under strong corruption with regret of order sqrt(dT log K) plus dC, matching the corruption-free rate and the dC lower bound up to logarithmic factors. For general compact action sets it yields d sqrt(T) plus dC regret, settling the statistical rate.
AI.motivation: Under strong corruption the adversary amplifies each unit of corruption by the inverse sampling probability of rarely drawn actions. The best known bound, from Liu et al. (2024), is a factor sqrt(d) above the corruption-free leading term, and whether d sqrt(T) plus dC regret is achievable was open.
AI.method: CRW-FTRL runs follow-the-regularized-leader with a radius-weighted entropy regularizer and a normalized kernel estimator whose corruption sensitivity is governed by per-action radii rather than inverse sampling probabilities. The radii are nondecreasing and chosen jointly with the sampling distribution through a monotone log-determinant barrier problem, so a negative linear term cancels both corruption bias and estimation error.
AI.result: For K actions in R^d, CRW-FTRL achieves regret of order sqrt(dT log K) plus dC with high probability against an adaptive adversary. Applied to a discretization of a general compact action set, it yields d sqrt(T) plus dC regret.
AI.conclusion: The results settle the statistical rate of corrupted adversarial linear bandits under strong corruption, matching the lower bound up to logarithmic factors.

title: Transportable Offline Reinforcement Learning in Presence of Unmeasured Confounding
summary: Offline reinforcement learning seeks to learn decision policies from previously collected data, but deployment environments may differ from the domains in which the data were collected, and logged variables may omit confounders that affected both historical actions and outcomes. We study offline policy learning under the joint challenges of domain discrepancy and unmeasured confounding, where multiple heterogeneous source datasets provide complementary information about a target domain. We develop a causally adjusted transportability framework combining transportability theory with instrumental variables, negative controls, and proxies to identify target-domain causal quantities. For confounded contextual bandits, identification reduces to systems of bridge-function integral equations, enabling minimax estimation from finite samples. Confidence sets for the identified quantities are then used for pessimistic policy optimization, yielding CAT-CCB. We extend the framework to episodic confounded Markov decision processes, where complementary sources identify target reward and transition mechanisms under structural and completeness conditions. Under Gaussian dynamics and linear function approximation, this yields CAT-CMDP. We establish high-probability finite-sample suboptimality guarantees that quantify the effects of approximation, estimation, source-to-target shift, offline coverage, and sample size. For bounded finite-dimensional linear classes, the contextual-bandit guarantee recovers the standard $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(N^{-1/2})$ rate. Numerical experiments support the effectiveness of the framework for learning target-domain policies from heterogeneous confounded data.
