Together, the results provide a principled approach when no single source dataset suffices for causal identification and policy optimization.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a causally adjusted transportability framework for offline policy learning when source domains differ from the target and logged data omit confounders. It yields pessimistic policy algorithms, CAT-CCB for confounded contextual bandits and CAT-CMDP for confounded MDPs, with high-probability finite-sample suboptimality guarantees.
AI.motivation: Deployment environments can differ from the domains where data were collected, and logged variables may omit confounders that affect both past actions and outcomes, while no single source dataset may suffice for causal identification and policy optimization.
AI.method: The framework combines transportability theory with instrumental variables, negative controls and proxies to identify target-domain causal quantities from multiple heterogeneous source datasets. For confounded contextual bandits, identification reduces to bridge-function integral equations estimated minimax from finite samples, and confidence sets feed pessimistic policy optimization. For episodic confounded MDPs under Gaussian dynamics and linear function approximation, the approach yields CAT-CMDP.
AI.result: The guarantees quantify the effects of approximation, estimation, source-to-target shift, offline coverage and sample size. For bounded finite-dimensional linear classes, the contextual-bandit guarantee recovers the standard O(N^-1/2) rate. Numerical experiments support the effectiveness of the framework on heterogeneous confounded data.
AI.conclusion: The framework gives a principled approach to learning target-domain policies when no single source dataset suffices for causal identification and policy optimization.

title: ParaTTT: Parallelizing Test-Time Training Layers with Deep Memories
comment: 34 pages, 7 figures. Project repository: this https URL
summary: Test-time training (TTT) layers replace the linear fast-weight memory of modern recurrent architectures with a small neural network trained online by gradient descent. This nonlinear memory is more expressive than the linear memories of Gated DeltaNet and Mamba-2, but is difficult to parallelize: existing implementations such as TTT-MLP rely on sequential, block-wise weight updates that run several times slower than chunkwise-parallel linear recurrences. Moreover, their block-wise execution only approximates the token-by-token online recurrence, whereas linear recurrences admit an exact chunkwise-parallel evaluation. We introduce ParaTTT (PTTT), an algorithm for parallelizing arbitrarily deep nonlinear memories by iteratively refining estimates of the inner-loop gradient trajectory. Starting from a guess of the hidden-layer gradients, each refinement consists of three chunkwise-parallel passes: a forward pass that evaluates the resulting feature trajectory, an exact gated-delta-rule pass that computes the readout trajectory and its feature gradients, and a backward pass that propagates these gradients into a new estimate. The exact online gradient descent recurrence is a fixed point of the iteration, while decoding requires no refinement iterations. We prove geometric convergence for a two-layer variant under sufficient contraction conditions. In practice, two iterations suffice. With two refinement steps at 4K context, PTTT evaluates the inner-loop trajectory $32\times$ faster than TTT-MLP with the block approximation at matched error, while the full 340M model trains $4.9\times$ faster. Models trained at 340M and 1.3B parameters match or exceed Gated DeltaNet and Mamba-2 and remain competitive with same-size Transformers on language-modeling perplexity and zero-shot accuracy, with better recall than the linear recurrences.

AI.tldr: ParaTTT parallelizes test-time training layers with deep nonlinear memories by iteratively refining the inner-loop gradient trajectory through chunkwise-parallel passes. It evaluates the inner-loop trajectory 32 times faster than TTT-MLP with the block approximation at matched error, and its 340M and 1.3B models match or exceed Gated DeltaNet and Mamba-2.
AI.motivation: TTT layers use nonlinear memories that are more expressive than linear ones but are hard to parallelize, and existing TTT-MLP runs several times slower than chunkwise-parallel linear recurrences while its block-wise updates only approximate the token-by-token online recurrence.
AI.method: Starting from a guess of the hidden-layer gradients, each refinement runs three chunkwise-parallel passes: a forward pass evaluating the feature trajectory, an exact gated-delta-rule pass computing the readout trajectory and its feature gradients, and a backward pass propagating these gradients into a new estimate. The exact online gradient descent recurrence is a fixed point of this iteration, and decoding needs no refinement.
AI.result: With two refinement steps at 4K context, the inner-loop trajectory is evaluated 32 times faster than TTT-MLP with the block approximation at matched error, and the full 340M model trains 4.9 times faster. Models at 340M and 1.3B match or exceed Gated DeltaNet and Mamba-2, remain competitive with same-size Transformers on language-modeling perplexity and zero-shot accuracy, and have better recall than linear recurrences.
AI.conclusion: Deep nonlinear test-time memories can be parallelized efficiently, with two refinement iterations sufficing in practice, and a two-layer variant has a geometric convergence proof under sufficient contraction conditions.

title: A Hybrid Physics-informed holomorphic neural networks Method
summary: Physics-informed holomorphic neural networks (PIHNNs) exploit complex-analytic representations to satisfy homogeneous PDEs by construction, but their extension to nonhomogeneous problems is nontrivial. We propose a hybrid physics-informed holomorphic neural network (HPIHNN) framework based on a decomposition of the solution into particular and homogeneous components. The particular component is computed by a spectral method on a simple extended domain, while the homogeneous component is approximated by a PIHNN trained only on the boundary with modified boundary data. The resulting formulation avoids meshing complex geometries and retains the dimensionality-reduction advantage of holomorphic representations. The method is applied to nonhomogeneous Poisson, Stokes, biharmonic, linear elasticity, and Helmholtz equations. Numerical experiments covering complex geometries, corner singularities, and nearly incompressible regimes demonstrate that the proposed method accurately resolves the corresponding solutions and, in the considered tests, generally achieves lower errors and shorter training times than standard PINNs. The results indicate that coupling spectral particular solutions with holomorphic neural approximations provides an efficient approach to nonhomogeneous PDEs on complex domains.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hybrid physics-informed holomorphic neural network (HPIHNN) that splits the solution into a particular part from a spectral method and a homogeneous part learned by a PIHNN trained on the boundary. In the considered tests it generally achieves lower errors and shorter training times than standard PINNs on nonhomogeneous Poisson, Stokes, biharmonic, linear elasticity and Helmholtz problems.
AI.motivation: Physics-informed holomorphic neural networks satisfy homogeneous PDEs by construction through complex-analytic representations, but extending them to nonhomogeneous problems is nontrivial.
AI.method: The solution is decomposed into particular and homogeneous components. The particular component is computed by a spectral method on a simple extended domain, and the homogeneous component is approximated by a PIHNN trained only on the boundary with modified boundary data. This avoids meshing complex geometries and keeps the dimensionality-reduction advantage of holomorphic representations.
AI.result: Experiments on complex geometries, corner singularities and nearly incompressible regimes show that the method accurately resolves the solutions and, in the considered tests, generally achieves lower errors and shorter training times than standard PINNs.
AI.conclusion: Coupling spectral particular solutions with holomorphic neural approximations is an efficient approach to nonhomogeneous PDEs on complex domains.

title: NAGO: Noise-Aware Generative Operator via Flow Matching
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 49 pages including appendices and checklist. Code: this https URL
summary: We introduce NAGO, a noise-aware generative operator for efficient sampling from invariant measures of stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs) in function space. Our central idea is to treat the source measure as a design variable rather than a fixed Gaussian default. We establish admissibility conditions for well-defined infinite-dimensional flows and show that the finite-band source--target covariance ratio controls the spectral stiffness of the marginal velocity field. This analysis yields an admissibility-constrained spectral-matching rule: choose a source that is sufficiently rough for well-posedness, then minimize covariance mismatch over the resolved Fourier modes. On three representative stochastic-field benchmarks, this source design improves few-step spectral accuracy and several complementary distributional and physical statistics. In a controlled Matern-field ablation, it reduces the accurate RK4 budget from about 30 steps for Gaussian functional flow matching to 3--5 steps, a $6$--$10\times$ reduction in neural ODE evaluations. These gains are strongest for stationary multiscale fields and depend on the metric, resolution, and guidance protocol.

AI.tldr: NAGO is a noise-aware generative operator that samples invariant measures of stochastic PDEs in function space with flow matching, treating the source measure as a design variable. In a Matern-field ablation it cuts the accurate RK4 budget from about 30 steps to 3 to 5 steps, a 6 to 10 times reduction in neural ODE evaluations.
AI.motivation: Flow matching usually takes a fixed Gaussian default as the source measure, whereas the authors argue the source should be designed to suit the stochastic field being sampled.
AI.method: The authors establish admissibility conditions for well-defined infinite-dimensional flows and show that the finite-band source-target covariance ratio controls the spectral stiffness of the marginal velocity field. This yields an admissibility-constrained spectral-matching rule: choose a source rough enough for well-posedness, then minimize covariance mismatch over the resolved Fourier modes.
AI.result: On three stochastic-field benchmarks, the source design improves few-step spectral accuracy and several complementary distributional and physical statistics. In a controlled Matern-field ablation, it reduces the accurate RK4 budget from about 30 steps for Gaussian functional flow matching to 3 to 5 steps. The gains are strongest for stationary multiscale fields and depend on the metric, resolution and guidance protocol.
AI.conclusion: Designing the source measure to match spectral covariance is a practical lever for efficient few-step sampling of stochastic-field distributions, with gains that depend on the setting.

title: The Role of Quantization in Loss Spikes
summary: Loss spikes in language model pretraining can waste substantial compute and derail otherwise healthy training runs. A primary driver of these instabilities is the growth and divergence of output logits in the final language modeling (LM) head. In this work, we study a particularly costly form of this instability associated with output logit growth: delayed, terminal divergences that emerge only after prolonged training, which we call time-bomb spikes. We find that these instabilities are preceded by rapidly growing quantization error in the LM head, which eventually culminates in a loss spike. Crucially, reducing numerical precision accelerates time-bomb spikes, while increasing precision improves stability. We then propose a simple yet effective mitigation that replaces AdamW on the LM head with SGD with momentum, suppressing logit growth and improving stability over long training horizons. Finally, we find that existing mitigation techniques from the literature (along with our own) all reduce quantization error, suggesting a shared numerical mechanism behind their effectiveness. Together, our results identify finite precision error as a hidden driver of time-bomb spikes and show that suppressing this error is key to stable long-horizon pretraining.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies time-bomb spikes, delayed and terminal loss spikes in language model pretraining, as preceded by growing quantization error in the LM head. Lower numerical precision accelerates them, and replacing AdamW on the LM head with SGD with momentum suppresses logit growth and improves long-horizon stability.
AI.motivation: Loss spikes waste compute and can derail healthy training runs, and a primary driver is the growth and divergence of output logits in the LM head. The paper studies a particularly costly delayed form of this, time-bomb spikes, which emerge only after prolonged training.
AI.method: The authors trace time-bomb spikes to rapidly growing quantization error in the LM head and compare precisions. They propose a simple mitigation that replaces AdamW on the LM head with SGD with momentum, and they examine existing mitigations from the literature alongside their own.
AI.result: Time-bomb spikes are preceded by rapidly growing quantization error in the LM head that culminates in a loss spike. Reducing numerical precision accelerates them, while increasing precision improves stability. SGD with momentum on the LM head suppresses logit growth and improves stability over long training horizons. Existing mitigations, and the authors' own, all reduce quantization error.
AI.conclusion: Finite-precision error is a hidden driver of time-bomb spikes and suppressing it is key to stable long-horizon pretraining, which suggests a shared numerical mechanism behind existing mitigations.

title: A Case Study of a Multi-Agent Kernel-Optimization Loop That Learns a New AI Accelerator
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Round 1 of the NPU Model Optimization Competition at MICRO 2026. Code: this https URL
summary: Frontier large language models write correct CUDA kernels for most single-operator benchmark tasks, yet their accuracy collapses on accelerators whose architecture and programming language they have rarely seen. We present a case study of an LLM agent loop built for such accelerators. Our example is the FuriosaAI RNGD NPU, programmed in a recent, sparsely documented Rust DSL, where the loop optimized three Gemma-4-12B decode kernels over 12 days on a shared, scarce device. The loop builds its own target knowledge: it writes and checks a summary of the DSL documentation, measures the chip with microbenchmarks, records compiler-derived legality rules, and revisits this knowledge when the toolchain changes, rechecking rules and measurements where it can. A role-based search over per-kernel Design Trees explores whole-kernel designs and accumulates small accepted changes in the best version of each kernel. Because device time is scarce and readings are noisy, cheap checks screen new designs before any device run, and late in the run a change was accepted only after repeated comparisons with the best kernel on the device. The final kernels reach a 9.293x geomean speedup over the official baseline, each within 1.25x of the cycles needed just to move its weights. Our prompts, profiler and acceptance test are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper is a case study of an LLM agent loop that optimized three Gemma-4-12B decode kernels for the FuriosaAI RNGD NPU, programmed in a sparsely documented Rust DSL, over 12 days on a shared, scarce device. The final kernels reach a 9.293x geomean speedup over the official baseline.
AI.motivation: Frontier LLMs write correct CUDA kernels for most single-operator benchmarks, but their accuracy collapses on accelerators whose architecture and programming language they have rarely seen.
AI.method: The loop builds its own target knowledge: it writes and checks a summary of the DSL documentation, measures the chip with microbenchmarks, records compiler-derived legality rules, and revisits this knowledge when the toolchain changes. A role-based search over per-kernel Design Trees explores whole-kernel designs and accumulates small accepted changes. Cheap checks screen new designs before any device run, and late in the run a change was accepted only after repeated comparisons with the best kernel on the device.
AI.result: The final kernels reach a 9.293x geomean speedup over the official baseline, each within 1.25x of the cycles needed just to move its weights.
AI.conclusion: An LLM agent loop that builds its own target knowledge can optimize kernels for a new accelerator under scarce and noisy device time, and the prompts, profiler and acceptance test are released.

title: Multi-Token Prediction Done Right
summary: Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) is now a common ingredient in language-model pre-training, as it improves downstream performance and enables faster inference through speculative decoding. We identify a flaw in standard MTP training, in which a residual component of the MTP gradient interferes with both next-token and multi-token learning, increasingly so with scale. Specifically, the MTP cross-entropy gradient can be decomposed exactly into a KL self-distillation term that pulls each MTP head toward the model's own next-token prediction (NTP) distribution and improves speculative decoding, and a residual that has a low signal-to-noise ratio and buries the useful KL signal. We introduce the KL gradient-recovery trick: when two distributions share a linear output head, the gradient of their KL divergence can be recovered exactly by combining their cross-entropy gradients through straight-through gradient routing. Unlike minimizing the KL directly, this trick requires no vocabulary-sized logit matrices and is compatible with standard fused cross-entropy kernels. This enables Soft Multi-Token Prediction (Soft-MTP), a one-line code change to MTP that removes the noisy residual and backpropagates only the KL self-distillation signal by reusing the existing NTP and MTP cross-entropy computations. Soft-MTP supports both DeepSeek- and Meta-style MTP, adds no parameters, and incurs no measurable overhead. From 167M to 1.2B parameters, Soft-MTP improves over standard MTP with lower NTP perplexity, faster speculative decoding and higher zero-shot accuracy at every scale, lower MTP perplexity from 689M onward, and stronger math and code reasoning after fine-tuning at 1.2B. Soft-MTP also matches, if not exceeds, direct KL divergence minimization on most metrics. Soft-MTP is, in effect, a free lunch for MTP optimization. Our code can be found at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Standard multi-token prediction (MTP) training carries a residual gradient term that interferes with learning, and the paper proposes Soft-MTP, a one-line change that backpropagates only the KL self-distillation signal. Soft-MTP improves over standard MTP at every scale from 167M to 1.2B parameters, with no added parameters and no measurable overhead.
AI.motivation: MTP improves downstream performance and speculative decoding, but its gradient contains a low signal-to-noise residual that buries the useful KL signal and interferes with next-token and multi-token learning, increasingly so with scale.
AI.method: The MTP cross-entropy gradient decomposes exactly into a KL self-distillation term that pulls each MTP head toward the model's next-token prediction distribution and a residual term. The KL gradient-recovery trick uses straight-through gradient routing to recover the KL gradient exactly from two cross-entropy gradients when the two distributions share a linear output head, without vocabulary-sized logit matrices and compatible with fused cross-entropy kernels.
AI.result: From 167M to 1.2B parameters, Soft-MTP improves over standard MTP with lower next-token prediction perplexity, faster speculative decoding and higher zero-shot accuracy at every scale, and lower MTP perplexity from 689M onward. At 1.2B it gives stronger math and code reasoning after fine-tuning, and it matches or exceeds direct KL divergence minimization on most metrics.
AI.conclusion: Removing the noisy residual while keeping the KL self-distillation signal is a simple, cost-free improvement to MTP optimization.

title: MUSE: Multi-Level Memory with Selective Runtime Injection for Scientific Coding Agents
summary: Historical experience can guide scientific coding at multiple levels, but task-level retrieval may miss implementation lessons that become relevant during execution. We introduce MUSE, a memory management framework combining multi-level memory with selective runtime injection for scientific coding agents. MUSE builds global, approach-level, and implementation-level memory from historical trajectories. At initialization, the agent receives global memory and problem-matched approach-level memory. During execution, current interactions are used to retrieve implementation-level memory. An LLM gate selects relevant experience and generates specific review advice, or skips injection. Across four benchmarks spanning numerical problem solving, kernel optimization, and scientific software repair, MUSE outperforms retrieval and memory baselines on all evaluation metrics. Ablations support the multi-level design and gated injection, while transfer experiments show that memory remains useful across kernel benchmarks. These results show that multi-level memory and selective runtime injection enable effective reuse of experience in scientific coding. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: MUSE is a memory framework for scientific coding agents that builds global, approach-level and implementation-level memory from historical trajectories and injects it selectively at runtime through an LLM gate. It outperforms retrieval and memory baselines on four benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Task-level retrieval of historical experience may miss implementation lessons that only become relevant during execution.
AI.method: Multi-level memory (global, approach-level, implementation-level) is built from historical trajectories. At initialization the agent receives global memory and problem-matched approach-level memory; during execution, current interactions are used to retrieve implementation-level memory. An LLM gate selects relevant experience and generates specific review advice, or skips injection.
AI.result: MUSE outperforms retrieval and memory baselines on all evaluation metrics across four benchmarks spanning numerical problem solving, kernel optimization and scientific software repair. Ablations support the multi-level design and gated injection, and transfer experiments show memory remains useful across kernel benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Multi-level memory combined with selective runtime injection enables effective reuse of experience in scientific coding.

title: Optimal Regret for Communication-Efficient Decentralized Online Learning
summary: In this paper, we investigate decentralized online convex optimization with compressed communication, where $n$ learners over a network jointly minimize a sequence of global loss functions based only on their local losses and compressed messages from their neighbors. The best known regret bounds for this problem are $O(\omega^{-1/2}n\rho^{-1}\sqrt{T\ln n})$ and $O(\omega^{-1}n\rho^{-2}\ln n\ln T)$ for convex and strongly convex loss functions, respectively, where $\rho\in(0,1)$ is the spectral gap of the communication matrix and $\omega\in(0,1]$ is the compression quality factor. Compared with the corresponding lower bounds of $\Omega(\omega^{-1/2}n\rho^{-1/4}\sqrt{T})$ and $\Omega(\omega^{-1}n\rho^{-1/2}\ln T)$, these upper bounds exhibit polynomial gaps in their dependence on $\rho^{-1}$. To close these gaps, we first develop Ascent-gossip, which combines an online compression strategy with a Chebyshev recursion and attains a faster consensus rate than existing compressed gossip methods. Furthermore, by adopting Ascent-gossip, we propose an online algorithm that achieves optimal regret bounds of $\widetilde O(\omega^{-1/2}n\rho^{-1/4}\sqrt{T})$ and $\widetilde O(\omega^{-1}n\rho^{-1/2}\ln T)$ for convex and strongly convex loss functions, respectively. Up to logarithmic factors in $n$ and $\rho^{-1}$, these results match the lower bounds in terms of $T$, $n$, $\rho$, and $\omega$.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Ascent-gossip, a compressed gossip method combining online compression with Chebyshev recursion, and an online algorithm built on it that attains regret bounds matching known lower bounds up to logarithmic factors.
AI.motivation: The best known regret bounds for decentralized online convex optimization with compressed communication have polynomial gaps in their dependence on the spectral gap rho, relative to known lower bounds.
AI.method: Ascent-gossip combines an online compression strategy with a Chebyshev recursion to reach a faster consensus rate than existing compressed gossip methods. The online algorithm adopts Ascent-gossip as its communication step.
AI.result: The proposed algorithm achieves regret of order omega^(-1/2) n rho^(-1/4) sqrt(T) for convex losses and omega^(-1) n rho^(-1/2) ln T for strongly convex losses, improving on the best known bounds, which scale as rho^(-1) and rho^(-2) respectively.
AI.conclusion: Up to logarithmic factors in n and rho, the bounds match the lower bounds in T, n, rho and omega, closing the gap for compressed decentralized online learning.

title: Learning a Prior-Data Fitted Network for Graph Foundation Models via Structural Causal Model Priors
summary: Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for learning transferable representations across different graphs and domains. However, existing GFMs face notable limitations, including limited pre-training scale or reliance on aligning with textual information in Large Language Models (LLMs). To overcome these limitations, recent studies have drawn inspiration from prior-data fitted networks (PFNs), which learn from large synthetic datasets and support multi-domain prediction backed by causal learning. However, existing graph PFNs encounter severe difficulties in modeling causal relationships within and across node and edge sets, generating diverse graph structures, and designing suitable architectures that can learn from complex synthetic datasets. To address these challenges, we propose **GSCM-PFN** (Graph SCM-based Prior-Data Fitted Network), a graph PFN pre-trained on synthetic data generated from an SCM-based prior that jointly models nodes and graph topology. Specifically, we (1) design a joint feature-edge-label structural causal model (SCM) to guide synthetic graph generation and capture causal relationships within and across node and edge sets; (2) introduce prior-guided node-edge dependency modeling to instantiate diverse graph generation strategies, and prove that our SCM-based generation prior is more expressive than existing priors; and (3) propose a feature-permutation-invariant dual-path graph network with theoretical guarantees for learning from diverse synthetic graphs. Experiments on 23 real-world benchmarks show that GSCM-PFN outperforms both conventional GFMs and PFN-based GFMs, without utilizing real-world graph data for pre-training. Code: this https URL

AI.tldr: GSCM-PFN is a graph prior-data fitted network pre-trained purely on synthetic graphs generated from a joint feature-edge-label structural causal model. It outperforms conventional and PFN-based graph foundation models on 23 real-world benchmarks without using real graph data for pre-training.
AI.motivation: Existing graph foundation models are limited by small pre-training scale or by reliance on aligning with textual information in LLMs, and existing graph PFNs struggle to model causal relationships within and across node and edge sets and to generate diverse graph structures.
AI.method: A joint feature-edge-label SCM guides synthetic graph generation, with prior-guided node-edge dependency modeling to instantiate diverse generation strategies. The authors prove that this SCM-based prior is more expressive than existing priors, and use a feature-permutation-invariant dual-path graph network with theoretical guarantees.
AI.result: GSCM-PFN outperforms both conventional graph foundation models and PFN-based graph foundation models across 23 real-world benchmarks, with no real-world graph data used for pre-training.
AI.conclusion: Pre-training on synthetic data from a causally structured graph prior can yield a transferable graph foundation model that competes with or surpasses models trained on real graphs.

title: How Much Do Teacher Bridges Matter in Interleaved On-Policy Distillation?
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student using teacher predictions on student-generated responses. Some methods insert teacher-written segments, or bridges, but disagree on how to train on those tokens. We compare no loss, forward KL and reverse KL on identical trajectories using Qwen3-1.7B as student and Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as teacher. We separate gradients by which model wrote each token. Under our short training runs and BF16 inference, pre-specified tests detected no added accuracy benefit from teacher text as context or as a training target. A one-paragraph bridge after the student's first paragraph is only 2.7% of the tokens and contributes a small gradient nearly orthogonal to the student-token gradient. In this main comparison, the three loss treatments gave similar gradient directions and were statistically equivalent in accuracy within a +/-5 percentage-point margin. An exploratory pilot placing the bridge where failed responses disagreed most with the teacher suggested a benefit from teacher-token loss. A pre-specified replication did not confirm this, and fourfold weighting showed no significant accuracy benefit. Two limitations bound these findings. Among the tested amounts of training on fixed responses, gains peaked after four updates before the student increasingly failed to stop generating. None of the tested online training variants met the criteria for stable stopping and improved accuracy. Our evaluations used BF16 inference, which rounds away most of the small weight changes. When evaluated in exact FP32, the tested replication models frequently reached the response-length limit. Our accuracy findings therefore concern BF16 inference; they do not establish that teacher-token supervision is generally unnecessary.

AI.tldr: A controlled comparison of no loss, forward KL and reverse KL on teacher-written bridge segments in interleaved on-policy distillation finds no detectable accuracy benefit from teacher text under short training and BF16 inference.
AI.motivation: Some on-policy distillation methods insert teacher-written bridge segments into student trajectories but disagree on how to train on those tokens.
AI.method: Identical trajectories are compared under three loss treatments (no loss, forward KL, reverse KL), with Qwen3-1.7B as student and Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as teacher. Gradients are separated by which model wrote each token. Pre-specified tests, an exploratory pilot that places the bridge where failed responses disagree most with the teacher, and a pre-specified replication are reported.
AI.result: Pre-specified tests detected no added accuracy benefit from teacher text as context or as a training target. The bridge is 2.7% of tokens and contributes a small gradient nearly orthogonal to the student-token gradient. The three loss treatments gave similar gradient directions and were statistically equivalent within a +/-5 percentage-point margin. The pilot suggested a benefit from teacher-token loss, which the pre-specified replication did not confirm, and fourfold weighting showed no significant benefit. Gains peaked after four updates on fixed responses, and no tested online variant met the criteria for stable stopping and improved accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The accuracy findings are specific to BF16 inference and short training; the paper does not establish that teacher-token supervision is generally unnecessary, since FP32 evaluation frequently hit the response-length limit.

title: Continual Adaptation Across Modalities: Learning and Forgetting in Unified Multimodal Models
summary: Unified multimodal models (UMMs), which can process and generate diverse modalities within a single framework, have recently emerged as a powerful paradigm. However, when these models undergo continual learning on multiple tasks across different modalities, their learning and forgetting dynamics remain poorly understood. In this paper, we systematically investigate how architectural design and adaptation method shape intra-modal learning and cross-modal interference between the generation and understanding sides. Specifically, we report three findings. First, the severity of cross-modal interference decreases with the degree of modality-specific parameter isolation. Second, a within-model asymmetry: the generation side of a UMM is markedly more fragile than its understanding side. Third, what post-training adds is the first to be forgotten: purely post-training capabilities such as personalized generation collapse by 84\% to 90\%, while pretraining capabilities remain stable. Together, these results clarify how parameter isolation and post-training fragility shape UMMs' learning and forgetting dynamics, offering a starting point for developing continually evolving UMMs.

AI.tldr: A systematic study of continual learning in unified multimodal models finds that cross-modal interference shrinks with modality-specific parameter isolation, the generation side is more fragile than the understanding side, and post-training capabilities are forgotten first.
AI.motivation: Unified multimodal models that handle several modalities within one framework are increasingly common, but their learning and forgetting dynamics under continual learning across modalities remain poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors investigate how architectural design and adaptation method shape intra-modal learning and cross-modal interference between the generation and understanding sides of the model.
AI.result: The severity of cross-modal interference decreases with the degree of modality-specific parameter isolation. The generation side is markedly more fragile than the understanding side. Purely post-training capabilities such as personalized generation collapse by 84% to 90%, while pretraining capabilities remain stable.
AI.conclusion: Parameter isolation and post-training fragility shape the learning and forgetting dynamics of unified multimodal models, offering a starting point for continually evolving models.

title: AtomSteer: Test-Time Constraint Steering for Atomistic Generative Models
summary: Diffusion and flow matching models offer scalable approaches to generating crystalline materials, molecular conformers, and protein-ligand complexes. However, satisfying crystallographic symmetry, structural geometry, and accurate stereochemistry remains challenging. Satisfying these requirements calls for corrections that preserve the geometry already captured by the pretrained model. In this work, we propose AtomSteer, a test-time inference framework for steering pretrained atomistic generative models with structural constraints. During sampling, AtomSteer corrects intermediate structure predictions with bounded local projections, graph-rigid stereochemical transformations, and projections over periodic symmetries, accepting updates that improve constraint satisfaction while limiting changes to the rest of the structure. We demonstrate AtomSteer across three pretrained backbones, FlowMM, ET-Flow, and Boltz-2, spanning de novo crystal generation and crystal structure prediction, molecular conformer generation, and protein-ligand complex structure prediction. AtomSteer improves space-group distribution coverage in de novo crystal generation and improves target space-group recovery in crystal structure prediction. AtomSteer improves molecular validity and E/Z stereochemical accuracy while retaining conformer ensemble fidelity. For protein-ligand complexes, AtomSteer reduces ligand E/Z errors relative to experimental reference structures while achieving competitive docking success and PoseBusters validity. Our method provides a unified framework for adding chemical and crystallographic control to existing atomistic generative models without retraining or architectural changes.

AI.tldr: AtomSteer is a test-time framework that steers pretrained atomistic generative models with structural constraints during sampling, improving crystal symmetry, molecular stereochemistry and protein-ligand E/Z accuracy without retraining.
AI.motivation: Diffusion and flow matching models for crystals, molecular conformers and protein-ligand complexes struggle to satisfy crystallographic symmetry, structural geometry and accurate stereochemistry, and corrections must preserve the geometry the pretrained model has already captured.
AI.method: During sampling, intermediate structure predictions are corrected with bounded local projections, graph-rigid stereochemical transformations, and projections over periodic symmetries. Updates are accepted only if they improve constraint satisfaction while limiting changes to the rest of the structure.
AI.result: Demonstrated on FlowMM, ET-Flow and Boltz-2 across de novo crystal generation, crystal structure prediction, molecular conformer generation and protein-ligand complex prediction. It improves space-group distribution coverage and target space-group recovery, improves molecular validity and E/Z accuracy while retaining conformer ensemble fidelity, and reduces ligand E/Z errors with competitive docking success and PoseBusters validity.
AI.conclusion: AtomSteer provides a unified way to add chemical and crystallographic control to existing atomistic generative models without retraining or architectural changes.

title: REVBRAIN: Real-time Probabilistic EEG Forecasting Using Residual Vector Quantization
summary: Real-time forecasting of resting-state EEG signals is required by applications like brain-state-dependent stimulation, where computer generated actions are coupled with ongoing neural oscillations. Recently, the deep learning model WaveNet was proposed for the forecasting task. It shows superior accuracy compared to the prevailing method, the linear autoregressive (AR) model, and provides a built-in uncertainty measure due to its probabilistic modeling framework. However, inference using WaveNet is too slow for real-time use due to its sample-by-sample autoregressive operation: a single forecast requires evaluating the model tens or hundreds of times depending on the length of the prediction window. In this paper, we present REVBRAIN, a probabilistic deep learning method that produces forecasts in real time by generating the forecast over the whole prediction horizon at once. This is achieved by tokenizing the output space using residual vector quantization (RVQ) and generating forecasts over the items in the tokenized space. We tested REVBRAIN for forecasting 200 ms of EEG time series in the alpha-frequency band (8-13 Hz) and compared our results against WaveNet model. We found that REVBRAIN achieved real-time inference on a laptop GPU and an over $50\times$ speedup compared to WaveNet, while reaching superior prediction accuracy. By achieving real-time inference speed, REVBRAIN enables incorporating accurate and probabilistic EEG forecasting into BCI applications, opening up new ways for investigating the functioning of the human brain.

AI.tldr: REVBRAIN is a probabilistic deep learning method for real-time EEG forecasting that generates the whole 200 ms prediction horizon at once by tokenizing the output with residual vector quantization. It runs over 50 times faster than WaveNet while achieving superior accuracy.
AI.motivation: WaveNet gives accurate probabilistic EEG forecasts but its sample-by-sample autoregressive inference is too slow for brain-state-dependent stimulation and other real-time BCI uses.
AI.method: The output space is tokenized using residual vector quantization, and forecasts are generated over the tokenized items for the whole prediction horizon at once. Forecasts of 200 ms of resting-state EEG in the alpha band (8-13 Hz) are compared against WaveNet.
AI.result: REVBRAIN achieves real-time inference on a laptop GPU, an over 50x speedup compared with WaveNet, and superior prediction accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The speed enables accurate probabilistic EEG forecasting to be used in BCI applications.

title: Persona Learning from Feedback for Personalized AI Assistants
summary: Personalizing AI assistants requires adapting their behavior to users' preferences and task contexts. Existing work elicits assistant personas through persona prompting or finetuning on persona-conditioned generations. However, persona descriptions alone do not identify what to change or preserve in a particular response, or which behaviors suit the current request. We introduce $\textit{Persona Learning from Feedback (PLF)}$, a framework that learns reusable, preference-grounded assistant personas as independent LoRA adapters on a shared frozen backbone. During training, a frozen self-teacher conditions on persona specifications and response-specific feedback to provide token-level supervision on each adapter's own generated prefixes. A feedback gate focuses corrective updates on responses judged to need improvement. At deployment, a supervised router uses the request or dialogue to select a single adapter or a fixed composition, without user-specific finetuning. We evaluate PLF on single-turn personalization with model-generated critiques and multi-turn tutoring with simulated students' reactions. Across both settings, PLF improves model-judged preference fit over fixed-persona policies and strong baselines including persona prompting and persona distillation, demonstrating how feedback-trained behaviors can be reused for adaptive assistant personalization without degrading general capabilities.

AI.tldr: Persona Learning from Feedback (PLF) trains reusable, preference-grounded persona adapters as independent LoRA modules on a frozen backbone and routes each request to one adapter or a fixed composition, improving preference fit over persona prompting and persona distillation.
AI.motivation: Persona prompts and persona-conditioned finetuning do not specify what to change or preserve in a particular response, or which behaviors suit the current request.
AI.method: Each persona is an independent LoRA adapter on a shared frozen backbone. A frozen self-teacher conditions on persona specifications and response-specific feedback to supply token-level supervision on each adapter's own generated prefixes, and a feedback gate focuses updates on responses judged to need improvement. A supervised router selects an adapter or fixed composition at deployment without user-specific finetuning.
AI.result: Evaluated on single-turn personalization with model-generated critiques and on multi-turn tutoring with simulated student reactions. PLF improves model-judged preference fit over fixed-persona policies and strong baselines including persona prompting and persona distillation, without degrading general capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Feedback-trained behaviors can be reused for adaptive assistant personalization.

title: Episodic looking - using reinforcement learning to bias perception enhances few-shot and continual learning with protection from forgetting
summary: There is a fundamental contradiction between the desire for models that can generalize, and models that can continuously adapt to recent input with changing statistics. These conditions, captured in few-shot and continual learning settings, can bias or disrupt learned representations. This harms generalization to a broader context, leaving the model unable to overcome input variance. This paper proposes a solution based on the Complementary Learning System architecture (CLS), in which a Short-Term Memory (STM) delegates generalization to a slow, statistical Long-Term Memory (LTM). Delegation is achieved by working in a space of robust, generalized perceptions produced by the LTM. With this separation, the STM can focus on memorizing recent input and avoiding interference between memories. We show that on an image classification task, the resulting CLS model is more resistant to forgetting in a domain-incremental continual learning setting than a baseline ResNet LTM, and generalizes more effectively in a few-shot setting than other continual learners. In the continual setting, overall accuracy is slightly worse than existing continual learning models, but with a different mix of performance characteristics. Results analysis suggests that the model is limited by the representations and representational plasticity of the LTM. In future work, we will seek to address this by replaying STM memories to the LTM.

AI.tldr: A Complementary Learning System model with a short-term memory that delegates generalization to a slow long-term memory is more resistant to forgetting than a ResNet baseline in domain-incremental learning and generalizes better in few-shot settings, though its continual accuracy is slightly lower than existing continual learners.
AI.motivation: Models that generalize and models that continually adapt to changing input statistics pull in opposite directions, and continual or few-shot learning can bias or disrupt learned representations.
AI.method: A Complementary Learning System architecture in which a Short-Term Memory (STM) memorizes recent input and delegates generalization to a slow, statistical Long-Term Memory (LTM), working in the space of generalized perceptions produced by the LTM.
AI.result: On an image classification task, the CLS model is more resistant to forgetting in a domain-incremental continual learning setting than a baseline ResNet LTM and generalizes more effectively in a few-shot setting than other continual learners. Overall continual accuracy is slightly worse than existing continual learning models, with a different mix of performance characteristics.
AI.conclusion: Results suggest the model is limited by the representations and representational plasticity of the LTM; the authors plan to address this by replaying STM memories to the LTM in future work.

title: Dual DeltaNet: Value-Side Memory Reorganization for Linear Attention
summary: Linear attention and state space models (SSMs) offer efficient alternatives to softmax attention by maintaining a fixed-size recurrent state, but this design requires careful management to preserve useful historical associations and limit interference. The delta rule helps reduce interference through correction of the value associated with each key, but it does not explicitly account for how related value features are distributed across the state. We observe that a state $\boldsymbol{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_k\times d_v}$ can be viewed as a bank of $d_k$ addresses storing $d_v$-dimensional values. While a key-side read $\boldsymbol{S}^\top\boldsymbol{k}$ retrieves the value associated with $\boldsymbol{k}$, a value-side read $\boldsymbol{S}\boldsymbol{e}$ aggregates addresses whose stored value features match the selector $\boldsymbol{e}$. Based on this observation, we propose Dual DeltaNet (DDN), which extends Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) with a two-sided delta rule. The key-side delta rule reads with the current key to correct its associated value, while the complementary value-side delta rule reads with selected features of the current value to reorganize the addresses it occupies. We derive a chunkwise parallel training algorithm and a rank-2 recurrence that increases arithmetic intensity during inference. Compared with KDA, GDN-2, and Mamba-3, DDN achieves the strongest overall performance across language modeling, zero-shot downstream tasks, and retrieval, while incurring modest training and inference overhead relative to KDA. Code: this https URL

AI.tldr: Dual DeltaNet extends Kimi Delta Attention with a second, value-side delta rule that reorganizes how the recurrent state stores values, achieving the strongest overall performance among the compared linear attention models at modest overhead relative to KDA.
AI.motivation: The delta rule corrects the value associated with each key in linear attention and SSM states, but does not account for how related value features are distributed across the state.
AI.method: The state is viewed as a bank of d_k addresses storing d_v-dimensional values. Alongside the key-side delta rule, a value-side delta rule reads with selected features of the current value to reorganize the addresses it occupies. The authors derive a chunkwise parallel training algorithm and a rank-2 recurrence that increases arithmetic intensity during inference.
AI.result: Compared with KDA, GDN-2 and Mamba-3, DDN achieves the strongest overall performance across language modeling, zero-shot downstream tasks and retrieval, with modest training and inference overhead relative to KDA.
AI.conclusion: Two-sided delta updates are a practical way to improve recurrent memory in linear attention.

title: Rethinking LLM Jailbreak Evaluation: Continuous Risk Landscapes Beyond Binary Outcomes
summary: A binary success indicator is a natural representation for discriminative tasks such as image classification under adversarial perturbations, where each input is mapped to a single prediction. However, generative tasks are fundamentally different: an LLM jailbreak prompt induces a distribution over open-ended trajectories, while a sampled response reveals only one path. Yet LLM jailbreak evaluation typically retains the binary response indicator underlying attack success rate, obscuring the surrounding structure of possible generations. We introduce a continuous, context-conditioned risk landscape over first-token branches, estimated by fixing candidate openings and repeatedly sampling their continuations. This continuous risk-landscape perspective reveals two complementary properties: current decoder exposure and safe rerouting capacity, which have been obscured by binary-indicator-based ASR. The resulting representation also provides a common basis for comparing clean prompts, attacked variants, and attack strength against a known adaptive defense. Across multiple target models and jailbreak attacks, we uncover risky branches beneath apparently safe outputs, identify qualitatively different ways attacks reshape the model's opening distribution, and show that attacks strongest before a defense do not necessarily remain the strongest after the adaptive defense reacts. These findings recast jailbreaks as deformations of the surrounding continuation-risk landscape, establishing a more informative foundation for understanding jailbreak behavior and developing safer language models.

AI.tldr: The paper replaces binary attack success rate with a continuous, context-conditioned risk landscape over first-token branches, showing that binary metrics hide risky continuations under apparently safe outputs and that attack rankings can change after an adaptive defense.
AI.motivation: Binary success indicators for LLM jailbreaks ignore that a prompt induces a distribution over open-ended trajectories, and a single sampled response reveals only one path.
AI.method: Candidate openings are fixed and their continuations are sampled repeatedly to estimate a continuous risk landscape over first-token branches. This yields two properties, current decoder exposure and safe rerouting capacity, and gives a common basis for comparing clean prompts, attacked variants and attack strength against a known adaptive defense.
AI.result: Across multiple target models and jailbreak attacks, the authors find risky branches beneath apparently safe outputs and identify qualitatively different ways attacks reshape the model's opening distribution. Attacks strongest before a defense do not necessarily remain the strongest after the adaptive defense reacts.
AI.conclusion: Jailbreaks can be understood as deformations of the surrounding continuation-risk landscape, which gives a more informative foundation for evaluating and developing safer language models.

title: Two-Stage Clipping: Linear-Time Approximate and Exact Mixed-Norm Projections for Transformers
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) based on Transformer architectures have achieved remarkable performance across artificial intelligence tasks, but their computational cost remains a major bottleneck. Structured sparsification provides a promising approach to reducing this cost. In particular, $\ell_{1,\infty}$ projections can induce column-wise sparsity in model matrices, but existing proximal methods (Prox) typically require $\mathcal{O}(nm\log(nm))$ operations for matrices in $\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$, limiting their computational and energy efficiency. In this paper, we introduce Two-Stage Clipping (TSC), an efficient structured sparsification operator inspired by bilevel optimization. Rather than solving a bilevel optimization problem in the strict sense, TSC decomposes the computation into two successive stages. First, group-level quantities are projected to allocate the global sparsity budget and identify active groups. Second, the resulting values are used as group-wise clipping thresholds for the matrix coefficients. For square attention matrices ($n \times n$), the complexity of our TSC method is $O(n^2)$, which is linear in the number of matrix coefficients. We establish a theoretical bound on the discrepancy between TSC and the exact proximal projection and show on synthetic data that the additional Euclidean approximation cost remains small in practice. Extensive benchmarks demonstrate substantial runtime improvements over proximal baselines and validate the theoretical norm identities underlying the proposed construction.

AI.tldr: Two-Stage Clipping (TSC) is a structured sparsification operator for l_{1,inf} projections in Transformers that runs in O(n^2) time on n x n attention matrices, substantially faster than proximal baselines that require O(nm log(nm)) operations.
AI.motivation: l_{1,inf} projections induce column-wise sparsity in LLM matrices, but existing proximal methods are costly at O(nm log(nm)) for n x m matrices, which limits computational and energy efficiency.
AI.method: Inspired by bilevel optimization but not solving it in the strict sense, TSC uses two successive stages. First, group-level quantities are projected to allocate the global sparsity budget and identify active groups. Second, the resulting values serve as group-wise clipping thresholds for the matrix coefficients.
AI.result: For square attention matrices the complexity is O(n^2), linear in the number of coefficients. The authors bound the discrepancy between TSC and the exact proximal projection, and on synthetic data the extra Euclidean approximation cost is small. Benchmarks show substantial runtime improvements over proximal baselines and validate the underlying norm identities.
AI.conclusion: TSC offers a linear-time route to structured sparsification of Transformer matrices, with a bounded approximation to the exact projection.

title: On-Policy Self-Distillation with Teacher Evolution
summary: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), which aligns a student model's token-level distribution with that of its self-teacher prompted by privileged context, has emerged as a promising direction to mitigate reward sparsity in sequence-level post-training paradigms. However, OPSD often fails to achieve continuous performance gains during training. In this paper, we find that the model's limited self-teaching capability underlies this phenomenon by generating unreliable guidance on certain samples. To address this problem, we propose Teacher-Evolution Self-Distillation (TESD), which enables the self-teacher to generate rollouts and receive environmental feedback based on task correctness and context independence. First, using these rewards as training objectives, we perform teacher-oriented optimization to continuously enhance the model's self-teaching capability during distillation. Second, by estimating teacher guidance reliability from these rewards, we apply adaptive student-oriented optimization to down-weight samples with unreliable guidance. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets and model scales show that TESD consistently outperforms representative token-level and sequence-level methods, highlighting the necessity of improving supervision quality in OPSD.

AI.tldr: Teacher-Evolution Self-Distillation (TESD) improves on-policy self-distillation by continually strengthening the self-teacher and down-weighting samples whose teacher guidance is unreliable, and outperforms representative token-level and sequence-level methods.
AI.motivation: On-Policy Self-Distillation often fails to yield continuous performance gains because the model's limited self-teaching capability produces unreliable guidance on certain samples.
AI.method: The self-teacher generates rollouts and receives environmental feedback based on task correctness and context independence. These rewards drive teacher-oriented optimization to enhance self-teaching during distillation, and estimated teacher-guidance reliability drives adaptive student-oriented optimization that down-weights samples with unreliable guidance.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple datasets and model scales show TESD consistently outperforms representative token-level and sequence-level methods.
AI.conclusion: Improving supervision quality is necessary for effective on-policy self-distillation.

title: CFKS: Continuum-Feature Kernel PDE Solvers
summary: Neural-network-based PDE solvers require architectural choices, particularly the number of layers and neurons per layer. Fixing a single Gaussian radial basis function (RBF) feature layer and taking the number of features to the continuum limit removes the need to prescribe a finite feature count or select individual feature centers, thereby reducing representation arbitrariness. Motivated by this principle, we introduce Continuum-Feature Kernel Solver (CFKS), a deterministic framework for PDEs obtained by analytically marginalizing a bounded continuum of Gaussian RBF features. CFKS works directly with the resulting continuum-feature mean kernel and its operator-applied counterparts, parameterized by prescribed Gaussian widths and bounded center distributions. For linear PDEs, CFKS leads to symmetric operator-kernel collocation systems with null-space enforcement of physical constraints. Nonlinear PDEs are addressed through linearized initialization and nonlinear least-squares residual minimization using analytical kernel derivatives and Jacobians. Residual-guided collocation enrichment and sequential space--time-slab marching provide additional resolution strategies, while prescribed multiscale kernel refinement helps resolve localized nonlinear structures. Finite-feature experiments confirm convergence of empirical value and operator Gram matrices toward their continuum counterparts. Numerical studies include oscillatory and multiscale ODEs, irregular-domain Poisson and biharmonic problems, singular perturbations, transient transport equations, and viscous Burgers' equation. The results establish CFKS as a direct computational connection between finite Gaussian-RBF representations and continuum-feature kernel PDE solvers. Codes: this https URL

AI.tldr: CFKS is a deterministic PDE solver framework that analytically marginalizes a continuum of Gaussian RBF features, removing the need to fix a feature count or feature centers, and handles linear and nonlinear PDEs through kernel collocation.
AI.motivation: Neural PDE solvers require architectural choices such as layer count and width, and finite RBF feature sets require prescribing feature counts and centers, which introduces representation arbitrariness.
AI.method: A continuum of Gaussian RBF features is marginalized analytically to give a continuum-feature mean kernel and operator-applied counterparts, parameterized by prescribed Gaussian widths and bounded center distributions. Linear PDEs yield symmetric operator-kernel collocation systems with null-space enforcement of constraints. Nonlinear PDEs use linearized initialization and nonlinear least-squares residual minimization with analytical kernel derivatives and Jacobians, supplemented by residual-guided collocation enrichment, space-time-slab marching and multiscale kernel refinement.
AI.result: Finite-feature experiments confirm convergence of empirical value and operator Gram matrices toward their continuum counterparts. Numerical studies cover oscillatory and multiscale ODEs, irregular-domain Poisson and biharmonic problems, singular perturbations, transient transport equations and viscous Burgers' equation.
AI.conclusion: CFKS establishes a direct computational connection between finite Gaussian-RBF representations and continuum-feature kernel PDE solvers.

title: Logical Guidance of Stochastic Interpolants
summary: Guidance and composition of generative models have applications in visual design, chemistry, and biology. Logical guidance composes conditional scores exactly for diffusion models. However, Flow Matching (FM) and Stochastic Interpolants (SI) learn velocity fields. We show that negation and exclusive disjunction admit exact conditional velocity composition on any interpolant, whereas conjunction, and therefore any formula containing one, is exact on Gaussian paths but in general incurs a drift-interaction error, so composed velocities need not sample the logical target. LOGSI solves this by using score-based re-equilibration as our principled mechanism and falling back to the Gaussian-path velocity rule as an approximate transport predictor. In non-Gaussian bridge problems, generation alternates transport steps with score re-equilibration steps. On image trans fer (EMNIST to CMNIST, CelebA) and QM9 source-to-target molecular editing with logical attribute constraints, LOGSI improves rule conformity at the same network-evaluation budget over composed-velocity baselines, while also improving fidelity on the image tasks. More broadly, LOGSI applies wherever stochastic interpolants need guidance and logical combinations of constraints are natural.

AI.tldr: LOGSI extends logical guidance to stochastic interpolants and flow matching, composing conditional velocities exactly for negation and exclusive disjunction, and correcting conjunction errors by alternating transport steps with score-based re-equilibration steps.
AI.motivation: Logical guidance composes conditional scores exactly for diffusion models, but flow matching and stochastic interpolants learn velocity fields, and naive velocity composition of conjunctions does not in general sample the logical target.
AI.method: Negation and exclusive disjunction admit exact conditional velocity composition on any interpolant. Conjunction is exact on Gaussian paths but incurs a drift-interaction error elsewhere, so LOGSI uses score-based re-equilibration as its principled mechanism and falls back to the Gaussian-path velocity rule as an approximate transport predictor. In non-Gaussian bridge problems, generation alternates transport steps with re-equilibration steps.
AI.result: On EMNIST to CMNIST and CelebA image translation, and on QM9 source-to-target molecular editing with logical attribute constraints, LOGSI improves rule conformity at the same network-evaluation budget over composed-velocity baselines, and also improves fidelity on the image tasks.
AI.conclusion: LOGSI applies wherever stochastic interpolants need guidance and logical combinations of constraints are natural.

title: ExplainCC: Explaining Correlated Clusters by Node Labels
summary: An increasingly important requirement for clustering algorithms is that decisions and outcomes need to be clearly understandable for human users. We address this requirement for the Correlation Clustering (CC) problem, in case the objects to be clustered are accompanied by labels. In CC one seeks to partition a set of objects into clusters based on pairwise similarity and dissimilarity information. Our proposed model only considers clusters that can be explained by a label tree, which is essentially a decision tree that partitions the objects according to labels. The goal is to find an explainable partition of the data that minimizes the CC objective function. We formalize this problem from a theoretical viewpoint, and prove several hardness of approximation results, also when constraining the size of the tree. Our proposed greedy method finds locally optimal splits, and works recursively in a top-down approach. To efficiently compute the best split, we carefully maintain certain counters. An experimental evaluation demonstrates its effectiveness. The proposed algorithm processes graphs with over million edges in a few minutes, can find the ground truth in synthetic data, and is able to produce interpretable clusters in real world networks.

AI.tldr: ExplainCC is a greedy top-down method for correlation clustering that restricts clusters to those explainable by a label tree, a decision tree over node labels, and scales to graphs with over a million edges.
AI.motivation: Clustering outcomes need to be understandable to human users, and existing correlation clustering does not restrict clusters to be explainable by object labels.
AI.method: The model only considers clusters that can be explained by a label tree, which partitions objects according to labels. A greedy method finds locally optimal splits recursively in a top-down manner, and maintains certain counters to compute the best split efficiently.
AI.result: The method processes graphs with over a million edges in a few minutes, recovers the ground truth on synthetic data, and produces interpretable clusters on real-world networks. The problem is shown to have hardness of approximation results, including when the tree size is constrained.
AI.conclusion: The approach yields explainable correlation clustering that is theoretically characterized and practically efficient.

title: On the Generalization Gap of Streaming Federated Learning with Markovian Data
summary: Streaming federated learning (SFL) allows clients to train a shared model from continuously arriving data without retaining large local datasets. Such streams often exhibit temporal dependence, yet its effect on generalization remains poorly understood. In this paper we study the expected generalization gap of the aggregated model when client data follow Markov processes, using information-theoretic and rate-distortion techniques. Our framework accommodates heterogeneous Markovian dynamics across clients and distinguishes temporal dependence from information acquired during local learning. We establish bounds under cross-entropy loss, specializing them to Linear Next-Token Prediction (LNTP) and Self-Attention Next-Token Prediction (SANTP). These results quantify the effects of client count, communication rounds, sample size, data dimension, mixing time, and context length. In particular, they reveal a communication--generalization tradeoff: although frequent aggregation may help optimization, it can weaken generalization guarantees. They also suggest a potential advantage of distributed over centralized streaming learning under a fixed total data budget. Temporal dependence enters through the square root of the mixing time. By analyzing the history-state process, we obtain refined bounds with improved context-length dependence under suitable mixing conditions. Experiments on GPT-style language-model pretraining with TinyStories and real-world time-series forecasting illustrate how collaboration and communication frequency influence generalization under temporal dependence

AI.tldr: This paper derives information-theoretic and rate-distortion generalization bounds for streaming federated learning on Markovian client data, showing a communication-generalization tradeoff and that temporal dependence enters through the square root of the mixing time.
AI.motivation: Streaming federated learning data often exhibits temporal dependence, whose effect on generalization of the aggregated model is poorly understood.
AI.method: The expected generalization gap of the aggregated model is studied when client data follow Markov processes, using information-theoretic and rate-distortion techniques. The framework allows heterogeneous Markovian dynamics across clients and separates temporal dependence from information acquired during local learning. Bounds under cross-entropy loss are specialized to Linear Next-Token Prediction and Self-Attention Next-Token Prediction, and a history-state process analysis gives refined context-length dependence under mixing conditions.
AI.result: The bounds quantify the effects of client count, communication rounds, sample size, data dimension, mixing time and context length. Frequent aggregation may help optimization but can weaken generalization guarantees, and distributed streaming may have an advantage over centralized streaming under a fixed total data budget. Experiments on GPT-style language-model pretraining with TinyStories and on real-world time-series forecasting illustrate these effects.
AI.conclusion: Collaboration and communication frequency shape generalization under temporal dependence, with a tradeoff between communication and generalization.

title: SatOps-Decision: Low-Latency Discriminative Decisions for Onboard Satellite Communication Operations
summary: We propose SatOps-Decision, a method for low-latency decisions in satellite communication operations. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first application of Jev-style general-purpose discriminative decision models to satellite operations, and the accompanying benchmark is the first dedicated to this approach. The learned scorer, a locally adapted Laya encoder with its native decision head, selects among supplied operational answers in a single forward pass. The benchmark combines authored operational contracts, controlled state changes and independently checked labels in an auditable construction. Evaluation prioritizes complete-request latency and raw decision accuracy; all main accuracy comparisons use the same 1,024 held-out questions, separate from training and development. SatOps-Decision's local scorer has a median latency of 90.3 ms per decision, versus 493.9 ms for Qwen3.5-0.8B generation and 388.4 ms for OneJev1.6-0.8B: $5.47\times$ and $4.30\times$ speedups based on median request times in the measured FP32/MPS implementations. Its mean raw accuracy is 85.3%, versus 42.5% for frozen Laya, 40.7% for Qwen generation and 58.6% for OneJev. As cloud accuracy references, original Jev 1.14/1.13 reach 87.4/81.9%.

AI.tldr: SatOps-Decision applies a locally adapted Laya encoder with a discriminative decision head to satellite communication operations, selecting among supplied answers in one forward pass, with a median latency of 90.3 ms and 85.3% mean raw accuracy on a new benchmark.
AI.motivation: Satellite operations need low-latency decisions, and no prior benchmark or application of general-purpose discriminative decision models targeted this domain.
AI.method: A locally adapted Laya encoder with its native decision head scores supplied operational answers in a single forward pass. The accompanying benchmark combines authored operational contracts, controlled state changes and independently checked labels. Evaluation uses complete-request latency and raw decision accuracy on the same 1,024 held-out questions.
AI.result: The local scorer has a median latency of 90.3 ms per decision, versus 493.9 ms for Qwen3.5-0.8B generation and 388.4 ms for OneJev1.6-0.8B, giving 5.47x and 4.30x speedups in the measured FP32/MPS implementations. Its mean raw accuracy is 85.3%, versus 42.5% for frozen Laya, 40.7% for Qwen generation and 58.6% for OneJev. Original Jev 1.14 and 1.13 reach 87.4% and 81.9% as cloud accuracy references.
AI.conclusion: A discriminative decision model can give lower latency and higher accuracy than generative baselines for satellite operations decisions, approaching cloud reference accuracy.

title: Latent Decision Flow Rewards for Clinical Guideline Reasoning
summary: Clinical practice guidelines encode evidence-based recommendations as conditional decision flows, which makes them a natural source of process supervision for training reasoning models. Two properties of clinical reasoning make this supervision difficult to use. A decision flow consistent with a guideline does not by itself determine the correct answer for a given patient, which we call the path--answer gap, and several valid decision flows can support the same clinical decision, which we call path multiplicity. Current training approaches address parts of this problem. Answer rewards supervise the final decision, and process rewards computed against a reference flow supervise one valid decision flow per case. Supervised fine-tuning on annotated flows teaches guideline-consistent reasoning but constrains the model to one trajectory per case and can reduce answer accuracy. We introduce GUIDER, a method that jointly optimizes a decision flow controller and a reasoning policy. The controller learns to generate plausible decision flows from guideline-derived supervision, and the policy learns to generate a decision flow and a final answer for each patient case. GUIDER computes the process reward for the policy over several controller-generated flows, which accounts for path multiplicity, and gates this reward on answer correctness, which addresses the path--answer gap. Joint training allows the process supervision to evolve with the policy. On MedGUIDE, GUIDER with Qwen3-14B achieves 82.5 weighted accuracy and 73.5 guideline adherence, 3.3 and 3.1 points above the strongest clinical reinforcement learning baseline. With Qwen3-14B and Gemma4-12B backbones, GUIDER also improves over CRPO, MRPO, and FaithMed on the out-of-domain benchmarks AMEGA-LLM, RealMedQA, and CancerGUIDE.

AI.tldr: GUIDER jointly trains a decision-flow controller and a reasoning policy for clinical guideline reasoning, computing a process reward over several controller-generated flows gated by answer correctness, and improves over clinical RL baselines on MedGUIDE and out-of-domain benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Guideline decision flows give process supervision, but the path-answer gap (a consistent flow does not determine the correct answer) and path multiplicity (several valid flows support one decision) are not handled by answer rewards, single-reference process rewards, or SFT on annotated flows.
AI.method: A controller learns to generate plausible decision flows from guideline-derived supervision, and a policy generates a decision flow and final answer per patient case. The process reward is computed over several controller-generated flows to account for path multiplicity and is gated on answer correctness to address the path-answer gap. Joint training lets the process supervision evolve with the policy.
AI.result: On MedGUIDE, GUIDER with Qwen3-14B achieves 82.5 weighted accuracy and 73.5 guideline adherence, 3.3 and 3.1 points above the strongest clinical reinforcement learning baseline. With Qwen3-14B and Gemma4-12B backbones, it also improves over CRPO, MRPO and FaithMed on AMEGA-LLM, RealMedQA and CancerGUIDE.
AI.conclusion: Jointly optimized, answer-gated process rewards over multiple flows give better guideline-consistent clinical reasoning than single-trajectory supervision.

title: Adversarial Self-Distillation
summary: Even though current safety-aligned language models are able to refuse harmful requests, their guard can still be bypassed by adversarial perturbations. As in other domains, adversarial training is considered a standard defense. However, due to the autoregressive nature of language generation, supervised finetuning on template refusals does not necessarily teach the model to refuse. Evidence of this is that the adversarially trained model still complies when the attacker injects a compliant prefill. We propose Adversarial Self-Distillation (ASD), which extends a model's own safe behavior to the space of adversarial perturbations. The teacher (the model itself given the clean prompt) can refuse the harmful request by default, or with the help of an additional instruction in its context. ASD distills this knowledge to the student (which is the same model under attack) at the prefixes that the student visits (due to on-policy sampling). These potentially include compliant openings. ASD achieves lower attack success than state-of-the-art defenses with little loss in multiple-choice accuracy, and it becomes able to recover a refusal even after a compliant opening.

AI.tldr: Adversarial Self-Distillation (ASD) makes a safety-aligned language model refuse adversarially perturbed harmful requests by distilling its own clean-prompt refusal behavior to the attacked student at the prefixes the student visits, achieving lower attack success with little loss in multiple-choice accuracy.
AI.motivation: Safety-aligned LLMs can be bypassed by adversarial perturbations, and supervised finetuning on template refusals does not teach the model to refuse, since the adversarially trained model still complies after an injected compliant prefill.
AI.method: The teacher is the model itself given the clean prompt, and it refuses by default or with an additional instruction in context. ASD distills this knowledge to the student, which is the same model under attack, at the prefixes the student visits through on-policy sampling, including potentially compliant openings.
AI.result: ASD achieves lower attack success than state-of-the-art defenses with little loss in multiple-choice accuracy, and the model can recover a refusal even after a compliant opening.
AI.conclusion: Extending a model's own safe behavior to the space of adversarial perturbations, on the states it actually visits, is an effective defense against jailbreaks.

title: Alpha-TCM: A Nine-Layer Framework for TCM-Guided Multimodal Inference and Structured-Prior Auditing
summary: Alpha-TCM makes two contributions under a central thesis: auditable systems should separate domain knowledge, case evidence, probabilistic inference, and downstream authority. First, it proposes a nine-layer TCM-oriented architecture covering semantic definitions, multimodal acquisition, quality control, provenance-bearing knowledge, probabilistic inference, longitudinal updating, constrained decisions, language interaction, and human governance. Each layer specifies its information contract, failure boundary, dependencies, and validation status. This is a system-design proposal, not a claim of complete clinical implementation. Second, a controlled synthetic prototype instantiates Layers 1-5 to audit the knowledge-evidence interface. Four conditional-Gaussian encoders process synthetic tongue images, pulse waveforms, inquiry fields, and text, while a frozen bridge predicts a five-dimensional synthetic outcome.
