A versioned contextual prior is compiled independently of the renderer. Fusion removes duplicated reference-prior information before adding context. Equal-information controls, prior regularization, graded contamination, and structural corruption test contextual benefits, Bayesian specificity, and conflict detection. Across ten paired seeds and four training sizes, contextual knowledge improved mean absolute error over marginal committee fusion at 600 and 1,200 cases, but not over equal-information neural controls. Fully incorrect context harmed performance at every size, while prior effects were inconsistent and conflict scores did not track case-level damage. The results support contextual structure in low-data synthetic settings, not a specifically Bayesian advantage. The prototype establishes no claims about TCM theory or clinical, diagnostic, therapeutic, causal, longitudinal, or transfer validity.

AI.tldr: Alpha-TCM proposes a nine-layer architecture for auditable TCM-guided multimodal inference and tests it with a controlled synthetic prototype, finding that contextual priors beat marginal committee fusion but not equal-information neural controls in low-data synthetic settings.
AI.motivation: Auditable systems need to separate domain knowledge, case evidence, probabilistic inference and downstream authority, and existing TCM-oriented systems lack an explicit architecture with per-layer information contracts and validation status.
AI.method: A nine-layer TCM-oriented architecture covering semantic definitions through human governance, with an information contract, failure boundary and validation status for each layer; a synthetic prototype instantiating layers 1-5 with four conditional-Gaussian encoders (tongue images, pulse waveforms, inquiry fields, text), a frozen bridge predicting a five-dimensional synthetic outcome, and a versioned contextual prior compiled independently of the renderer, with fusion that removes duplicated reference-prior information before adding context.
AI.result: Across ten paired seeds and four training sizes, contextual knowledge improved mean absolute error over marginal committee fusion at 600 and 1,200 cases but not over equal-information neural controls; fully incorrect context harmed performance at every size, prior effects were inconsistent, and conflict scores did not track case-level damage.
AI.conclusion: The results support contextual structure in low-data synthetic settings rather than a specifically Bayesian advantage; the paper is a system-design proposal that makes no claims about TCM theory or about clinical, diagnostic, therapeutic, causal, longitudinal or transfer validity.

title: Rennala NSGD: Asynchronous Stochastic Optimization Beyond Euclidean Geometry
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 111 pages, 2 algorithms, 3 tables
summary: The empirical success of matrix-aware optimizers, such as Muon (Jordan et al., 2024) and Shampoo (arXiv:1802.09568), highlights the potential of non-Euclidean geometry for deep learning, including large language model (LLM) training. Despite this progress, the theoretical understanding of stochastic optimization in general normed spaces remains limited, particularly in distributed settings. We analyze minibatch stochastic gradient descent (SGD) for smooth nonconvex optimization with respect to an arbitrary norm on a finite-dimensional space. Using the framework of $\kappa$-regular normed spaces (arXiv:0809.0813), we derive high-probability oracle complexity bounds under a light-tail condition stated directly in the dual norm induced by the update norm. The bounds make the dependence on geometry explicit through the regularity constant $\kappa$ of the dual space. In the Euclidean case, our bound recovers the standard minibatch SGD rate up to logarithmic factors. For some non-Euclidean geometries and noise models, it is sharper than bounds obtained by converting a Euclidean noise assumption, reducing a linear dimension dependence to a logarithmic one. Building on this framework, we introduce Rennala NSGD, a semi-asynchronous distributed algorithm, and establish wall-clock time complexity guarantees under fixed, heterogeneous worker computation times. In the Euclidean case ($\kappa=1$), our bound matches the parameter dependence of classical Rennala SGD up to logarithmic factors.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes minibatch SGD for smooth nonconvex optimization under an arbitrary norm, deriving high-probability oracle complexity bounds whose geometry dependence is explicit, and introduces Rennala NSGD, a semi-asynchronous distributed algorithm with wall-clock guarantees under heterogeneous worker times.
AI.motivation: Matrix-aware optimizers such as Muon and Shampoo show the value of non-Euclidean geometry for deep learning, but theory for stochastic optimization in general normed spaces, particularly in distributed settings, remains limited.
AI.method: The analysis uses the framework of kappa-regular normed spaces and a light-tail condition stated directly in the dual norm induced by the update norm; the regularity constant kappa of the dual space makes the geometry dependence explicit; Rennala NSGD is built on this framework for fixed, heterogeneous worker computation times.
AI.result: In the Euclidean case the bound recovers the standard minibatch SGD rate up to logarithmic factors; for some non-Euclidean geometries and noise models it is sharper than bounds obtained by converting a Euclidean noise assumption, reducing a linear dimension dependence to a logarithmic one; with kappa = 1 it matches the parameter dependence of classical Rennala SGD up to logarithmic factors.
AI.conclusion: The choice of norm can materially change guarantees for stochastic and distributed optimization, and for some geometries the analysis gives dimension-dependence gains over Euclidean-conversion bounds.

title: Auditable Hierarchical Inference with Multimodal Evidence and Bayesian Active Inquiry
summary: Most multimodal classifiers assume that all useful evidence is available upfront, whereas clinical inquiry is sequential. We present a synthetic evaluation framework separating objective multimodal inference from active inquiry. An objective model maps synthetic tongue, bilateral multipressure pulse, and acoustic observations to eight syndrome families. A provenance-bearing Knowledge Core and training-only answer model support Bayesian narrowing over 33 fine terms using 25 typed questions, while seven safety questions remain outside the diagnostic posterior. Weak shared symptom factors limit fine-term influence on objective phenotypes, and an objective-only probe tests leakage. In a preregistered 600-case synthetic evaluation, objective family accuracy was 87.0%. Cost-sensitive expected information gain (cost-EIG) raised family accuracy to 95.5% and exact fine-term accuracy to 42.5%, versus 92.7% and 33.0% for an unoptimized fixed-order baseline. Selective family accuracy reached 96.9% at 95.3% coverage. However, cost-EIG asked more questions on average than fixed order (9.795 versus 9.352). Missing-audio routing retained 94.0% family accuracy, and a workflow invariant enforced abstention when all objective modalities were absent. Permuting fine-term answer likelihoods reduced family accuracy to 78.7%. Five of six frozen checks passed, but the question-efficiency hypothesis failed. Comparisons are descriptive because only aggregate, not paired case-level, outputs were retained. These results establish a reproducible synthetic workflow, not clinical diagnostic or treatment validity.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a synthetic framework that separates objective multimodal inference from Bayesian active inquiry; cost-sensitive expected information gain improves family and exact fine-term accuracy over a fixed-order questioning baseline, but asks more questions on average.
AI.motivation: Most multimodal classifiers assume all useful evidence is available upfront, whereas clinical inquiry is sequential, so the paper asks how objective multimodal inference should be combined with adaptive questioning.
AI.method: An objective model maps synthetic tongue, bilateral multipressure pulse and acoustic observations to eight syndrome families; a provenance-bearing Knowledge Core and a training-only answer model support Bayesian narrowing over 33 fine terms using 25 typed questions, while seven safety questions remain outside the diagnostic posterior; an objective-only probe tests leakage; cost-sensitive expected information gain (cost-EIG) selects questions.
AI.result: In a preregistered 600-case synthetic evaluation, objective family accuracy was 87.0%; cost-EIG raised family accuracy to 95.5% and exact fine-term accuracy to 42.5%, versus 92.7% and 33.0% for an unoptimized fixed-order baseline; selective family accuracy reached 96.9% at 95.3% coverage; cost-EIG asked more questions on average (9.795 versus 9.352); missing-audio routing retained 94.0% family accuracy; permuting fine-term answer likelihoods reduced family accuracy to 78.7%; five of six frozen checks passed, but the question-efficiency hypothesis failed.
AI.conclusion: The workflow is reproducible in a synthetic setting, but the comparisons are descriptive because only aggregate, not paired case-level, outputs were retained, and the results establish neither clinical diagnostic nor treatment validity.

title: Skillful and realistic precipitation forecasting with reinforced diffusion
summary: Accurate precipitation forecasting remains elusive as physics-based models struggle to resolve mesoscale convection and machine learning often yields physically inconsistent, blurred results that consistently underestimate extreme events. We present FitzRoy, the first system that simultaneously achieves state-of-the-art predictive skill and physical realism over the continental United States. Through a reinforced diffusion framework, where a conditional discrete diffusion model is refined via reinforcement learning, FitzRoy effectively resolves the long-standing trade-off between pointwise accuracy and structural fidelity. Across lead times up to 24 hours, FitzRoy consistently matches or exceeds state-of-the-art models while preserving structural realism and capturing extreme events. Its low-latency inference further enables deployment in real-time operational settings. In case studies such as the 2025 Texas Hill Country floods and the 2026 Missouri floods, FitzRoy signals record-breaking accumulations that existing models largely missed. By bridging the gap between realism and skill, FitzRoy establishes a new frontier for high-fidelity precipitation forecasting.

AI.tldr: FitzRoy is a precipitation forecasting system that refines a conditional discrete diffusion model with reinforcement learning, matching or exceeding state-of-the-art skill while preserving physical realism over the continental United States, and it captured record-breaking floods that existing models largely missed.
AI.motivation: Physics-based models struggle to resolve mesoscale convection, while machine learning forecasts are often physically inconsistent, blurred and biased low for extreme events, leaving a long-standing trade-off between pointwise accuracy and structural fidelity.
AI.method: A reinforced diffusion framework in which a conditional discrete diffusion model is refined via reinforcement learning, designed for low-latency inference in operational settings.
AI.result: Across lead times up to 24 hours, FitzRoy consistently matches or exceeds state-of-the-art models while preserving structural realism and capturing extreme events; in case studies of the 2025 Texas Hill Country floods and the 2026 Missouri floods it signals record-breaking accumulations that existing models largely missed.
AI.conclusion: The authors argue the system bridges the gap between realism and skill and establishes a new frontier for high-fidelity precipitation forecasting; the abstract reports no quantitative skill scores.

title: Loss is Not Behavior: A Unified Output-Space Analysis of Gradient-Based Machine Unlearning
summary: Gradient-based machine unlearning methods typically ``unlearn'' by optimizing forget and retain losses, but similar losses do not necessarily imply similar output-space behavior. Prior work has shown that high forget loss alone does not certify that unlearning has produced retraining-like output behavior. We therefore ask: when a gradient-based unlearner differs from the model that would have been learned on only the retain data, what structure does the resulting output-space gap have? We derive closed-form expressions for this gap in linear regression, with an extension to nonlinear models via a generalized Gauss-Newton and local linearity approximations. Our analysis puts various gradient-based methods under a unified framework parametrized by geometry, reweighting, and projection. Two leverage matrices emerge that capture the forget-retain entanglement under the retrained model geometry: forget self-leverage and retain cross-leverage. We show both theoretically and empirically that these two leverage matrices drive the impact of the forget residual on the forget and retain outputs, and existing methods account for this geometry only partially. Our framework yields precomputable leverage diagnostics for auditing forget sets to identify what type of gradient-based unlearning is likely to be successful.

AI.tldr: The paper derives closed-form expressions for the output-space gap between gradient-based unlearning and retraining in linear regression, extends them to nonlinear models, and shows that two leverage matrices govern the forget and retain outputs, yielding precomputable diagnostics for auditing forget sets.
AI.motivation: Gradient-based unlearning optimizes forget and retain losses, but similar losses do not imply retraining-like output behavior, and prior work showed that high forget loss alone does not certify successful unlearning.
AI.method: Closed-form output-space gap in linear regression, extended to nonlinear models via a generalized Gauss-Newton approximation and local linearity; a unified framework parametrized by geometry, reweighting and projection that covers various gradient-based methods; two leverage matrices, forget self-leverage and retain cross-leverage, defined under the retrained model geometry.
AI.result: Theoretically and empirically, the two leverage matrices drive the impact of the forget residual on the forget and retain outputs, and existing methods account for this geometry only partially.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides precomputable leverage diagnostics for auditing forget sets, identifying what type of gradient-based unlearning is likely to succeed.

title: Routed Continual Learning
summary: Agents deployed at scale repeatedly encounter related problems, and it is natural to let them learn from each other's experience rather than starting over each time. Unfortunately, there is no single way to retain that experience that works well across settings, and no way to know in advance which future problems a given experience will help with. A global history preserves every detail but becomes expensive and mixes together experience that may not belong together; compressing that history into one fixed representation limits the cost but can throw away valuable details. We introduce Routed Continual Learning (Routed CL), an architecture that decides how to partition and retain experience. Past trajectories are grouped into clusters, each of which maintains state using one memory system from a fixed library. Before each run, an LLM-based router either reuses an existing cluster or creates a new one, basing its decision on the problem statement, memory system descriptions, and cluster summaries. We also introduce Context Memory Adapter, which mediates between the memory system and the agentic loop. We evaluate the architecture on a heterogeneous stream that interleaves 301 instances from the six CL-Bench tasks with 97 banking instances from $\tau^3$-Bench. Across four language models and five matched rollouts, Routed Continual Learning raises normalized reward over a single global in-context learning (ICL) history by 15-30% of the maximum attainable normalized reward, achieves higher mean normalized reward than ICL-only clustering, and reduces estimated API cost by 65-72% relative to Global ICL. These results support approaching continual learning as a routing problem that chooses both a learning mechanism and a state cluster rather than committing to one representation globally.

AI.tldr: Routed Continual Learning partitions agent experience into clusters, each maintained by one memory system from a fixed library, with an LLM router choosing reuse or creation per problem; it raises normalized reward over a global in-context history by 15-30% of the maximum attainable normalized reward while cutting estimated API cost by 65-72%.
AI.motivation: Agents deployed at scale should learn from shared experience, but a global history is expensive and mixes unrelated experience, while a single fixed representation can discard valuable detail, and no one retention method works well across settings.
AI.method: Past trajectories are grouped into clusters, each using one memory system from a fixed library; before each run an LLM-based router either reuses an existing cluster or creates a new one, based on the problem statement, memory system descriptions and cluster summaries; a Context Memory Adapter mediates between the memory system and the agentic loop.
AI.result: On a heterogeneous stream interleaving 301 instances from six CL-Bench tasks with 97 banking instances from tau3-Bench, across four language models and five matched rollouts, Routed CL raised normalized reward over a single global ICL history by 15-30% of the maximum attainable normalized reward, achieved higher mean normalized reward than ICL-only clustering, and reduced estimated API cost by 65-72% relative to Global ICL.
AI.conclusion: The results support treating continual learning as a routing problem that chooses both a learning mechanism and a state cluster, rather than committing to one representation globally.

title: Causal Attention on CPU: A Cache-Aware and Load-Balanced Scheduling Kernel for Prefill
summary: Agentic AI drives significant productivity gains across diverse domains, but concurrent long-context prefills from multiple agents can saturate GPU compute resources. Although CPUs offer a viable alternative, existing CPU attention kernels fall short in adapting to multi-tier cache hierarchies and lack effective thread scheduling. To address this, we introduce CACPU, a high-performance attention kernel featuring tiered cache blocking and an in-kernel task dispatching mechanism designed for causal full-sequence prefilling. CACPU achieves up to a 2.01x speedup over PyTorch SDPA, FlexAttention, and SGLang attention kernels. Integrated into SGLang, it reduces Time to First Token (TTFT) of Llama-3.1-8B by up to 1.74x while preserving model accuracy.

AI.tldr: CACPU is a CPU attention kernel for causal full-sequence prefill that uses tiered cache blocking and in-kernel task dispatching; it reaches up to 2.01x speedup over PyTorch SDPA, FlexAttention and SGLang attention kernels and cuts Llama-3.1-8B time to first token by up to 1.74x in SGLang while preserving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Concurrent long-context prefills from multiple agents can saturate GPU compute, and CPUs are a viable alternative, but existing CPU attention kernels adapt poorly to multi-tier cache hierarchies and lack effective thread scheduling.
AI.method: A high-performance attention kernel with tiered cache blocking for multi-tier cache hierarchies and an in-kernel task dispatching mechanism, designed for causal full-sequence prefilling and integrated into SGLang.
AI.result: Up to 2.01x speedup over PyTorch SDPA, FlexAttention and SGLang attention kernels; within SGLang it reduces Time to First Token of Llama-3.1-8B by up to 1.74x while preserving model accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Cache-aware blocking and in-kernel scheduling make CPU attention a practical option for prefill under concurrent agentic workloads.

title: Discovering Jailbreaks via Curriculum of Models
summary: Automated jailbreak discovery aims to find prompts that elicit prohibited behaviors from safety-trained language models, helping developers identify vulnerabilities before deployment. One class of approaches uses reinforcement learning to train an investigator model to generate prompts that elicit a specified behavior from a target model. However, training directly against a safety-trained target is difficult because nearly all prompts are refused, leaving the investigator with a sparse reward signal. Prior work addresses this with the propensity bound (PRBO), a proxy reward estimated by sampling responses from a more compliant target, and then adjusting for how likely those responses would have been under the original target. We introduce Curriculum of Models (CoM), an alternative method that trains the investigator against a sequence of modified versions of the target, progressing gradually from a version that readily exhibits the specified behavior to the original target. For jailbreak discovery, training begins against a target version that rarely refuses harmful requests, and advances to the next, harder version once the investigator reliably elicits the behavior from the current one. We evaluate CoM on elicitation tasks involving CBRN materials, explosives, and illicit drugs, using two open-weight targets, gemma-4-31b-it and gpt-oss-120b. We compare against PRBO and direct training on the original target without a curriculum. When the investigator is trained to elicit a single behavior, CoM finds successful jailbreaks more reliably than either baseline. When trained on multiple behaviors simultaneously, the CoM-trained investigator can elicit held-out behaviors, though PRBO-trained investigators achieve higher success rates. Our results suggest that a simple curriculum over target models offers a promising approach for addressing sparse rewards in rare-behavior elicitation.

AI.tldr: Curriculum of Models (CoM) trains a jailbreak investigator against a sequence of progressively harder versions of the target model to ease the sparse-reward problem in rare-behavior elicitation; it finds successful jailbreaks more reliably than PRBO and direct training for single behaviors, while PRBO-trained investigators reach higher success rates in the multi-behavior setting.
AI.motivation: Training an investigator directly against a safety-trained target yields sparse rewards because nearly all prompts are refused, and the prior propensity bound method (PRBO) addresses this with a proxy reward estimated from a more compliant target.
AI.method: CoM trains the investigator against modified versions of the target, starting from a version that readily exhibits the specified behavior and advancing to the next, harder version once the investigator reliably elicits the behavior, ending at the original target; evaluated on CBRN, explosives and illicit drug elicitation tasks using gemma-4-31b-it and gpt-oss-120b as targets, against PRBO and direct training on the original target.
AI.result: With single-behavior training, CoM finds successful jailbreaks more reliably than either baseline; with multi-behavior training, the CoM-trained investigator can elicit held-out behaviors, though PRBO-trained investigators achieve higher success rates.
AI.conclusion: A simple curriculum over target models is a promising approach to sparse rewards in rare-behavior elicitation, though the multi-behavior results favor PRBO on success rate.

title: What to randomize matters: a controlled study of volume, axis and representation in low-data molecular generation
summary: Chemical language models can struggle to generate new molecules when trained on small datasets, where a model may reproduce training examples rather than learn a useful generative distribution. Randomized SMILES augmentation varies atom traversal, whereas Sequential Attachment-based Fragment Embedding (SAFE) also allows the order of fragment blocks to vary. How these distinct sources of representational variation affect low-data molecular generation has not been clearly studied. Here, using 1,000 seed molecules to train an autoregressive sequence model, we compare canonical SAFE with randomized SAFE at increasing corpus sizes, isolate atom-order and fragment-order axes of SAFE randomization, and compare fully randomized SAFE with randomized SMILES at molecule-by-molecule matched training corpora. Three findings emerge. First, randomization of SAFE alone raises the genuine yield of novel molecules more than 450-fold, turning a model that merely reproduces its training set into a practical molecular generator. Second, the two axes of randomization act jointly rather than additively: atom order alone reaches a tenth, and fragment order alone a seventh, of the genuine yield obtained when both vary, which is four times their combined contribution. Third, at matched corpus size and compute, randomized SAFE delivers 2.8 times the genuine yield of randomized SMILES. Welch tests with Games-Howell post-hoc comparisons resolve every difference on the primary outcomes. In the low-data regime, thus, what one randomizes rather than only how much determines whether augmentation produces new molecules or merely new spellings of the training set.

AI.tldr: Randomizing SAFE raises the genuine yield of novel molecules more than 450-fold for an autoregressive model trained on 1,000 seed molecules, and atom-order and fragment-order randomization act jointly; at matched corpus size and compute, randomized SAFE gives 2.8 times the genuine yield of randomized SMILES.
AI.motivation: Chemical language models trained on small datasets tend to reproduce training examples rather than learn a useful generative distribution, and how distinct sources of representational variation (SMILES atom traversal versus SAFE fragment order) affect low-data generation has not been clearly studied.
AI.method: Using 1,000 seed molecules to train an autoregressive sequence model, the authors compare canonical SAFE with randomized SAFE at increasing corpus sizes, isolate atom-order and fragment-order axes of SAFE randomization, and compare fully randomized SAFE with randomized SMILES at molecule-by-molecule matched training corpora, using Welch tests with Games-Howell post-hoc comparisons.
AI.result: Randomizing SAFE alone raises the genuine yield of novel molecules more than 450-fold; atom order alone reaches one tenth, and fragment order alone one seventh, of the yield obtained when both vary; at matched corpus size and compute, randomized SAFE delivers 2.8 times the genuine yield of randomized SMILES; the statistical tests resolve every difference on the primary outcomes.
AI.conclusion: In the low-data regime, which representation is randomized matters, not only how much, in determining whether augmentation produces new molecules or merely new spellings of the training set.

title: Discovery of Diverse and Realistic Financial Tail-Risk Using Generative Flow Networks
summary: Accurate modeling of rare, high-impact financial events is essential for robust risk management. Sampling-based techniques such as Sequential Markov Chain Monte Carlo (SMCMC) generate diverse scenarios but inefficiently explore high-risk regions, while Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) converges on narrow sets of scenarios, limiting diversity. We present GRID, which uses Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) -- samplers that draw objects in proportion to a reward -- to systematically generate diverse and realistic financial tail-risk scenarios. Building on continuous GFlowNets, GRID introduces a flexible mixture-policy architecture with variable-specific distribution families for high-dimensional, sequential macro-financial data, together with plausibility constraints that keep generated trajectories realistic. A central practical advantage is robustness to reward-proxy imperfection: because GFlowNets sample proportionally rather than maximize, they remain broadly exploratory even when the oracle's out-of-sample accuracy is low -- an unavoidable reality in financial forecasting. On three real-world crises, GRID improves scenario diversity, realism, and tail-risk coverage over RL and MCMC baselines, and ablations over oracle architectures and distribution families yield practical insights into continuous GFlowNet behavior under noisy rewards.

AI.tldr: GRID uses continuous GFlowNets with a mixture-policy architecture and plausibility constraints to generate diverse, realistic financial tail-risk scenarios; on three real-world crises it improves scenario diversity, realism and tail-risk coverage over RL and MCMC baselines and remains exploratory under noisy reward oracles.
AI.motivation: Sampling-based methods such as Sequential MCMC explore high-risk regions inefficiently, while deep reinforcement learning converges on narrow sets of scenarios, limiting the diversity needed to model rare, high-impact financial events.
AI.method: Builds on continuous GFlowNets, which sample objects in proportion to a reward, adding a flexible mixture-policy architecture with variable-specific distribution families for high-dimensional sequential macro-financial data, together with plausibility constraints that keep generated trajectories realistic; ablations examine oracle architectures and distribution families.
AI.result: On three real-world crises, GRID improves scenario diversity, realism and tail-risk coverage over RL and MCMC baselines, and the ablations yield insights into continuous GFlowNet behavior under noisy rewards.
AI.conclusion: Proportional sampling makes GRID robust to reward-proxy imperfection, which matters in financial forecasting where the oracle's out-of-sample accuracy is often low.

title: Contextual Embeddings Beyond the Gold Chunk
summary: Contextual embeddings represent chunks of a document with respect to the document's global context. These models are typically trained and evaluated under the assumption that a relevant document contains only a single relevant chunk. In this work, we argue that in real-world use cases a retriever should not only find answers spread over several chunks but also surface the evidence needed to verify them. To address this, we introduce pplx-embed-v2-context, a family of contextual embedding models trained by distilling graded chunk-level relevance from a query-aware context compression model. This removes the need for gold-chunk labels and makes the training targets independent of the chunking. We utilize a vision-language backbone for training and release pplx-embed-v2-context in 9B and 0.6B sizes with compatible embedding spaces. On the evaluation side, we introduce two benchmarks that label both the chunks that answer a query and the evidence needed to verify the answer. Context-bench is a controlled diagnostic, and Q2D-Chunk is built from real-world search queries. To encourage further research, we also publish Q2D-Chunk as a public leaderboard. Our 9B model sets a new state of the art on both benchmarks and ConTEB. We find that the visual retrieval capabilities of our 9B model transfer from its vision-language base model and propose to extend chunking to image inputs. We demonstrate that our models achieve state-of-the-art performance among dense retrievers on visual ViDoRe-V3 and that performance improves with granular image chunking.

AI.tldr: pplx-embed-v2-context is a family of contextual embedding models trained by distilling graded chunk-level relevance from a query-aware compression model; its 9B model sets a new state of the art on two new benchmarks and ConTEB, and chunking is extended to images with state-of-the-art dense retrieval on visual ViDoRe-V3.
AI.motivation: Contextual embedding models are typically trained and evaluated assuming a relevant document contains only one relevant chunk, whereas real use requires finding answers spread across several chunks and the evidence needed to verify them.
AI.method: Models trained by distilling graded chunk-level relevance from a query-aware context compression model, which removes the need for gold-chunk labels and makes the training targets independent of chunking; a vision-language backbone; released in 9B and 0.6B sizes with compatible embedding spaces; two benchmarks, Context-bench (a controlled diagnostic) and Q2D-Chunk (built from real search queries, published as a public leaderboard).
AI.result: The 9B model sets a new state of the art on Context-bench, Q2D-Chunk and ConTEB; its visual retrieval capability transfers from the vision-language base model; it achieves state-of-the-art performance among dense retrievers on visual ViDoRe-V3, and performance improves with granular image chunking.
AI.conclusion: Relevance distillation without gold-chunk labels, together with chunking extended to image inputs, supports retrieval of both answers and the evidence that verifies them.

title: Geometric Time Score Estimators: Bridging Self-Predictive Representations and Generative Occupancy Models For Reinforcement Learning
summary: In reinforcement learning (RL), temporal reasoning is essential for estimating the density of future outcomes under a policy's occupancy measure. While self-predictive representations have been a dominant paradigm for occupancy density estimation, we find that they yield surprisingly poor estimates. On the other hand, generative occupancy models can produce remarkably accurate samples from the occupancy measure. Yet, they cannot easily recover occupancy densities, limiting their use for control despite their expressivity. In this paper, we propose Geometric Time Score Estimators (GTSE), a framework that bridges the two paradigms by learning occupancy density estimators along probability paths. We analyze how GTSE implicitly induces better occupancy estimators through improved representation learning and show how to directly extract self-predictive representations from this framework. Through experiments across several locomotion and manipulation tasks, we show that GTSE improves performance over state-of-the-art methods by $2\times$ to $6\times$ in goal-conditioned RL settings, and that the representations learned using our framework transfer effectively to downstream RL tasks. Website: this https URL

AI.tldr: GTSE learns occupancy density estimators along probability paths, bridging self-predictive representations and generative occupancy models in RL; it improves over state-of-the-art methods by 2x to 6x in goal-conditioned RL, and its learned representations transfer to downstream RL tasks.
AI.motivation: Self-predictive representations are a dominant paradigm for occupancy density estimation but yield surprisingly poor estimates, while generative occupancy models sample accurately but cannot easily recover densities, which limits their use for control.
AI.method: The Geometric Time Score Estimators framework learns occupancy density estimators along probability paths; the authors analyze how it implicitly induces better occupancy estimators through improved representation learning, and show how to extract self-predictive representations directly from the framework.
AI.result: Across several locomotion and manipulation tasks, GTSE improves over state-of-the-art methods by 2x to 6x in goal-conditioned RL settings, and the representations learned with the framework transfer effectively to downstream RL tasks.
AI.conclusion: GTSE unifies occupancy density estimation and representation learning for RL, and its representations are useful beyond the original tasks.

title: Structural-Test Geometry as an Inductive Bias for Partially Observable World Models
summary: Predictive world-model objectives need not organize latent histories according to distinctions required for later control. With privileged simulator access during training, should response-derived structural information be predicted, decoded, or imposed directly on latent geometry--and how do these choices compare with structured belief distillation? We define posterior-marginalized structural tests whose response distributions induce a pseudometric over histories, then train quotient-preserving (QP) world models by aligning shared latent Euclidean distances to that metric. Across a fixed six-task diagnostic suite, the largest differences appear under held-out structural variation: QP improves planning success by 26.1 points $[21.5,30.7]$ over metric decoding and 6.4 points $[3.8,9.0]$ over structured belief distillation. On GridWorld, metric decoding accurately recovers held-out structural distances ($\rho=.91$) while its native latent geometry remains more distorted than QP's (paired IQD difference $.22$ $[.20,.24]$), showing that relational recoverability and direct geometric alignment can diverge.

AI.tldr: Quotient-preserving (QP) world models align latent Euclidean distances to a pseudometric induced by posterior-marginalized structural tests, improving planning under held-out structural variation; the paper also shows that relational recoverability and direct geometric alignment can diverge.
AI.motivation: Predictive world-model objectives need not organize latent histories by the distinctions that later control requires, and it is unclear whether response-derived structural information should be predicted, decoded or imposed directly on latent geometry, or how these choices compare with structured belief distillation.
AI.method: Defines posterior-marginalized structural tests whose response distributions induce a pseudometric over histories, then trains QP world models by aligning shared latent Euclidean distances to that metric; compared against metric decoding and structured belief distillation on a fixed six-task diagnostic suite.
AI.result: The largest differences appear under held-out structural variation: QP improves planning success by 26.1 points (95% interval 21.5 to 30.7) over metric decoding and by 6.4 points (3.8 to 9.0) over structured belief distillation; on GridWorld, metric decoding recovers held-out structural distances accurately (rho 0.91) while its native latent geometry remains more distorted than QP's (paired IQD difference 0.22, interval 0.20 to 0.24).
AI.conclusion: Direct geometric alignment to structural tests can yield better planning than relational decoding, and accurate relational recovery does not guarantee a well-organized latent geometry.

title: Lev-3B: A Data Recipe for Compact Probabilistic Log Decision Models
summary: Many log-analysis tasks involve choosing among known options, such as detecting anomalous sessions or identifying attack techniques, and benefit from calibrated probabilities. We present Lev-3B, an open 3B-parameter decision model built on Granite-4.1-3B-Base with a shared pointer readout, and study its training recipe. The recipe has two key parts. First, training follows a curriculum: the model learns bounded natural-language decisions, using no log data, before it sees any logs. Second, the log stage mixes the target tasks with general log data spanning 35 auxiliary tasks unrelated to either evaluation task. We evaluate one shared checkpoint on sources seen in training and on sources excluded from training, calibration and model selection. The two-stage recipe transfers substantially better than training on log data alone. Adding general log data improves performance on excluded sources. At a fraction of their serving cost, Lev-3B outperforms prompted frontier models on anomaly detection, including on an excluded logging system, but trails them on attack-technique classification. Its probabilities are well calibrated on familiar sources, but on the excluded logging system it confidently misses anomalies. We release the checkpoint, recipe, data manifests, and prediction-level artifacts.

AI.tldr: Lev-3B is an open 3B-parameter log decision model trained with a curriculum that moves from bounded natural-language decisions to log data mixed with general log tasks; it outperforms prompted frontier models on anomaly detection at a fraction of their serving cost but trails them on attack-technique classification.
AI.motivation: Log-analysis tasks that involve choosing among known options, such as detecting anomalous sessions or identifying attack techniques, benefit from calibrated probabilities, and the paper studies how to train a compact decision model for them.
AI.method: Built on Granite-4.1-3B-Base with a shared pointer readout; a two-stage recipe in which the model first learns bounded natural-language decisions with no log data, then a log stage mixes the target tasks with general log data spanning 35 auxiliary tasks unrelated to the evaluation tasks; one shared checkpoint is evaluated on seen sources and on sources excluded from training, calibration and model selection.
AI.result: The two-stage recipe transfers substantially better than training on log data alone, and adding general log data improves performance on excluded sources; Lev-3B outperforms prompted frontier models on anomaly detection, including on an excluded logging system, but trails them on attack-technique classification; its probabilities are well calibrated on familiar sources but it confidently misses anomalies on the excluded logging system.
AI.conclusion: A compact model can be competitive for log decisions, but good calibration on familiar sources does not guarantee reliability on unseen logging systems; the authors release the checkpoint, recipe, data manifests and prediction-level artifacts.

title: Planned Restlessness: Delayed Meta Bandits with Budgets
summary: We study episodic finite-horizon Bayesian bandits, or meta-bandits, with independent arms. Each episode draws fresh arm qualities from unknown recurring priors. Observations arrive after known delays, and plays obey hard per-episode caps and total budgets. A play earns reward and informs both the current quality and the recurring prior: the learner must explore, use, and generalize. We formulate a common planning optimization over learning trajectories. Its LP relaxation values experiments through current reward, resource consumption and continuation: the value of future decisions from the learning state produced. Dual prices separate the arms into local programs and certify every admissible policy, including hierarchical Thompson sampling. Execution enforces the hard constraints while preserving the promised learning transitions or accounting for their loss. The framework also represents risk-sensitive objectives and prices purchased observations and buyout options. Delayed reports create planned restlessness: an arm's information changes while it is not played, through reports of its own earlier plays arriving on a known calendar. For stationary priors, finite reward alphabets, bounded report lag and nonbinding budgets, posterior sampling over the recurring priors bounds the price of not knowing them by $O(\sqrt{N})$ over $N$ episodes, with other parameters fixed. For one undelayed $T$-step episode with arms capped at $T/X$ plays each, we obtain the LP-relative approximation factor $1+(2\pi X)^{-1/2}+O(X^{-1})$, improving previous factors, with a matching lower bound for the leading term.

AI.tldr: The paper formulates an LP-based planning framework for episodic Bayesian bandits with delayed reports and hard budgets, shows that posterior sampling bounds the price of not knowing recurring priors by O(sqrt(N)) over N episodes, and gives an LP-relative approximation factor of 1 + (2 pi X)^(-1/2) + O(1/X) for one undelayed episode.
AI.motivation: Meta-bandit learners must explore, exploit and generalize across episodes with unknown recurring priors, under delayed observations and per-episode and total budgets, and prior work offered weaker approximation factors without a common planning optimization covering these constraints.
AI.method: A common planning optimization over learning trajectories whose LP relaxation values an experiment through its current reward, resource consumption and the value of the continuation learning state; dual prices separate the arms into local programs and certify every admissible policy, including hierarchical Thompson sampling; execution enforces the hard constraints while preserving the promised learning transitions or accounting for their loss; the framework also represents risk-sensitive objectives and prices purchased observations and buyout options.
AI.result: For stationary priors, finite reward alphabets, bounded report lag and nonbinding budgets, posterior sampling over the recurring priors bounds the price of not knowing them by O(sqrt(N)) over N episodes; for one undelayed T-step episode with arms capped at T/X plays each, the LP-relative approximation factor is 1 + (2 pi X)^(-1/2) + O(1/X), improving previous factors, with a matching lower bound for the leading term.
AI.conclusion: The LP framework and its dual pricing certify near-optimal policy structure for delayed Bayesian bandits with budgets, and delayed reports create planned restlessness, in which an arm's information changes while it is not being played.

title: Communication-Efficient Clustered Federated Learning in Non-IID Wireless Networks
summary: Current and emerging mobile networks face increasing privacy, scalability, and performance challenges as distributed learning becomes essential for advanced 6G services. These challenges are amplified by the presence of non-IID data, naturally arising in heterogeneous wireless environments, that degrade the performance of standard Federated Learning (FL) approaches. To address non-IID data across clients, we propose a Clustered Federated Learning (CFL) framework that assigns clients to specialized models during training. Data-domain clustering initializes model-based clustering, enabling identification and exploitation of client similarities without sharing raw data while reducing communication cost. Motivated by mmWave beam selection, we evaluate our methods on a wireless simulation dataset (DeepMIMO) and complement it with two non-IID benchmarks (FEMNIST, Rotated CIFAR-10) to isolate different non-IID characteristics. Our best configurations improve accuracy over IFCA by 4.8 pp on DeepMIMO and 10.6 pp on FEMNIST while reducing downlink data volume by 83.1 % on FEMNIST compared to IFCA. We demonstrate that different clustering strategies suit different non-IID characteristics. These results show that our CFL methods enable resource-efficient, and high-performance distributed learning in future 6G networks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a clustered federated learning framework for non-IID wireless clients in which data-domain clustering initializes model-based clustering; its best configurations beat IFCA by 4.8 points on DeepMIMO and 10.6 points on FEMNIST while cutting downlink data volume by 83.1% on FEMNIST.
AI.motivation: Non-IID data arising in heterogeneous wireless environments degrades standard federated learning, and privacy, scalability and performance challenges grow as distributed learning becomes essential for 6G services.
AI.method: Clustered federated learning that assigns clients to specialized models during training; data-domain clustering initializes model-based clustering without sharing raw data and reduces communication cost; evaluated on DeepMIMO (a wireless simulation motivated by mmWave beam selection) and on two non-IID benchmarks, FEMNIST and Rotated CIFAR-10.
AI.result: The best configurations improve accuracy over IFCA by 4.8 percentage points on DeepMIMO and 10.6 percentage points on FEMNIST, and reduce downlink data volume by 83.1% on FEMNIST compared with IFCA; different clustering strategies suit different non-IID characteristics.
AI.conclusion: The CFL methods offer resource-efficient, high-performance distributed learning for future 6G networks, and the best clustering strategy depends on the type of non-IID heterogeneity.

title: The Utility of Physics-Informed Machine Learning in Solar Power Production Forecasting
summary: Physics-informed machine learning (PIML) and hybrid modeling have attracted significant attention as approaches for combining physical knowledge with the flexibility of deep learning. In this work, we investigate whether these approaches deliver their commonly claimed benefits for large-scale photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting. We develop two hybrid forecasting architectures that integrate the ADR physical PV efficiency model with the TSMixer neural forecasting architecture through feature augmentation and residual learning. The proposed models are evaluated on a dataset comprising over 3 million samples from 3,713 PV installations across 33 European countries. We assess convergence speed, forecasting accuracy, transferability across geographical regions, and data efficiency. Although the physics-informed models seem to exhibit slightly faster convergence during training, they do not achieve consistent improvements in test-set accuracy, generalization, or performance under limited training data compared to the purely data-driven baseline. These findings suggest that, for modern deep forecasting architectures trained on large datasets, explicitly incorporating the ADR physical model provides limited practical benefit for day-ahead PV forecasting.

AI.tldr: Two hybrid models that combine the ADR physical PV efficiency model with the TSMixer forecasting architecture show little practical benefit over a purely data-driven baseline for day-ahead PV forecasting; the physics-informed variants converge slightly faster but do not improve test accuracy, generalization or data efficiency.
AI.motivation: Physics-informed machine learning and hybrid modeling are widely claimed to combine physical knowledge with the flexibility of deep learning, but their benefits for large-scale photovoltaic power forecasting have not been established.
AI.method: Two hybrid architectures integrate the ADR physical PV efficiency model with the TSMixer neural forecasting architecture through feature augmentation and residual learning, evaluated on over 3 million samples from 3,713 PV installations across 33 European countries.
AI.result: The physics-informed models show slightly faster convergence during training but no consistent improvement in test-set accuracy, generalization, transferability across geographical regions or performance under limited training data, compared with the purely data-driven baseline.
AI.conclusion: For modern deep forecasting architectures trained on large datasets, explicitly incorporating the ADR physical model provides limited practical benefit for day-ahead PV forecasting.

title: Why Speculative Decoding Works Better Than Predicted on Sparse MoE Models
comment: Accepted as at NeurIPS 2026 main track conference
summary: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates autoregressive inference by leveraging the memory bound nature of decoding, verifying multiple draft tokens in a single forward pass. For mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, prior work predicts a concave speedup-batch size relationship, with gains peaking at intermediate batch sizes due to expert saturation. We evaluate this across 10 sparse MoE models (30B--1T parameters, 8--512 experts) and find recent fine-grained models break this trend, showing higher speedup at low batch size. We find verification cost is governed not only by activated-expert bytes, but also by temporal overlap across draft tokens and GPU execution dynamics. At low batch size, MoE layers in fine-grained models account for a much smaller share of runtime than of weights; on H100, kernel profiling attributes this mainly to higher bandwidth utilization of MoE kernels relative to attention, with L2 absorbing repeated reads of co-routed experts. Across draft tokens, routing overlap further reduces the unique experts activated during verification relative to independence assumptions. We model this effect using a maximum-entropy Iterative Proportional Fitting (IPF) framework that predicts unique expert counts from routing-overlap statistics with less than 4\% error, and substantially narrows the gap to real-model curves and captures the qualitative low-batch trend from synthetic routing.

AI.tldr: Speculative decoding on sparse MoE models often beats predictions from the prior concave speedup-batch-size model, especially for recent fine-grained models at low batch size; a maximum-entropy IPF framework predicts unique expert counts from routing-overlap statistics with less than 4% error.
AI.motivation: Prior work predicts a concave speedup-batch-size relationship for speculative decoding on MoE models, with gains peaking at intermediate batch sizes due to expert saturation, but recent fine-grained models break this trend.
AI.method: Evaluation across 10 sparse MoE models (30B to 1T parameters, 8 to 512 experts), kernel profiling on H100, and a maximum-entropy Iterative Proportional Fitting framework that predicts unique expert counts from routing-overlap statistics.
AI.result: Fine-grained models show higher speedup at low batch size; at low batch size their MoE layers account for a much smaller share of runtime than of weights, which kernel profiling attributes mainly to higher bandwidth utilization of MoE kernels relative to attention, with L2 absorbing repeated reads of co-routed experts; routing overlap further reduces the unique experts activated during verification; the IPF model predicts unique expert counts with less than 4% error, substantially narrows the gap to real-model curves and captures the low-batch trend from synthetic routing.
AI.conclusion: Verification cost is governed not only by activated-expert bytes but also by temporal overlap across draft tokens and GPU execution dynamics, which explains why speculative decoding can exceed earlier predictions on fine-grained MoE models.

title: Benchmarking Graph Neural Networks for AC Power Flow: The Role of Inductive Biases and Physical Constraints
summary: Fast and accurate models for AC power flow (ACPF) are increasingly important as modern electrical grids require more frequent system analyses. Graph neural networks (GNNs) naturally exploit electrical grid topology, yet the effects of architectural design choices on predictive performance remain poorly understood given differences in graph representations and evaluation settings across studies. We present a unified benchmark of representative GNN architectures for ACPF prediction under a common experimental framework. All models use identical preprocessing and training procedures and comparable parameter budgets, isolating the impact of message-passing mechanisms and inductive biases. We also analyze errors by distance from the slack bus and systematically ablate key design components. We evaluate predictive accuracy and physical consistency on the IEEE 14-bus and IEEE 118-bus systems. Results indicate that anisotropic message-passing architectures offer the most favorable trade-off between predictive accuracy and physical consistency under the studied parameter and topology constraints. Explicit edge features encoding line impedances and global context aggregation are particularly important for representing electrical interactions and system-wide dependencies, especially for voltage-angle predictions on the topologically bottlenecked IEEE-118 grid. Under a budget with approximately fixed parameters, two or three message-passing layers generally provide the best balance between depth and representation width, while additional depth offers no consistent improvement. Ablations also show that standard residual and root connections are not necessarily beneficial in shallow models, and that aggregation operators involve trade-offs between statistical accuracy and physical consistency. These results provide practical guidelines for designing graph-based power system models.

AI.tldr: A unified benchmark of GNN architectures for AC power flow, run under a common experimental framework, finds that anisotropic message-passing gives the best trade-off between predictive accuracy and physical consistency on the IEEE 14-bus and 118-bus systems, with explicit edge features and two or three layers generally working best.
AI.motivation: GNNs naturally exploit electrical grid topology for fast AC power flow, but the effects of architectural design choices are poorly understood because graph representations and evaluation settings differ across studies.
AI.method: A unified benchmark with identical preprocessing, training procedures and comparable parameter budgets, isolating message-passing mechanisms and inductive biases; error analysis by distance from the slack bus; systematic ablations of key design components; evaluation of predictive accuracy and physical consistency on IEEE 14-bus and 118-bus systems.
AI.result: Anisotropic message-passing architectures offer the most favorable trade-off; explicit edge features encoding line impedances and global context aggregation matter, especially for voltage-angle prediction on the topologically bottlenecked IEEE-118 grid; under approximately fixed parameters, two or three message-passing layers give the best depth-width balance, and extra depth brings no consistent gain; residual and root connections are not necessarily beneficial in shallow models; aggregation operators trade statistical accuracy against physical consistency.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides practical guidelines for designing graph-based power system models.

title: Rethinking GFlowNet Training: Negative Reinforce Dynamics
summary: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) are models that learn to sample discrete objects proportional to a target reward. They are trained by minimizing balance errors over sampled trajectories, which inherently ties correctness to exploration: if a region is not visited, balance cannot be enforced there. Adaptive exploration is therefore crucial, yet standard training relies on a semi-gradient update that treats the sampling distribution as fixed at each optimization step. On the other hand, the full gradient reveals a second mechanism that reduces the observed errors in an anti-exploratory manner. In this paper, we establish a connection between the full gradient and min-min dynamics between the GFlowNet and a decoupled sampler, showing that the sampler reduces observed violations by avoiding high-error regions. This insight motivates a bridge between two-player games and single-policy dynamics, which underpins the design of our proposed method, Negative Reinforce Dynamics (NRD). By tying the parameters of an adversarial game together, we recover a single-policy dynamic that extends exploration while maintaining correctness. In standard benchmarks, our method outperforms existing approaches in both convergence speed and exploration efficiency, without training a separate teacher or auxiliary exploration policy.

AI.tldr: Negative Reinforce Dynamics (NRD) trains GFlowNets through a single-policy dynamic derived from min-min dynamics between the GFlowNet and a decoupled sampler, extending exploration while maintaining correctness; on standard benchmarks it outperforms existing approaches in convergence speed and exploration efficiency without a separate teacher or exploration policy.
AI.motivation: Standard GFlowNet training uses a semi-gradient update that treats the sampling distribution as fixed at each step, which ties correctness to exploration, so adaptive exploration is crucial, yet the second mechanism revealed by the full gradient is not exploited.
AI.method: Connects the full gradient to min-min dynamics between the GFlowNet and a decoupled sampler, showing the sampler reduces observed violations by avoiding high-error regions; bridges two-player games and single-policy dynamics by tying the parameters of an adversarial game together, recovering a single-policy dynamic.
AI.result: On standard benchmarks the proposed method, Negative Reinforce Dynamics, outperforms existing approaches in both convergence speed and exploration efficiency, without training a separate teacher or auxiliary exploration policy.
AI.conclusion: Tying the parameters of the adversarial game yields a practical single-policy method that extends GFlowNet exploration while preserving correctness.

title: Fed-IGTD: A federated learning-based framework for tabular-to-image encoding
summary: Tabular-to-image encoding methods, which transform tabular data into image-like representations, have shown promising results in predictive tasks. Despite their benefits, these methods follow a centralized paradigm, in which the data are collected and models are trained on a central device. This raises privacy and security concerns, particularly the risk of data leakage, unauthorized data collection and access to users' private information. Federated Learning (FL) provides a decentralized framework in which multiple clients jointly optimize a shared model without directly sharing training data. We introduce Fed-IGTD, a horizontal FL-based approach in which clients share a common feature space and upload only local statistics, from which the server reconstructs the global correlation matrix and obtains a feature-to-pixel mapping to train a convolutional neural network via Federated Averaging (FedAvg). We studied two differential privacy (DP) mechanisms: (i) a one-shot Gaussian mechanism protecting the correlation-aggregation step; and (ii) a client-level DP-FedAvg variant protecting the training with privacy loss composed via a Renyi-DP accountant. We evaluated Fed-IGTD on five datasets under a systematic sweep of non-IID severity and privacy budgets. Privacy protection applied to the mapping-construction step has little impact on predictive performance. By contrast, DP-FedAvg substantially degrades utility at moderate privacy budgets with a small client cohort (K=5). Ablation study indicates that this degradation is driven mainly by the injected noise rather than by uniform averaging or update clipping. Macro-F1 exhibits sensitivity to performance degradation than accuracy under non-IID heterogeneity and class imbalance.

AI.tldr: Fed-IGTD is a horizontal federated learning framework for tabular-to-image encoding in which clients share only local statistics and the server builds a feature-to-pixel mapping for a CNN trained with FedAvg, with two differential privacy options. Privacy on the mapping step has little effect on accuracy, while DP-FedAvg substantially degrades utility at moderate privacy budgets with a small client cohort.
AI.motivation: Existing tabular-to-image encoding methods follow a centralized paradigm that collects data on a central device, raising privacy, data leakage and unauthorized access risks.
AI.method: Clients with a common feature space upload only local statistics, from which the server reconstructs the global correlation matrix, obtains a feature-to-pixel mapping and trains a convolutional neural network via Federated Averaging. Two differential privacy mechanisms are studied: a one-shot Gaussian mechanism on the correlation aggregation, and a client-level DP-FedAvg variant with Renyi-DP accounting.
AI.result: Evaluated on five datasets under a sweep of non-IID severity and privacy budgets. Privacy protection on the mapping-construction step has little impact on predictive performance, whereas DP-FedAvg substantially degrades utility at moderate budgets with K=5 clients; an ablation attributes this mainly to the injected noise. Macro-F1 is more sensitive than accuracy to degradation under non-IID heterogeneity and class imbalance.
AI.conclusion: Privacy can be applied to the mapping-construction step at little cost, but client-level DP training with few clients is costly, so the privacy-utility trade-off depends strongly on where noise is injected.

title: Assessing feature scorer results on high-dimensional datasets with t-SNE
summary: While vast literature on high-dimensional data visualization is available, there are not many works regarding the visualization of feature scorers and their results. Feature scorers are algorithms that assign numerical importance to each feature of multi-dimensional datasets. These importance scores can be used in several applications, such as feature selection, knowledge discovery, and machine learning interpretability. There are several feature scorers to choose from, and often no single metric or ground truth is available to guarantee the quality of their results. In this scenario, visualization can become valuable to support the decision of which method to choose and how good its results are. For this goal, this work presents "weighted t-SNE." It modifies the relationship between data points in the embedded 2D space to reflect the importance of each dimension of the original datasets as assessed by a feature scorer. This research discusses how to implement weighted t-SNE, proposes the silhouette coefficient as a numerical evaluation of the results, and shows several examples of its use in practice. Synthetic and real-world tabular datasets are used in the experiments together with nine feature scorers, ranging from Mutual Information to neural networks. Each feature scorer produces unique visualizations, and weighted t-SNE can be used to compare and choose the one that better suits a given dataset and task. Weighted t-SNE can also visually show the importance of features learned by machine learning models and help us see how they are organizing the data, increasing their interpretability.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes weighted t-SNE, which reweights relationships between points in a 2D embedding by the importance each feature scorer assigns to each dimension, so the resulting visualizations help compare and choose feature scorers.
AI.motivation: Feature scorers assign numerical importance to features, but there is often no single metric or ground truth to judge their quality, and little prior work visualizes their results.
AI.method: Weighted t-SNE modifies the relationships between data points in the embedded 2D space to reflect per-dimension importance from a feature scorer, and the silhouette coefficient is proposed as a numerical evaluation of the embeddings.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic and real-world tabular datasets with nine feature scorers, ranging from Mutual Information to neural networks, show that each scorer produces a distinct visualization, so weighted t-SNE can be used to compare scorers and choose the one that suits a dataset and task.
AI.conclusion: Weighted t-SNE supports choosing feature scorers for a given task and can also visualize feature importance learned by machine learning models, improving interpretability.

title: Representation Complexity Along Learning Trajectories: Trading Width for Precision and Time
summary: What computational role does overparameterisation play during learning? Information-plane analyses suggest that neural networks can traverse representations substantially more complex than those required by their final predictors. We explore when this transient complexity serves a computational purpose by comparing the representation complexity needed for prediction with that needed to make an unknown target statistically visible through gradient feedback. We introduce an oracle model of neural network learning and use Kolmogorov \(n\)-widths to quantify effective representation complexity. Our main technical result transfers complexity bounds from the forward representation to the corresponding gradient-query features. Combined with statistical-query lower bounds, this gives a task-agnostic lower bound on the initial effective width required for target-dependent gradient information to become detectable. For \(k\)-sparse parity in \(D\) dimensions, a known target admits an \(O(k)\)-width representation, while the general bound already implies a polynomial separation between representation and discovery. We then exploit parity's invariance under coordinatewise sign reflections to identify a sharper unsigned effective width, which removes sign distinctions invisible to the parity information channel. At a transfer-compatible measurement resolution, its critical scale is \(\widetilde{\Theta}_k\left( D^{k-1}\tau^2 \right)\), up to logarithmic factors. Thus, the representation resources required to discover a predictor can substantially exceed those required to represent it once learned. Interpreting precision through accumulation over fresh samples yields a corresponding width-time frontier. Experiments support the predicted dimension dependence and examine how optimisation and generalisation depart from this idealised frontier.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that the representation complexity needed to discover a target during learning can far exceed the complexity needed to represent the predictor once learned, illustrated by a polynomial separation for k-sparse parity.
AI.motivation: Information-plane analyses suggest networks traverse representations more complex than their final predictors, but it is unclear whether this transient complexity serves a computational purpose.
AI.method: An oracle model of neural network learning uses Kolmogorov n-widths to quantify effective representation complexity, and transfers complexity bounds from the forward representation to gradient-query features. Combined with statistical-query lower bounds, this gives a task-agnostic lower bound on the initial effective width needed for target-dependent gradient information to become detectable; a sharper unsigned effective width is used for parity.
AI.result: For k-sparse parity in D dimensions, the target admits an O(k)-width representation, while the critical scale of the unsigned effective width is Theta-tilde_k(D^(k-1) tau^2), up to logarithmic factors. Experiments support the predicted dimension dependence and examine how optimisation and generalisation depart from the idealised frontier.
AI.conclusion: The representation resources needed to discover a predictor can substantially exceed those needed to represent it once learned, and accumulating precision over fresh samples yields a width-time frontier.

title: FairSplit: Decomposing the Embedding Space for Fair Classification
summary: Fair classification faces a twofold challenge: maintaining high classification accuracy while limiting reliance on sensitive information. Our method FairSplit achieves this by learning a decomposition of the embedding space into a Fair Space used for prediction and a Sensitive Space that isolates sensitive information. During training, the model must simultaneously learn the classification task and separate fair from sensitive information. The Sensitive Space gives sensitive attributes a destination, so the Fair Space can be used for prediction without relying on them. This decomposition is guided via a learnable mask and the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) as a measure of statistical dependence. We provide theoretical guarantees showing that the demographic parity gap is upper-bounded by both (i) the learned dimensionality of the Fair Space and (ii) the HSIC between the Fair Space and sensitive attributes. FairSplit effectively handles multiclass tasks and non-binary sensitive attributes, overcoming key limitations of existing fair classification methods. Experiments on established fairness benchmarks show that FairSplit achieves competitive accuracy-fairness trade-offs. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: FairSplit decomposes the embedding space into a Fair Space used for prediction and a Sensitive Space that absorbs sensitive information, achieving competitive accuracy-fairness trade-offs on established fairness benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Fair classification must keep accuracy high while limiting reliance on sensitive information, and existing fair classification methods have key limitations, including in multiclass tasks and with non-binary sensitive attributes.
AI.method: A learnable mask splits the embedding into a Fair Space for prediction and a Sensitive Space, guided by the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) as a measure of statistical dependence between the spaces and the sensitive attributes.
AI.result: Theory shows that the demographic parity gap is upper-bounded by both the learned dimensionality of the Fair Space and the HSIC between the Fair Space and the sensitive attributes. Experiments on established fairness benchmarks show competitive accuracy-fairness trade-offs, and the method handles multiclass tasks and non-binary sensitive attributes.
AI.conclusion: Assigning sensitive information an explicit destination in a separate space gives a principled way to reduce the demographic parity gap while preserving predictive accuracy.

title: Exponential-Nemytskii Neural Operators: Learning Field Evolution Across Step Sizes
summary: In variable-step operator learning, agreement at observed step sizes does not by itself determine predictions at other temporal resolutions. We propose an operator whose step-size dependence is prescribed by a first-order Duhamel approximation of semilinear dynamics. It combines exact linear propagation with a local nonlinear function of the field and its derivatives, allowing evaluation below the observation interval without supervision densely sampled across step sizes. Under suitable conditions and at fixed spatial resolution, we prove that agreement between models at two step sizes controls their prediction differences throughout a prescribed range. We also give conditions for local identifiability of both components from two step sizes, supporting interpretation of the learned structure. A latent extension applies the same construction to learned fields. We evaluate the base model on two synthetic problems and the extension on two real datasets against several baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an operator learning model whose step-size dependence follows a first-order Duhamel approximation of semilinear dynamics, so predictions can be made at step sizes not seen in training, with guarantees on agreement across step sizes and local identifiability of its components.
AI.motivation: In variable-step operator learning, agreement at observed step sizes does not by itself determine predictions at other temporal resolutions, and densely sampled supervision across step sizes is not available.
AI.method: The operator combines exact linear propagation with a local nonlinear function of the field and its derivatives, following the first-order Duhamel approximation; a latent extension applies the same construction to learned fields.
AI.result: Under suitable conditions at fixed spatial resolution, agreement between models at two step sizes provably controls their prediction differences over a prescribed range, and both components are locally identifiable from two step sizes. The base model is evaluated on two synthetic problems and the latent extension on two real datasets against several baselines.
AI.conclusion: The prescribed step-size structure allows evaluation below the observed interval with controlled prediction differences and gives an interpretable learned structure.

title: Reinforcement Learning for the Game of Balatro: A Fast Simulator and Two-Policy Training Approach
comment: Accepted at EXAG 2026 (AIIDE Workshop on Experimental AI in Games)
summary: Balatro, a 2024 roguelike deckbuilder, presents three difficulties that have historically derailed reinforcement learning methods: a 3,000-action state-dependent action space, horizons of several hundred decisions with sparse rewards, and pervasive stochasticity in both card draws and shop generation. Published RL results on the game remain scarce. We introduce an end-to-end pipeline comprising (i) a high-throughput Rust simulator that is automatically state-diffed against the live game client via BalatroBot, (ii) a condensed observation-action interface with dynamic per-step masking of legal moves, and (iii) a multi-agent PPO architecture that decomposes play into a tactical blind policy and a strategic shop policy that share the full game state but act in disjoint phases. Long-horizon credit assignment is partially addressed by per-agent reward routing with explicit cross-agent credit. On the main joint run, training metrics show a sharp phase transition in which the first-blind clear rate converges above 99% and mean episode return increases by roughly an order of magnitude, plateauing at a mean maximum ante of 3 out of 8; single-agent baselines under identical rewards oscillated between greedy and hoarding failure modes and did not stably clear the first blind. These results establish the two-policy decomposition as a strong reactive baseline for Balatro and localise the remaining gap to long-horizon strategic planning rather than tactical blind play.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an end-to-end reinforcement learning pipeline for the roguelike Balatro, including a fast Rust simulator and a two-policy multi-agent PPO, whose joint run reaches a first-blind clear rate above 99% but plateaus at a mean maximum ante of 3 out of 8.
AI.motivation: Balatro's 3,000-action state-dependent action space, horizons of several hundred sparse-reward decisions and pervasive stochasticity have historically derailed RL methods, and published RL results on the game are scarce.
AI.method: A high-throughput Rust simulator is automatically state-diffed against the live game client via BalatroBot; a condensed observation-action interface applies dynamic per-step masking of legal moves; and a multi-agent PPO splits play into a tactical blind policy and a strategic shop policy that share the full game state but act in disjoint phases, with per-agent reward routing and explicit cross-agent credit.
AI.result: The joint run shows a sharp phase transition in which the first-blind clear rate converges above 99% and mean episode return rises by roughly an order of magnitude, plateauing at a mean maximum ante of 3 out of 8. Single-agent baselines under identical rewards oscillated between greedy and hoarding failure modes and did not stably clear the first blind.
AI.conclusion: The two-policy decomposition is a strong reactive baseline for Balatro, and the remaining gap lies in long-horizon strategic planning rather than tactical blind play.

title: BASILISC: Bayesian Alignment of Siamese-Integrated Latents for Inferring Single-cell Correspondence
comment: 12 pages main text, 3 figures, 1 table; supplementary material with 10 figures and 10 tables (38 pages total). Code to be released on publication. Currently under review
summary: Single-cell assays study the genome one cell at a time. Unimodal assays measure one molecular layer, the newer multimodal assays measure several. Most data are single-modality, so integrating them relies on models trained on multimodal assays, where the cell correspondence across modalities is known. These models return a matching, but rarely a confidence measure. We present BASILISC (Bayesian Alignment of Siamese-Integrated Latents for Inferring Single-cell Correspondence), a framework for matching single-cell representations with uncertainty on the correspondence itself. A BASILISC model is a probabilistic siamese network over the two modalities with a predictive distribution over the correspondence for a cross-modal pair of cells. We instantiate it at two levels: at the cell-type level the question is whether two cells share a cell type, at the cell level which cell is the partner in the other modality. To our knowledge, this is the first uncertainty score on a learned cross-modal correspondence evaluated against a known ground-truth pairing.
