BASILISC learns a similarity across modalities that reflects cell lineage: an unseen cell type is matched to its lineage relative, matching still works on such held-out types (balanced accuracy 0.86 on unseen against 0.93 on seen types), and the predictive uncertainty rises on these out-of-distribution cells. The uncertainty score also selects high-quality matches for downstream analysis: discarding the least certain fifth of the pairs raises accuracy from 0.93 to 0.98. At the cell level, a deep ensemble of the deterministic matcher reaches 0.062 matching accuracy on the benchmark test set, above the competition winner; on the Bayesian matcher's assignment, the posterior flags the wrong matches that cross a cell-type boundary better than a deterministic read of the same scores (AUROC 0.68 against 0.64).

AI.tldr: BASILISC is a probabilistic siamese framework that matches single cells across modalities and attaches an uncertainty score to each correspondence, and this score flags unreliable matches.
AI.motivation: Models trained on multimodal assays return cell matchings for integrating single-modality data but rarely provide a confidence measure for the cross-modal correspondence.
AI.method: A probabilistic siamese network over the two modalities gives a predictive distribution over the correspondence of a cross-modal cell pair, instantiated at the cell-type level (whether two cells share a cell type) and at the cell level (which cell is the partner). The learned similarity reflects cell lineage.
AI.result: Balanced accuracy is 0.86 on unseen cell types against 0.93 on seen types, and predictive uncertainty rises on these out-of-distribution cells. Discarding the least certain fifth of the pairs raises accuracy from 0.93 to 0.98. At cell level, a deep ensemble of the deterministic matcher reaches 0.062 matching accuracy on the benchmark test set, above the competition winner, and the posterior flags wrong matches that cross a cell-type boundary better than the deterministic scores (AUROC 0.68 against 0.64).
AI.conclusion: The uncertainty score is a useful signal, evaluated against a known ground-truth pairing, for selecting high-quality cross-modal matches and detecting out-of-distribution cells.

title: When Does Closed-Loop Curriculum Adaptation Help GRPO? An Analysis on Countdown
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, Accepted at IEEE ICTAI 2026
summary: Reinforcement fine-tuning has become an effective post-training paradigm for improving the reasoning ability of large language models, but it remains sample-inefficient when the training distribution is mismatched to the model's current capability. In group-relative objectives such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), problems that are too hard often produce uniformly failed rollouts, while problems that are too easy provide little useful advantage signal. In this work, we introduce CLOSEDLOOPGAUSSIAN, a lightweight adaptive curriculum method for efficient reinforcement fine-tuning on ordered reasoning tasks. Instead of following a fixed easy-to-hard schedule, CLOSEDLOOPGAUSSIAN preserves the structure of an Easy-to-Hard Gaussian sampler while dynamically adjusting its pace and spread using periodic probe estimates of per-difficulty accuracy. The controller accelerates training when the model is ahead of a reference curriculum, slows down when the model falls behind, and broadens sampling when earlier difficulties regress. This feedback mechanism keeps training focused on tasks that are challenging but still learnable, without changing the reward function, model architecture, or underlying GRPO optimizer. Experiments on symbolic arithmetic reasoning task show that CLOSEDLOOPGAUSSIAN improves exact-match accuracy over vanilla GRPO and fixed open-loop curricula, with the strongest gains in intermediate-difficulty regimes where group-relative learning signals are most informative. Codes are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: CLOSEDLOOPGAUSSIAN is an adaptive curriculum for GRPO that adjusts the pace and spread of an Easy-to-Hard Gaussian sampler using periodic probes of per-difficulty accuracy, improving exact-match accuracy on symbolic arithmetic over vanilla GRPO and fixed curricula.
AI.motivation: GRPO is sample-inefficient when the training distribution is mismatched to model capability: overly hard problems yield uniformly failed rollouts, overly easy problems give little advantage signal, and fixed easy-to-hard schedules do not adapt.
AI.method: The controller accelerates when the model is ahead of a reference curriculum, slows when it falls behind, and broadens sampling when earlier difficulties regress, using periodic probe estimates of per-difficulty accuracy. The reward function, model architecture and GRPO optimizer are unchanged.
AI.result: On a symbolic arithmetic reasoning task, the method improves exact-match accuracy over vanilla GRPO and fixed open-loop curricula, with the strongest gains at intermediate difficulty where group-relative learning signals are most informative.
AI.conclusion: Closed-loop difficulty adaptation keeps training focused on tasks that are challenging but still learnable, offering a lightweight way to improve the efficiency of reinforcement fine-tuning.

title: Closed Gates Leak: Decomposing Adjacent-Layer Cancellation in Gated Language Models
summary: In transformer language models with gated multilayer perceptrons (MLPs), adjacent layers write partly against each other into the residual stream. Previous work interpreted this cancellation as layers proposing features and the next layer selectively rejecting the inappropriate ones. We decompose the cancellation by removing the previous layer's write from the input of the next MLP: what the next layer writes along that write splits into what it writes anyway and how much less its MLP writes because the write is present, which we call the damping, and we trace the damping to the neurons that carry it. In gated MLPs the damping is carried by neurons whose gates are closed. SiLU and GELU are slightly negative below zero, so a closed gate still passes a small negative multiple of what the neuron reads, and a neuron whose output weight points along its input weight then subtracts a fraction of the direction it read. Summed over such neurons, closed gates contract the average direction a gated MLP reads, and the previous layer's write is not singled out: the same layer's write at another token is damped as much or more, and the eigenvalue signature from which that work concluded that the correction is selective appears for another token's write as well. Over training the damping grows while what the next layer writes anyway stays flat, and cancellation begins when the damping overtakes it; annealing the negative side of the gate activation away in continued pretraining removes the damping and the cancellation. Adjacent-layer cancellation is therefore weak evidence about which features a model rejects: it is produced by a contraction that gated MLPs apply, on average over directions, to whatever they read.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that adjacent-layer cancellation in gated MLP transformers comes from a contraction that closed gates apply, on average over directions, to whatever they read, rather than from selective rejection of particular features.
AI.motivation: Prior work interpreted adjacent-layer cancellation in the residual stream as the next layer selectively rejecting features proposed by the previous layer, and the mechanism behind this cancellation was not decomposed.
AI.method: The previous layer's write is removed from the input of the next MLP, and the resulting change is split into what the layer writes anyway and a damping term, which is traced to neurons with closed gates. For SiLU and GELU, slightly negative outputs below zero pass a small negative multiple of the read input, so neurons whose output weight points along their input weight subtract a fraction of the direction they read.
AI.result: Damping grows over training while the component written anyway stays flat, and cancellation begins when damping overtakes it. The same layer's write at another token is damped as much or more, and the eigenvalue signature used in prior work also appears for other tokens. Annealing the negative side of the gate activation in continued pretraining removes both the damping and the cancellation.
AI.conclusion: Adjacent-layer cancellation is therefore weak evidence about which features a model rejects, because it is produced by a general contraction that gated MLPs apply to what they read.

title: Generating Critic-Guided Synthetic Experience in Latent World Models
summary: Learning from offline datasets is limited in scalability, as collecting new experience is often costly or unsafe in the real world. World models offer an alternative way to generate new experience through a learned dynamics model, yet learning policies in latent space is limited due to compounding errors in imagined rollouts. To this end, we propose using the world model as a local transition generator, leveraging critic guidance to choose actions inside that model to generate synthetic experiences. We study action refinement methodologies, introducing Critic-Guided Synthetic Experience (CGSE) generation in world models. Specifically, CGSE augments an existing offline dataset by sampling candidate actions using an offline policy and refining each to maximize a first-order approximation of the $Q$-function within a trust region. We then use a frozen latent world model to imagine the future state given each updated action, and use the critic to choose the best one, appending this synthetic transition to the replay buffer. Our method requires no additional real-environment interaction or test-time planner, as it generates synthetic experience offline using the world model. On three OGBench manipulation tasks, CGSE improves an offline policy by a relative improvement of $7.1\%$ on the average success rate.

AI.tldr: CGSE augments an offline dataset with synthetic transitions generated inside a frozen latent world model using critic-selected, trust-region-refined actions, improving an offline policy's average success rate by a relative 7.1% on three OGBench manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Learning from offline datasets is limited in scale because collecting new real-world experience is costly or unsafe, and policy learning in latent world models suffers from compounding errors in imagined rollouts.
AI.method: Candidate actions are sampled from an offline policy and each is refined within a trust region to maximize a first-order approximation of the Q-function. A frozen latent world model imagines the next state for each refined action, the critic chooses the best one, and the resulting synthetic transition is appended to the replay buffer. No additional real-environment interaction or test-time planner is required.
AI.result: On three OGBench manipulation tasks, CGSE improves the offline policy by a relative 7.1% on the average success rate.
AI.conclusion: Using the world model as a local transition generator guided by the critic is a practical way to expand offline datasets without additional environment interaction.

title: From Local Recovery to Unified Generation: Discovering Triple Set in Knowledge Graphs via Observation-Anchored Latent Diffusion
summary: Triple set prediction (TSP) is to recover missing relational triples in a knowledge graph by predicting the triple set instead of isolated links. Existing approaches predominantly rely on the subgraph-based completion paradigm, where the original graph is first partitioned into local subgraphs which are then independently completed. Such a paradigm suffers from fragmented structural reasoning, limited cross subgraph dependency modeling, and missing predictions across subgraphs. This paper proposes LatentDiff, a novel unified latent generative framework for TSP, which reformulates knowledge graph completion as latent space graph generation. LatentDiff first learns a compact latent representation using a relation-aware residual-quantized knowledge graph autoencoder, which encodes the whole graph into relation-aware latent embeddings, quantizes them with chunked residual codebooks, and reconstructs triples through a factorized decoder. On top of this latent space, we introduce an observation-anchored latent graph diffusion model, where the target latent graph representation is perturbed toward the observed latent. The reverse process recovers missing triples through progressive latent denoising. Experiments on three benchmark datasets show that LatentDiff outperforms the SOTA in terms of F_{tsp} by 5.4 percentage points on average. Code: this https URL.

AI.tldr: LatentDiff reformulates knowledge graph triple set prediction as latent graph generation, using a relation-aware residual-quantized autoencoder and an observation-anchored latent diffusion model, and outperforms the state of the art in F_tsp by 5.4 percentage points on average across three benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Subgraph-based completion partitions the graph into local subgraphs that are completed independently, which causes fragmented structural reasoning, limited cross-subgraph dependency modelling and missing predictions across subgraphs.
AI.method: A relation-aware residual-quantized knowledge graph autoencoder encodes the whole graph into latent embeddings, quantizes them with chunked residual codebooks and reconstructs triples with a factorized decoder. On this latent space, an observation-anchored latent graph diffusion model perturbs the target latent graph toward the observed latent, and missing triples are recovered by progressive latent denoising.
AI.result: On three benchmark datasets, LatentDiff outperforms the state of the art in F_tsp by 5.4 percentage points on average.
AI.conclusion: Unified latent generative modelling of the whole graph is a stronger alternative to subgraph-based completion for triple set prediction.

title: Uncertainty-Guided Cross-Modal Alignment for Diffusion-Based IoT Intrusion Detection
comment: 7 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Accepted at NeurIPS DynaFront 2026
summary: Diffusion models evolve noisy states toward a learned data distribution, so their sampling behavior depends on the geometry of the representation in which denoising occurs. This dependence is especially important for multimodal data: independently trained encoders can map synchronized views to incompatible latent regions, while uniform alignment can let an uncertain view distort the shared geometry. To address this gap, we introduce a novel reliability-guided alignment rule that uses normalized VAE posterior variance to control directional cross-modal influence before diffusion training. We study this issue in minority-attack generation for imbalanced Internet-of-Things intrusion detection. Tabular flow attributes, a DeepInsight image, and a packet sequence are encoded by modality-specific variational autoencoders. Per-modality normalized VAE posterior variances provide bounded, sample-specific weighting signals in an asymmetric stop-gradient alignment objective. We use these quantities as heuristic encoder-derived reliability proxies rather than calibrated probabilistic uncertainties. The full modality-specific latent means obtained after alignment fine-tuning are standardized and modeled jointly by a class-conditional EDM; a second-order sampler then generates paired attack-conditioned latent blocks for the three decoders. In controlled experiments on TON-IoT, uncertainty-aware alignment obtains the highest mean precision, recall, density, and coverage among three diffusion variants. Augmenting only the training split yields ROC-AUC 0.9515, PR-AUC 0.8954, balanced accuracy 0.8395, and attack-class F1 0.7940 on an untouched real test set. Among the two variants with matched alignment fine-tuning, posterior-variance-based weighting improves both tabular generative fidelity and downstream detection relative to uniform weighting.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes reliability-guided cross-modal alignment, which weights an asymmetric stop-gradient alignment objective by normalized VAE posterior variance, and then trains a class-conditional EDM to generate minority attack samples for IoT intrusion detection on TON-IoT.
AI.motivation: Independently trained encoders can map synchronized views to incompatible latent regions, and uniform alignment lets an uncertain view distort the shared geometry, which matters for generating minority attacks in imbalanced IoT intrusion detection.
AI.method: Tabular flow attributes, a DeepInsight image and a packet sequence are encoded by modality-specific variational autoencoders. Per-modality normalized posterior variances serve as bounded, sample-specific weights in an asymmetric stop-gradient alignment objective; they are treated as heuristic reliability proxies rather than calibrated uncertainties. The aligned latent means are modelled jointly by a class-conditional EDM, and a second-order sampler generates paired attack-conditioned latent blocks for the three decoders.
AI.result: In controlled experiments on TON-IoT, uncertainty-aware alignment obtains the highest mean precision, recall, density and coverage among three diffusion variants. Augmenting only the training split yields ROC-AUC 0.9515, PR-AUC 0.8954, balanced accuracy 0.8395 and attack-class F1 0.7940 on an untouched real test set, and posterior-variance weighting improves both tabular generative fidelity and downstream detection over uniform weighting.
AI.conclusion: Reliability-guided weighting of cross-modal alignment improves both the fidelity of synthetic tabular data and the downstream detection of minority attacks.

title: Clean Sheets and Checkpoints: Evidence Complexity for Certifying Sequential Agent Risk
summary: Dangerous-capability evaluations often test an AI agent from prepared states at ordered milestones. A clean sheet records no successes. What it certifies about a campaign of $B$ attempts depends on what a failed attempt erases. We model the task as a chain of $k$ milestones divided into checkpoint segments and ask how many zero audit responses certify, at level $\alpha$, a completion probability of at most $\epsilon$. For segments chosen before the audit, counting possible completion windows gives a certificate for any specified budget. The bound also covers adaptive deployment processes that follow the chain's transitions, provided their success probabilities after every complete history are capped by the corresponding audit success probabilities. The audit does not test this transport assumption. In rare-risk phase interiors, each segment is either rarely completed within the budget (active) or nearly always completed (free). The minimum expected number of zero responses is asymptotic to $\log(1/\alpha)\,(B^a/(a!\,\epsilon))^{1/K_A}$, where the $a$ active segments contain $K_A$ milestones and are those at least as long as a budget-dependent threshold. The certificate attains this constant. Every asymptotically optimal evaluator must divide its expected response count equally among active milestones in the limit, with a vanishing share elsewhere. Where a single segment passes from active to free, each of its milestones receives a smaller limiting share than an active milestone; a crossover-aware certificate attains the optimal constant. For selected segments with known or unqueried prefix steps, counting failed cycles can sharpen the certificate.

AI.tldr: The paper gives the number of zero-success audit responses needed to certify, at level alpha, that a sequential AI agent's completion probability is at most epsilon, together with an asymptotically optimal allocation of those responses across milestones.
AI.motivation: Dangerous-capability evaluations test an AI agent from prepared states at ordered milestones, and a clean sheet with no recorded successes certifies something that depends on what a failed attempt erases.
AI.method: The task is modelled as a chain of k milestones divided into checkpoint segments. For segments chosen before the audit, counting possible completion windows gives a certificate for any specified budget, and this extends to adaptive deployment processes whose success probabilities are capped by the audit probabilities. In rare-risk regimes each segment is either active (rarely completed within the budget) or free (nearly always completed), and the certificate attains the asymptotically optimal constant.
AI.result: The minimum expected number of zero responses is asymptotically log(1/alpha) times (B^a/(a! epsilon))^(1/K_A), where the a active segments contain K_A milestones. Optimal evaluators divide their responses equally among active milestones in the limit, with a vanishing share elsewhere, and a crossover-aware certificate attains the optimal constant for a segment passing from active to free. Counting failed cycles can sharpen the certificate for selected segments with known or unqueried prefix steps.
AI.conclusion: The paper gives the optimal response count and allocation for certifying sequential agent risk from clean audits, under a transport assumption that the audit itself does not test.

title: A Novel Approach to Evaluating Evaluation Metrics for Multi-Output Structured Prediction
comment: Extended version of the AAAI 2026 paper, including the technical appendix. 18 pages, 8 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: In multi-output structured prediction tasks, while only one ground truth label may be provided in the training data, multiple equally valid outputs may be possible, making reliable evaluation a persistent challenge. We postulate that human evaluators implicitly use task-specific invariants, e.g., object boundaries in colorized images or named entities in translations, to judge if an output is acceptable. Under this assumption, we introduce a notion of approximate task-specific invariants and use them as diagnostic tools to evaluate a variety of existing metrics for vision and language tasks. We use these task invariants as part of a framework to systematically test metric reliability by encouraging domain-relevant invariants in model outputs via an augmented loss function. In our experiments, we observe that enforcing invariants with an augmented loss yields substantial improvements in popular distributional metrics while more traditional metrics change only marginally. Through this invariants-driven evaluation, we expose where standard metrics fail to detect meaningful differences, and we highlight the conditions under which distributional metrics succeed or still fall short.

AI.tldr: The paper uses approximate task-specific invariants as diagnostic tools to test evaluation metrics for multi-output structured prediction, finding that enforcing invariants substantially improves distributional metrics while traditional metrics change only marginally.
AI.motivation: Multi-output structured prediction often has several equally valid outputs but only one ground-truth label, so reliable evaluation is a persistent challenge, while human evaluators implicitly rely on task invariants such as object boundaries or named entities.
AI.method: Approximate task-specific invariants are introduced and used in a framework that encourages domain-relevant invariants in model outputs through an augmented loss function, in order to systematically test the reliability of existing metrics for vision and language tasks.
AI.result: Enforcing invariants with the augmented loss yields substantial improvements in popular distributional metrics, while more traditional metrics change only marginally, exposing where standard metrics fail to detect meaningful differences.
AI.conclusion: Invariant-driven evaluation shows where distributional metrics succeed and where they still fall short.

title: ACAM-J-MARS: Multi-Atlas Riemannian Spectral Representations for Decoding Advanced Meditation States from fMRI
summary: Inferring jhana-type advanced concentration absorption meditation (ACAM-J) states from fMRI data is challenging due to the spatially distributed nature of meditation-related effects, substantial inter-individual variability that can exceed within-subject state differences, and limited sample sizes. Conventional machine-learning approaches often formulate this problem as unimodal, Euclidean, atlas-based classification, thereby neglecting the non-Euclidean geometry of functional connectivity matrices and underrepresenting temporal information in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI); these limitations can lead to suboptimal classification performance. We propose ACAM-J-MARS (\textbf{M}ulti-\textbf{A}tlas \textbf{R}iemannian \textbf{S}pectral representation), which computes functional connectivity using multiple atlases, represents symmetric positive definite (SPD) connectivity matrices on a Riemannian manifold, projects them into a log-Euclidean tangent space, and augments connectivity-derived features with low-frequency BOLD spectral energy to better resolve subtle state differences under heterogeneous variability. Evaluated on 204 segments from 22 practitioners, ACAM-J-MARS improves performance across multiple backbone models, achieving a balanced accuracy of 0.757 for early versus late ACAM-J classification and 0.545 for three-class classification, corresponding to a 10.8-point absolute improvement over the strongest baseline. These findings suggest that the proposed representation improves the decoding of advanced meditative brain states and may enable downstream applications such as closed-loop neurofeedback and real-time psychophysiological brain-computer interfaces.

AI.tldr: ACAM-J-MARS decodes jhana-type advanced concentration meditation states from fMRI by combining multi-atlas Riemannian connectivity representations with low-frequency BOLD spectral energy, reaching balanced accuracy 0.757 for early versus late states and 0.545 for three-class classification.
AI.motivation: Decoding these states is difficult because meditation effects are spatially distributed, inter-individual variability can exceed within-subject state differences, and samples are limited, while conventional atlas-based Euclidean classifiers ignore the non-Euclidean geometry of connectivity matrices and underrepresent temporal information.
AI.method: Functional connectivity is computed with multiple atlases, and the symmetric positive definite connectivity matrices are represented on a Riemannian manifold and projected into a log-Euclidean tangent space. These features are augmented with low-frequency BOLD spectral energy.
AI.result: Evaluated on 204 segments from 22 practitioners, the method improves performance across multiple backbone models, achieving balanced accuracy 0.757 for early versus late ACAM-J classification and 0.545 for three-class classification, a 10.8-point absolute improvement over the strongest baseline.
AI.conclusion: The representation better resolves subtle differences between meditative brain states and may support applications such as closed-loop neurofeedback and real-time brain-computer interfaces.

title: Analyzing Condensation on Patterned Surfaces via Deep Learning
summary: Dropwise condensation is key to power and water systems. State-of-the-art condensation surfaces are often inhomogeneous, either patterned by design or random defects. Inhomogeneous surface features dictate the rates of each stage of dropwise condensation-nucleation, growth, coalescence, and shedding. Characterizing these rates requires the precise detection of thousands of droplets. Yet, existing segmentation methods are unable to detect droplets on inhomogeneous surfaces. We developed TileSAM3, a universal droplet segmentation tool built on the Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM3). Hierarchical tiling with per-tile inference followed by post-processing extended SAM3's detection cap and raised the effective resolution of small droplets. We created two datasets: High Quality Droplet Dataset (N=365,826; HQDD) with homogeneous surfaces and Low Quality Droplet Dataset (N=63,577; LQDD) with patterned, defect-laden surfaces under adverse lighting. TileSAM3 closely reproduced thresholding annotations on HQDD, surpassed it over sixfold on LQDD (Average Precision 0.57 versus 0.088), and outperformed other deep learning models on all metrics evaluated. Combined with KD-tree tracking, TileSAM3 identified localized nucleation and coalescence in narrow active bands on a stiffness-patterned surface. TileSAM3 enables analysis of understudied inhomogeneous substrates with poor lighting and videography which facilitates faster, lower cost research of condensation materials.

AI.tldr: TileSAM3 is a droplet segmentation tool built on SAM3 that uses hierarchical tiling to segment droplets on inhomogeneous condensation surfaces, reaching Average Precision 0.57 on the low-quality patterned dataset where thresholding annotations reach 0.088.
AI.motivation: Dropwise condensation on inhomogeneous surfaces requires precise detection of thousands of droplets to characterize nucleation, growth, coalescence and shedding, but existing segmentation methods cannot detect droplets on such surfaces.
AI.method: Hierarchical tiling with per-tile inference followed by post-processing extends SAM3's detection cap and raises the effective resolution for small droplets. Two datasets were created: the High Quality Droplet Dataset (N=365,826, homogeneous surfaces) and the Low Quality Droplet Dataset (N=63,577, patterned, defect-laden surfaces under adverse lighting). Combined with KD-tree tracking, the tool identifies localized nucleation and coalescence.
AI.result: TileSAM3 closely reproduces thresholding annotations on the high-quality dataset, surpasses them by more than sixfold on the low-quality dataset (AP 0.57 versus 0.088), and outperforms other deep learning models on all evaluated metrics. On a stiffness-patterned surface it identifies localized nucleation and coalescence in narrow active bands.
AI.conclusion: The tool enables analysis of understudied inhomogeneous substrates under poor lighting, which supports faster and lower-cost research on condensation materials.

title: Sparse Autoencoders as Implicit Diversification Regularisers for Cross-Sectional Cryptocurrency Returns
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures. Accepted at the 7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance (ICAIF '26)
summary: Factor models are central to asset pricing and portfolio construction, but neural factors are often difficult to interpret, and their effect on portfolio risk is unclear. A sparse autoencoder (SAE) may address both concerns by describing daily returns across many assets with only a few active features. We ask whether this sparse representation produces stable financial factors and better-diversified portfolios. We study cryptocurrency returns, use equities as a secondary test, and compare the SAE with common benchmarks in a time-ordered evaluation. We find consistently lower volatility in SAE portfolios and link this result to lower correlations among the selected assets. However, the SAE does not outperform a simple contrarian strategy on risk-adjusted return, and its factor identities are not stable across training runs. Our contribution is to show that sparse coding can support portfolio diversification, while clearly separating this risk effect from claims about alpha or stable factor identities.

AI.tldr: Sparse autoencoder factor portfolios for cryptocurrency returns show consistently lower volatility, linked to lower correlations among selected assets, but do not outperform a simple contrarian strategy on risk-adjusted return.
AI.motivation: Neural factors in asset pricing are often hard to interpret and their effect on portfolio risk is unclear, and a sparse autoencoder may address both concerns by describing many assets' daily returns with few active features.
AI.method: A sparse autoencoder represents daily cryptocurrency returns across many assets, with equities as a secondary test, and is compared with common benchmarks in a time-ordered evaluation.
AI.result: Sparse autoencoder portfolios show consistently lower volatility, linked to lower correlations among the selected assets. However, the autoencoder does not outperform a simple contrarian strategy on risk-adjusted return, and its factor identities are not stable across training runs.
AI.conclusion: Sparse coding can support portfolio diversification, and the paper keeps this risk effect separate from claims about alpha or stable factor identities.

title: Where Position Matters: Profiling-Guided Layer-Wise RoPE Allocation in Transformers
summary: Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) typically uses uniform coverage across Transformer layers despite heterogeneous positional requirements. Phase-off interventions reveal non-uniform, model-specific rotary-phase dependence, while coverage interventions relate it to coverage-upgrade benefits. We propose profiling-guided layer-wise RoPE allocation, assigning high/low coverage under a fixed budget using early coverage-benefit profiles. The framework supports fixed-width query/key representations and physical rotary-dimension allocation in Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA). Normalized-depth mapping transfers profiles within model families, enabling small-model measurements to guide larger-model allocations before pretraining. A brief analysis relates selection and transfer to score calibration and inter-layer interactions. From-scratch experiments demonstrate validation-loss improvements over available budget-matched baselines, while analytical resource accounting identifies favorable quality--storage--compute trade-offs for physical MLA. These results connect positional demand to transferable, efficient architecture design.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes profiling-guided layer-wise RoPE allocation, which assigns high or low rotary coverage to each layer under a fixed budget using early coverage-benefit profiles, and improves validation loss over budget-matched baselines in from-scratch experiments.
AI.motivation: RoPE typically uses uniform coverage across Transformer layers despite heterogeneous positional requirements, and phase-off and coverage interventions reveal non-uniform, model-specific rotary-phase dependence.
AI.method: Layers are assigned high or low coverage under a fixed budget using early coverage-benefit profiles. Normalized-depth mapping transfers profiles within model families, so measurements on small models can guide allocations for larger models before pretraining. The framework supports fixed-width query/key representations and physical rotary-dimension allocation in Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA).
AI.result: From-scratch experiments show validation-loss improvements over available budget-matched baselines, and analytical resource accounting identifies favorable quality, storage and compute trade-offs for physical MLA.
AI.conclusion: Connecting positional demand to transferable profiles yields efficient architecture design that carries across model sizes.

title: IMRouter: Imbalance-aware Temporal Pattern Routing for LLM-based Time Series Forecasting
summary: Accurate time series forecasting (TSF) is essential for Web applications, such as traffic monitoring and online resource management. Recent advances in leveraging pre-trained large language models (LLMs) have shown promising performance in TSF. However, existing LLM-based TSF methods largely optimize the overall forecasting objective while overlooking temporal pattern imbalance (TPI), where different temporal patterns occur at highly unequal frequencies. Our empirical analysis reveals that TPI is prevalent across widely used TSF benchmarks, with substantially higher forecasting errors on less frequent patterns. To address this issue, we propose IMRouter (Imbalance-aware Temporal Pattern Routing), a novel framework that mitigates TPI-induced biases in both temporal representation learning and cross-modal alignment. Specifically, IMRouter introduces Pattern-Adaptive Temporal Representation Learning (PATR), which leverages gradient conflict and local gradient density to guide expert specialization. By penalizing incompatible expert assignments with density-aware weighting, PATR reduces the dominance of frequent optimization signals in router training. Furthermore, Routing-Guided Semantic Alignment (RGSA) transfers the pattern-specific knowledge learned by the router to cross-modal alignment through mutual information maximization, preserving distinctive temporal information across different patterns. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of IMRouter, particularly in improving forecasting performance on less frequent temporal patterns.

AI.tldr: IMRouter addresses temporal pattern imbalance in LLM-based time series forecasting, improving accuracy on less frequent temporal patterns through imbalance-aware expert routing and mutual-information-based cross-modal alignment.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based forecasting methods optimize the overall objective and overlook temporal pattern imbalance, in which patterns occur at highly unequal frequencies; the authors' analysis shows this imbalance is prevalent across widely used benchmarks, with substantially higher errors on less frequent patterns.
AI.method: Pattern-Adaptive Temporal Representation Learning (PATR) uses gradient conflict and local gradient density to guide expert specialization, penalizing incompatible expert assignments with density-aware weighting to reduce the dominance of frequent optimization signals in router training. Routing-Guided Semantic Alignment (RGSA) transfers the pattern-specific knowledge learned by the router to cross-modal alignment through mutual information maximization.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of IMRouter, particularly in improving forecasting performance on less frequent temporal patterns.
AI.conclusion: Correcting for pattern-frequency bias in both temporal representation learning and cross-modal alignment improves forecasting for rare temporal patterns.

title: Strongly Adaptive Online Learning Achieves Uniform Discounted Regret
summary: Discounted regret measures the performance of an online learner by assigning exponentially decaying weights to past losses, reflecting the greater importance of recent losses in non-stationary online learning. While previous work obtains uniform discounted regret bounds over a continuous range of discount factors using a specialized meta-algorithm, its results are limited to convex functions. In this paper, we demonstrate that strongly adaptive regret bounds can directly imply uniform discounted regret guarantees for convex, strongly convex, and exp-concave loss functions. Our key observation is that discounted regret against a fixed comparator admits an exact decomposition into a convex combination of interval regrets. For convex functions, this reduction yields an $O(\sqrt{\log T/(1-\lambda)})$ discounted regret bound for all discount factors $\lambda\in(0,1)$, matching the previous rate over a broader range of discount factors. For strongly convex and exp-concave functions, we provide regret bounds of $O\left(\log T\left(1+\log\frac{1}{1-\lambda}\right)\right)$.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that strongly adaptive regret bounds directly imply uniform discounted regret guarantees for convex, strongly convex and exp-concave losses, using an exact decomposition of discounted regret into a convex combination of interval regrets.
AI.motivation: Prior uniform discounted regret bounds over a continuous range of discount factors relied on a specialized meta-algorithm and were limited to convex functions.
AI.method: Discounted regret against a fixed comparator admits an exact decomposition into a convex combination of interval regrets, so guarantees for discounted regret follow from strongly adaptive regret bounds.
AI.result: For convex losses, the bound O(sqrt(log T/(1-lambda))) holds for all discount factors lambda in (0,1), matching the previous rate over a broader range. For strongly convex and exp-concave losses, the regret bounds are O(log T (1 + log(1/(1-lambda)))).
AI.conclusion: Strongly adaptive online learning yields uniform discounted regret guarantees across a broader class of loss functions.

title: There Is No Free Lunch in RLVR: Every pass@1 Gain Has a pass@k Price
comment: 19 pages, 4 figures. Code and verification package (34/34 automated checks): this https URL
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) makes a language model solve more problems on the first try and fewer when given many tries: it raises pass@1 while the base model overtakes it at large sampling budget k. Is this a failure of RL to add reasoning, or a transient that more training removes? We settle the question with a theorem. The reversal is a price, and we compute its exact rate. Modeling RLVR as an exponential tilt of a base policy over strategies shared across prompts, we prove that under exclusive specialization every update that raises pass@1 strictly lowers the success of some prompt; a strictly positive price on prompts (Stiemke duality) is the exact condition, and being merely the best strategy on a prompt is provably not enough. When the loss reaches the hardest prompts, it forces a pass@k crossover, and the number of crossings is at most the sign variation of the shift in per-prompt success, a totally positive bound that is tight and that recovers the known single-crossover result as its order-preserving case. The crossover is not a bug to patch: a constrained update traces the exact pass@1 versus pass@k frontier, and removing the crossover entirely costs the entire pass@1 gain. The same tilt identity yields entropy collapse and the entropy-performance law with an identifiable exponent, unifying two literatures under one mechanism. Reinforcement cannot widen the reasoning frontier; it can only move along it, at a price we make measurable by a diagnostic that reads the bound, the order-preserving test, and the price from any evaluation log. There is no free lunch, only a price.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that RLVR raises pass@1 only by lowering the success of some prompts, so the pass@1 gain comes with a pass@k crossover. The price is exact and measurable from an evaluation log.
AI.motivation: RLVR raises pass@1 but the base model overtakes it at large sampling budget k, and it was unclear whether this reflects a failure of RL to add reasoning or a transient that more training removes.
AI.method: RLVR is modeled as an exponential tilt of a base policy over strategies shared across prompts. Under exclusive specialization, the authors prove a strictly positive price on prompts (Stiemke duality) is the exact condition for the trade-off, and they bound the number of pass@k crossings by the sign variation of the per-prompt success shift, a totally positive bound.
AI.result: The bound is tight and recovers the known single-crossover result as its order-preserving case. A constrained update traces the exact pass@1 versus pass@k frontier, and removing the crossover entirely costs the whole pass@1 gain. The same tilt identity yields entropy collapse and an entropy-performance law with an identifiable exponent.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement cannot widen the reasoning frontier, it can only move along it, and the price can be read from any evaluation log using the bound, the order-preserving test and the price.

title: Multi-Solution Inverse Design of Pixelated Patch Antennas Using an Autoregressive Transformer
summary: Deep-learning-based inverse design has emerged as a promising framework for pixelated patch antenna synthesis by enabling broader exploration of discrete geometry spaces and reducing design time compared with conventional template-based methods. Existing methods, including surrogate-assisted metaheuristic optimization, tandem inverse networks, and diffusion models, have advanced the field but still face practical limitations. Metaheuristic methods such as binary particle swarm optimization (BPSO) are sensitive to initialization and search hyperparameters and are often time-consuming, tandem networks have difficulty capturing the one-to-many nature of inverse antenna design, and diffusion models may require excessive complexity and data for moderate-scale binary layout synthesis. In this paper, an autoregressive (AR) transformer is presented for the inverse design of 10 x 10 pixelated patch antennas. Its sequential discrete generation process enables the synthesis of multiple feasible structures for a given target response. The pretrained model is further fine-tuned for dual-band design using step-shaped target responses with sharp spectral transitions, allowing intuitive band specification without manually constructing detailed S11 curves. Compared with BPSO, our proposed method generates valid and diverse antenna candidates more efficiently. Fabricated and measured examples confirm that distinct pixelated layouts can realize the desired antenna responses, thereby demonstrating the multi-solution capability of the proposed framework.

AI.tldr: The paper applies an autoregressive transformer to inverse design of 10 x 10 pixelated patch antennas, generating multiple feasible layouts for one target response. Fabricated and measured examples confirm the designs.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches have limitations: binary particle swarm optimization is sensitive to initialization and hyperparameters and is time-consuming, tandem networks struggle with the one-to-many nature of inverse antenna design, and diffusion models may need excessive complexity and data for moderate-scale binary layouts.
AI.method: An autoregressive transformer generates the discrete layout sequentially, pretrained for the inverse design of 10 x 10 pixelated patch antennas and then fine-tuned for dual-band design using step-shaped target responses with sharp spectral transitions.
AI.result: Compared with BPSO, the method generates valid and diverse antenna candidates more efficiently. Fabricated and measured examples show distinct pixelated layouts realizing the desired responses.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates multi-solution capability for pixelated antenna synthesis and allows intuitive band specification without hand-constructing detailed S11 curves.

title: Learning to Bound: Monotonic, Calibrated Neural Upper Bounds for MPE Inference
summary: Probabilistic graphical models (PGMs) compactly encode structured joint distributions, but Most Probable Explanation (MPE), which finds the highest-probability assignment to unobserved variables, remains computationally intractable in large, densely structured models. Anytime systematic search, such as branch-and-bound (B&B), is a popular approach, but its efficiency depends on tight admissible upper bounds that are often prohibitively expensive to compute using classical methods like Mini-Bucket Elimination (MBE). We introduce Learning to Bound (L2B), a data-driven framework that amortizes bound computation cost by training a neural predictor. L2B targets two key properties required for effective search bounds: admissibility, which is achieved via statistical calibration techniques, and progressive tightening as evidence accumulates, which is enforced through structural architectural constraints that ensure monotonicity by construction. Across challenging benchmarks, L2B delivers tighter, monotonic bounds at orders-of-magnitude lower cost on every PGM family, and yields measurable improvements when integrated with branch-and-bound on high-treewidth instances.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Learning to Bound (L2B), a neural predictor that amortizes the cost of upper bounds for MPE inference and enforces admissibility through calibration and monotonic tightening by construction. It gives tighter bounds at much lower cost and improves branch-and-bound on high-treewidth instances.
AI.motivation: Most Probable Explanation is intractable in large, densely structured probabilistic graphical models, and the tight admissible bounds needed for anytime branch-and-bound are expensive with classical methods such as Mini-Bucket Elimination.
AI.method: A data-driven framework trains a neural predictor to output bounds. Admissibility is obtained through statistical calibration techniques, and progressive tightening as evidence accumulates is enforced through structural architectural constraints that guarantee monotonicity.
AI.result: Across challenging benchmarks, L2B delivers tighter, monotonic bounds at orders-of-magnitude lower cost on every PGM family, and yields measurable improvements when integrated with branch-and-bound on high-treewidth instances.
AI.conclusion: Learned, calibrated and monotone bounds can make branch-and-bound search for MPE more efficient on instances where classical bound computation is prohibitive.

title: TaxoMFM: A Taxonomy-Aware Foundation Model for the Human Gut Microbiome
summary: Existing gut microbiome foundation models typically use flat taxon representations, limiting their ability to exploit known taxonomic hierarchies. We introduce TaxoMFM, a microbiome foundation model that integrates taxonomic structure into self-supervised learning. TaxoMFM jointly learns abundance patterns across taxonomic ranks and relative proportions within groups through taxonomy-aware encoding and hierarchical compositional reconstruction. We further construct TaxoGut-HPP, comprising 100,806 gut microbiome profiles from 231 source cohorts and covering 40 classification and 8 regression tasks. TaxoMFM achieves competitive performance across disease, gut health, host trait, and liver ultrasound phenotype prediction. In cross-cohort zero-shot transfer, where target cohorts are excluded from both pretraining and downstream adaptation, TaxoMFM achieves AUROCs of 0.838, 0.736, and 0.722 for colorectal cancer, type 2 diabetes, and inflammatory bowel disease, respectively. Further analyses show that TaxoMFM recovers community changes across taxonomic scales, while preserving community information and producing consistent representations under database updates and species-vocabulary shifts. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: TaxoMFM is a gut microbiome foundation model that encodes known taxonomic hierarchies through self-supervised learning. It achieves competitive prediction performance and cross-cohort zero-shot transfer on disease phenotypes.
AI.motivation: Existing gut microbiome foundation models use flat taxon representations and so cannot exploit known taxonomic hierarchies.
AI.method: The model uses taxonomy-aware encoding and hierarchical compositional reconstruction to jointly learn abundance patterns across taxonomic ranks and relative proportions within groups. The authors also construct TaxoGut-HPP, comprising 100,806 gut microbiome profiles from 231 source cohorts, covering 40 classification and 8 regression tasks.
AI.result: TaxoMFM achieves competitive performance across disease, gut health, host trait and liver ultrasound phenotype prediction. In cross-cohort zero-shot transfer, where target cohorts are excluded from pretraining and downstream adaptation, it reaches AUROCs of 0.838, 0.736 and 0.722 for colorectal cancer, type 2 diabetes and inflammatory bowel disease.
AI.conclusion: The model recovers community changes across taxonomic scales and stays consistent under database updates and species-vocabulary shifts, supporting taxonomy-aware pretraining for microbiome data.

title: Class-aware Latent Attention Replay (CLAR): Class Incremental Hazard Diagnosis for Resilient AI in the Manufacturing Industrial Internet
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems provide critical computation services in the Manufacturing Industrial Internet (MII), and their resilience depends on timely diagnosis of hazards across the data, AI pipeline, and cyber-physical layers. During operation, new hazard types keep emerging with only a few samples each, hazards co-occur, and the diagnosis model runs on memory-constrained computation nodes. Replay-based class-incremental learning (CIL) can learn new hazard classes while revisiting a small memory of past samples, but existing methods assume single-label, balanced streams, store high-dimensional raw samples, and select them independently of the classifier. We propose Class-aware Latent Attention Replay (CLAR), which combines a dual buffer that stores mostly compact latent representations with a few raw samples, an Attention Leverage Score (ALS) that upper-bounds the classifier logit and guides class-balanced reservoir sampling, and an exponential-moving-average teacher that slows latent-space drift. For an idealized buffer model, we prove that the buffer is class-balanced and follows an ALS-weighted class distribution, and that below a critical per-class capacity, ALS-guided replay has a lower replay-gradient error than class-balanced uniform replay. In the case study, On hazard diagnosis data from an MII testbed, CLAR achieves the highest mean average weighted F1 score among the evaluated replay methods with the same buffer size

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CLAR, a replay-based class-incremental learning method for diagnosing hazards in manufacturing industrial internet systems under memory constraints. It achieves the highest mean average weighted F1 among the evaluated replay methods at the same buffer size.
AI.motivation: Hazard diagnosis in the Manufacturing Industrial Internet involves new hazard classes with few samples each, co-occurring hazards and memory-constrained nodes, while existing replay methods assume single-label balanced streams, store high-dimensional raw samples and select samples independently of the classifier.
AI.method: CLAR combines a dual buffer storing mostly compact latent representations plus a few raw samples, an Attention Leverage Score that upper-bounds the classifier logit and guides class-balanced reservoir sampling, and an exponential-moving-average teacher that slows latent-space drift.
AI.result: For an idealized buffer model, the authors prove the buffer is class-balanced and follows an ALS-weighted class distribution, and that below a critical per-class capacity ALS-guided replay has lower replay-gradient error than class-balanced uniform replay. On hazard diagnosis data from an MII testbed, CLAR achieves the highest mean average weighted F1 among the evaluated replay methods with the same buffer size.
AI.conclusion: Classifier-aware, latent-based replay can support resilient class-incremental hazard diagnosis on resource-constrained industrial nodes.

title: RetroChessBench: A Benchmark for Reconstructing and Proving Chess Histories
comment: 22 pages, 2 figures. Benchmark and RL environment: this https URL
summary: Frontier language models such as GPT 6 Astra have contributed to research mathematics, demonstrating substantial reasoning capabilities. Yet serious reasoning failures persist even in tasks governed by explicit rules. We demonstrate this in retrograde chess which is a playground for pure reasoning, where solvers reconstruct legal histories and distinguish possible events from forced ones. We introduce RetroChessBench, a 12-task benchmark covering exact-length constructions, unique endings, and exhaustive answer sets, with references, rubrics, and a terminal-reward environment. In two trials per task and condition, GPT 6 Astra High fails to produce the required final answer in 22/24 attempts without tools and 18/24 with code execution; mean terminal RL rewards are 14.75% and 27.19%, respectively. The examples identify faulty deductions: failed responses reject legal histories and treat temporary obstructions as permanent. Online retrograde archives often provide puzzles and final move sequences without detailed derivations. We hypothesize that limited exposure to these missing explanations in web-derived training data contributes to the observed reasoning failures. This questions how far frontier mathematical reasoning really generalizes beyond familiar solution patterns. Claims of general intelligence require evidence that models can transfer learnt principles to areas with few worked examples.

AI.tldr: RetroChessBench is a 12-task benchmark of retrograde chess that tests whether models can reconstruct legal histories and distinguish possible from forced events. Frontier models fail most attempts, with and without code execution.
AI.motivation: Frontier language models have contributed to research mathematics, yet serious reasoning failures persist on tasks governed by explicit rules, and it is unclear how far mathematical reasoning generalizes beyond familiar solution patterns.
AI.method: The benchmark covers exact-length constructions, unique endings and exhaustive answer sets, with references, rubrics and a terminal-reward environment. Each task is run in two trials per condition.
AI.result: GPT 6 Astra High fails to produce the required final answer in 22/24 attempts without tools and 18/24 with code execution, with mean terminal RL rewards of 14.75% and 27.19%, respectively. Failed responses reject legal histories and treat temporary obstructions as permanent.
AI.conclusion: The authors hypothesize that the scarcity of detailed derivations in web-derived training data contributes to these failures, and they argue that claims of general intelligence require transfer of principles to areas with few worked examples.

title: MulClip: A table-free activation function with monotonic and folding regimes for reservoir computing on microcontrollers
comment: 15 pages (7 pages main text, 8 pages appendices), 2 figures
summary: This letter proposes MulClip, a lightweight activation function for reservoir computing (RC) on microcontrollers (MCUs). In a ring reservoir, a representative sparse RC topology, multiply-accumulate operations are few, and evaluating tanh accounted for 75% of the state-update time on a Cortex-M4. MulClip introduces curvature into the response using only comparison, absolute value, multiplication, and subtraction, and places its clipping threshold not at the extremum but at the point where the response returns to zero after passing the extremum. As a result, a single function has both a monotonic regime and a nonmonotonic folding regime that increases the expressiveness of a single unit. Which regime is used is determined by the usual hyperparameter search, e.g., over the input scale, so no task-specific threshold tuning is required. The state-update time measured on hardware was 0.34 times that of tanh and shorter than that of any of the 11 evaluated tanh approximations. In PC-based evaluation, third-order MulClip achieved a 22% lower NMSE than tanh on NARMA-20, where the pre-activations remained in the monotonic regime, and on 8-bit parity it raised the accuracy from 0.76-0.78 for the monotonic-clip variant without folding to 0.97-0.98. For these two tasks, on-device inference yielded nearly the same values as on the PC.

AI.tldr: MulClip is a table-free activation function for reservoir computing on microcontrollers that adds curvature with only comparison, absolute value, multiplication and subtraction. It runs in 0.34 times the state-update time of tanh on a Cortex-M4 and achieves lower error on NARMA-20 and higher accuracy on 8-bit parity.
AI.motivation: On microcontrollers, evaluating tanh accounts for 75% of the state-update time in a ring reservoir, which has few multiply-accumulate operations.
AI.method: MulClip places its clipping threshold at the point where the response returns to zero after passing the extremum, so a single function has a monotonic regime and a nonmonotonic folding regime. The regime is selected by the usual hyperparameter search, for example over the input scale, without task-specific threshold tuning.
AI.result: The state-update time measured on hardware is 0.34 times that of tanh and shorter than that of any of the 11 evaluated tanh approximations. In PC-based evaluation, third-order MulClip achieves 22% lower NMSE than tanh on NARMA-20, and on 8-bit parity it raises accuracy from 0.76-0.78 for the monotonic-clip variant to 0.97-0.98. On-device inference yields nearly the same values as on the PC for these tasks.
AI.conclusion: The folding regime increases the expressiveness of a single unit, making MulClip a fast and accurate alternative to tanh for reservoir computing on microcontrollers.

title: More Is Better? Exploring Latent Correspondence in Federated Hypergraph Learning
summary: Federated hypergraph learning with latent cross-client hyperedge correspondence poses fundamental identifiability and computational challenges, as the same local release can correspond to multiple global hypergraph structures. We characterize the tractability of recovering these latent correspondences, showing tractable pairwise assignment but generally intractable multi-client hyperedge matching. Building on this characterization, we derive a cross-entropy decomposition that reveals when local prediction can outperform predictors fitted with additional cross-client information. Motivated by this principle, we introduce Federated Adaptive Spectral Training with Representation Alignment (FedASTRA), which learns correspondence-invariant diffusion representations through adaptive heat diffusion and masked latent prediction while communicating model parameters only. We establish its asymptotic optimality with respect to the permitted local information and prove global population-risk convergence under explicit conditions on recovery, representation, and update alignment. Experiments on eight real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of FedASTRA against identifier-free federated graph and hypergraph methods. On ogbn-papers100M, FedASTRA reaches the performance-communication Pareto frontier, achieving 50.07 Accuracy and 29.73 Macro-F1 while communicating only 59.60 MiB per round.

AI.tldr: The paper characterizes which latent cross-client hyperedge correspondences are tractable to recover in federated hypergraph learning and proposes FedASTRA, which communicates only model parameters. It reaches the performance-communication Pareto frontier on ogbn-papers100M.
AI.motivation: Federated hypergraph learning with latent cross-client hyperedge correspondence has identifiability and computational challenges, since one local release can correspond to multiple global hypergraph structures.
AI.method: The authors show pairwise assignment is tractable but multi-client hyperedge matching is generally intractable, and derive a cross-entropy decomposition that indicates when local prediction can beat predictors using extra cross-client information. FedASTRA learns correspondence-invariant diffusion representations through adaptive heat diffusion and masked latent prediction.
AI.result: On eight real-world datasets FedASTRA is effective against identifier-free federated graph and hypergraph methods. On ogbn-papers100M it reaches 50.07 Accuracy and 29.73 Macro-F1 while communicating 59.60 MiB per round. The authors establish asymptotic optimality with respect to the permitted local information and prove global population-risk convergence under explicit conditions.
AI.conclusion: Correspondence-invariant representations learned from local data can match or exceed methods that use cross-client identifiers, with a favorable communication cost.

title: Safe Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning: Zero Constraint Violation and Primal-Averaging Convergence
summary: Many applications of multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) require policies that balance conflicting objectives while satisfying safety constraints. We study safe MORL with zero constraint violation throughout learning, covering both cumulative and stepwise constraints. A key challenge is to explore sufficiently under unknown dynamics and constraint costs without violating the constraints. For a given preference over objectives, we develop an algorithm to learn a safe Pareto optimal policy by combining optimistic reward estimates with pessimistic cost bounds. With high probability, every policy executed over $T$ episodes incurs zero constraint violation. The algorithm returns a safe Markov policy induced by the averaged occupancy measure and achieves an $\widetilde{O}(1/\sqrt{T})$ suboptimality gap under smooth Tchebycheff scalarization. We further develop a preference-free algorithm that first explores safely without a prespecified preference and then computes a safe policy for any given preference without further interaction. Over $T$ exploration episodes and $K$ planning iterations, it retains the same safety guarantee and achieves an $\widetilde{O}(1/\sqrt{T}+1/\sqrt{K})$ suboptimality gap. Both algorithms require knowledge of a policy that strictly satisfies the constraints and its costs. We then relax these requirements, incurring at most constant cumulative violation. To our knowledge, we provide the first sample-efficient MORL algorithms that guarantee safety for every executed policy.

AI.tldr: The paper gives safe multi-objective RL algorithms with zero constraint violation during learning, combining optimistic reward estimates with pessimistic cost bounds. They achieve a suboptimality gap of O~(1/sqrt(T)) and a preference-free variant also covers K planning iterations.
AI.motivation: Multi-objective RL applications need policies that balance conflicting objectives while satisfying safety constraints, and the challenge is to explore enough under unknown dynamics and constraint costs without violating the constraints.
AI.method: For a given preference, the algorithm learns a safe Pareto optimal policy by combining optimistic reward estimates with pessimistic cost bounds, returning a safe Markov policy induced by the averaged occupancy measure. A preference-free algorithm explores safely first and then computes a safe policy for any given preference without further interaction.
AI.result: With high probability every policy executed over T episodes incurs zero constraint violation, and the suboptimality gap under smooth Tchebycheff scalarization is O~(1/sqrt(T)). The preference-free method achieves O~(1/sqrt(T)+1/sqrt(K)) over T exploration episodes and K planning iterations with the same safety guarantee. Relaxed versions incur at most constant cumulative violation.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides the first sample-efficient MORL algorithms that guarantee safety for every executed policy, although the base versions require a known strictly feasible policy and its costs, which the relaxations weaken.

title: Dobb: Shard-Local Preconditioning in Block-Diagonal Eigenbases
summary: Training language models whose parameters and optimizer state exceed a single node's memory requires sharding these tensors across devices. Under tensor parallelism (TP) or fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP), matrix-aware optimizers such as Muon introduce communication to perform global matrix operations across shards. We propose Dobb (Distributed Optimizer with Block-diagonal Eigenbases), a matrix-aware optimizer designed to compute updates locally within parameter shards. Dobb approximates the input-activation second moment with diagonal blocks and tracks a complete basis within each block. It projects momentum into these bases, applies sign normalization to the coefficients, and reconstructs the update. When each block lies within one shard under TP or FSDP, Dobb applies its matrix update locally, requiring no communication beyond data-parallel synchronization of the activation second moments. We benchmark Dobb against Dion, a distributed matrix-aware optimizer designed to retain the benefits of orthonormalized updates while reducing communication. On GPT-2 XL (1.56B parameters), Dobb with 16 blocks reaches a validation loss of 2.476, compared with 2.511 for Dion at rank fraction 1/16. Under FSDP on 32 H100 GPUs, Dobb reduces the amortized optimizer-call time from 124.1 ms for Dion to 9.2 ms.

AI.tldr: Dobb is a matrix-aware optimizer that computes its updates locally within parameter shards under tensor or fully sharded data parallelism, so it needs no communication beyond data-parallel synchronization of activation second moments. It matches or beats Dion on validation loss and cuts optimizer-call time sharply.
AI.motivation: Matrix-aware optimizers such as Muon introduce communication to perform global matrix operations across shards when parameters and optimizer state are sharded across devices.
AI.method: Dobb approximates the input-activation second moment with diagonal blocks, tracks a complete basis within each block, projects momentum into these bases, applies sign normalization to the coefficients and reconstructs the update. When each block lies within one shard, the update is applied locally.
AI.result: On GPT-2 XL (1.56B parameters), Dobb with 16 blocks reaches a validation loss of 2.476, compared with 2.511 for Dion at rank fraction 1/16. Under FSDP on 32 H100 GPUs, the amortized optimizer-call time drops from 124.1 ms for Dion to 9.2 ms.
AI.conclusion: Shard-local preconditioning in block-diagonal eigenbases can retain the benefits of matrix-aware updates while avoiding the communication cost of global matrix operations.

title: Accuracy is not compatibility: two Evo 2 checkpoints hinge on one FP8 matrix multiplication
comment: 18 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Data: this https URL ; code: this https URL
summary: FP8 formats specify how values are stored, not how products are summed; this gap can break checkpoints. Evo 2, a DNA language model, documents a Hopper FP8 requirement for its 1B and 40B checkpoints. On two Blackwell (sm_120) GPUs both fail the developers' forward test (the 7B passes); on an RTX 5070 Ti the 40B's next-base accuracy is 25.7%, near guessing. Greater accuracy breaks them, as BioNeMo saw for the 40B on Hopper: natively, 99.996% of one projection's outputs are correctly rounded (H100: about 30%), and fp32 accumulation of the same operands fails. Our H100 FP8 GEMM emulator, mmaemu (bit-exact on captured 1B projections), localises the dependence to the 1B's first projection (of 21), where exact sums fail but pass when shrunk by the H100's 1.4% (measured in-sample), not 2.1%. The 40B fails with only its first projection native. Emulating only that projection, weights unchanged, raises 40B BRCA1 variant-classification AUROC from 0.434 to 0.869 (H100: 0.868) on the RTX 5070 Ti, despite a narrow forward-test miss, and 0.481 to 0.867 on an RTX PRO 6000. We tested one model family but not training origin; releases should specify reference arithmetic.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that two Evo 2 DNA language model checkpoints fail on Blackwell GPUs because of how one FP8 matrix multiplication sums products, and that emulating a single projection natively restores variant-classification AUROC. The authors argue that releases should specify their reference arithmetic.
AI.motivation: FP8 formats specify storage but not how products are summed, and this gap can break checkpoints. Evo 2 documents a Hopper FP8 requirement for its 1B and 40B checkpoints, and it was unclear where the dependence on FP8 arithmetic lies.
AI.method: The authors use mmaemu, an H100 FP8 GEMM emulator that is bit-exact on captured 1B projections, to localize the dependence to the first projection of the 1B model (of 21). They emulate only that projection in the 40B model, keeping weights unchanged.
AI.result: On two Blackwell (sm_120) GPUs both checkpoints fail the developers' forward test, while the 7B passes. On an RTX 5070 Ti the 40B model's next-base accuracy is 25.7%. Emulating only the first projection raises 40B BRCA1 variant-classification AUROC from 0.434 to 0.869 on the RTX 5070 Ti (H100: 0.868) and from 0.481 to 0.867 on an RTX PRO 6000.
AI.conclusion: Greater accuracy in the matrix product can break checkpoints tuned to Hopper FP8 arithmetic, so model releases should specify their reference arithmetic. The authors tested one model family only.

title: LinQuant: Functional Invariances for Low-Precision Linear Recurrences
comment: 35 pages, 16 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Linear recurrences are emerging as practical alternatives to softmax attention in large language models, appearing in both standalone and hybrid architectures. However, despite their rapid emergence, low-precision inference remains much less developed for these models than for softmax attention. During prefill, chunkwise-parallel algorithms cast much of the recurrence as dense matrix multiplications, suggesting a natural path to low-precision execution. Simply quantizing these operations in their native form, however, can be fragile. In this work, we identify functional invariances that preserve the full-precision computation while making the operands more amenable to quantization. Building on this observation, we introduce LinQuant, a framework for low-precision recurrent prefill based on seven such invariances, including rotations, diagonal rescalings, and alternative placements of recurrent decay and write factors. We derive when these transformations remain valid across common recurrence families spanning linear, gated, and delta-rule updates, and show that they provide complementary degrees of freedom for improving low-precision accuracy. Finally, we translate this framework to production by augmenting SSDi8, an existing low-precision prefill pipeline for Mamba-2, with the applicable invariances. LinQuant improves perplexity at matched latency on Mamba-2 1.3B, 2.7B, and 8B and Nemotron-H 8B, demonstrating the practical utility of invariance-based quantization for recurrent models.

AI.tldr: LinQuant is a framework for low-precision prefill of linear recurrences built on seven functional invariances that preserve full-precision computation while making operands easier to quantize. It improves perplexity at matched latency on Mamba-2 and Nemotron-H models.
AI.motivation: Linear recurrences are emerging alternatives to softmax attention, but low-precision inference for them is much less developed, and simply quantizing the chunkwise-parallel operations in their native form can be fragile.
AI.method: The authors identify seven invariances, including rotations, diagonal rescalings and alternative placements of recurrent decay and write factors, derive when they remain valid across linear, gated and delta-rule recurrence families, and augment SSDi8, an existing low-precision prefill pipeline for Mamba-2, with the applicable invariances.
AI.result: LinQuant improves perplexity at matched latency on Mamba-2 1.3B, 2.7B and 8B and on Nemotron-H 8B.
AI.conclusion: Invariance-based quantization gives complementary degrees of freedom for improving low-precision accuracy and is practically useful for recurrent models.

title: Softmax Routing Dynamics in Mixture-of-Experts Models: Collapse and Recovery
summary: Softmax routing in mixture-of-experts models can concentrate probability on a subset of experts, suppressing access to the others. We study how this concentration forms, why it persists, and how suppressed probabilities recover. For fixed experts, a stationary-loss barrier identifies the face supporting the optimal routed output. In a common-target square-loss model with freely trainable expert outputs, slow adaptation tracks fixed-expert dynamics on finite horizons, while every fixed positive adaptation rate yields an interior routing limit. An exact normal-velocity decomposition separates complementary-expert covariance from relative gradient advantage. Under positive two-sided power bounds along recovery paths, uniform over initial masses, the resulting coefficient's order of vanishing gives logarithmic or power-law recovery times. Integrations of constructed fields reproduce these orders. An exact discrete log-odds identity relates neural updates to threshold crossing. In paired Transformer-MoE training, removing a class-conditional router-gradient contrast delays confirmed recovery and reduces accumulated log-odds on fixed tokens, both with and without capacity constraints.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how softmax routing in mixture-of-experts models collapses onto a subset of experts, why this persists, and how suppressed experts recover. It derives logarithmic or power-law recovery times and shows that removing a class-conditional router-gradient contrast delays recovery in Transformer-MoE training.
AI.motivation: Softmax routing can concentrate probability on a few experts and suppress access to the others, and the formation, persistence and recovery of this concentration were not well understood.
AI.method: For fixed experts, a stationary-loss barrier identifies the face supporting the optimal routed output. In a common-target square-loss model with trainable expert outputs, an exact normal-velocity decomposition separates complementary-expert covariance from relative gradient advantage, and recovery times are derived under positive two-sided power bounds.
AI.result: Under these bounds the recovery time is logarithmic or power-law in the coefficient's order of vanishing, and integrations of constructed fields reproduce these orders. In paired Transformer-MoE training, removing a class-conditional router-gradient contrast delays confirmed recovery and reduces accumulated log-odds on fixed tokens, with and without capacity constraints.
AI.conclusion: Router gradient contrasts drive recovery of suppressed experts, and the exact discrete log-odds identity links neural updates to threshold crossing.

title: End-to-End Guarantees for Masked Diffusion Models under Conditional Mixing
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Diffusion Language Models: Foundations, Efficiency, and Reasoning (DiffuLM). 26 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables
summary: Masked diffusion models train a denoiser on masked cross-entropy and generate by unmasking many positions in parallel. Existing MDM sampling bounds assume an exact denoiser or leave its error uncontrolled while training bounds cover only the masking distribution on which the model was trained. We present an end-to-end guarantee for a learned denoiser under conditional mixing (CM): stationary sources (e.g. floored order-$r$ Markov and two-sided-Doeblin hidden-Markov sources) for which revealing distant visible tokens moves a masked token's posterior on average exponentially little in the distance with correlation length $\tau_c$. We show the empirical risk minimizer trained under any masking distribution attains per-token excess $\varepsilon'$ on that distribution from $\varepsilon'^{-\mathcal{O}(\tau_c\log|\mathcal{V}|)}$ training sequences, independent of sequence length $N$ -- one sample budget serves every decoding schedule when each schedule's denoiser is trained under its own weighting. We further show that the exponent's order $\Theta(\tau_c\log|\mathcal{V}|)$ is minimax-optimal up to constants; more efficient rates require added structure. With this, we bound the end-to-end KL as $\mathrm{KL}(\pi\Vert p_{\mathrm{alg}})\leq \varepsilon+N\varepsilon'$ under a dilated schedule of $T=\mathcal{O}(\tau_c\log(N|\mathcal{V}|/\varepsilon))$ denoising steps versus $\Omega(N)$ steps for a fixed random order on an explicit CM source. Finally, we show that block-autoregressive samplers chain across blocks with no added error and that a $\Lambda$-looped order-$r$ message-passing class on order-$r$ sources achieves polynomial sample complexity, with approximation error improving per loop until saturation at $\Lambda r\approx \tau_c\log(1/\varepsilon')$. Experiments on released and retrained models support our results' qualitative predictions.
