AI.tldr: The paper gives an end-to-end KL guarantee for masked diffusion models with learned denoisers under conditional mixing, and shows a dilated schedule needs far fewer denoising steps than a fixed random order. The sample complexity exponent is minimax-optimal up to constants.
AI.motivation: Existing sampling bounds for masked diffusion models assume an exact denoiser or leave its error uncontrolled, and training bounds cover only the masking distribution on which the model was trained.
AI.method: The analysis assumes stationary sources with conditional mixing, such as floored order-r Markov and two-sided-Doeblin hidden-Markov sources, where revealing distant visible tokens moves a masked token's posterior exponentially little with correlation length tau_c. The empirical risk minimizer is analyzed under any masking distribution, and block-autoregressive samplers and a Lambda-looped message-passing class are also studied.
AI.result: Training sequences needed for per-token excess error are independent of sequence length N, with exponent Theta(tau_c log|V|), minimax-optimal up to constants. The end-to-end KL is bounded by epsilon plus N times epsilon' under a dilated schedule of T = O(tau_c log(N|V|/epsilon)) steps, versus Omega(N) steps for a fixed random order. Block-autoregressive chaining adds no error, and the looped class achieves polynomial sample complexity.
AI.conclusion: Experiments on released and retrained models support the qualitative predictions, and more efficient rates require added structure beyond conditional mixing.

title: Smooth Action Chunking Via Movement-Primitive Representations for Imitation Learning
summary: Imitation learning has become a widely adopted approach for vision-based robot policies, owing to its conceptual simplicity, scalability, and ability to leverage large-scale datasets. As these policies have grown more capable, action chunking has become their standard interface. At each decision step the policy outputs several future actions at once. Backbones from diffusion policies to large vision-language-action models all share it. Whatever backbone produces the chunk, its temporal structure is learned only implicitly. The commanded trajectory is therefore jerky both within a chunk and between successive chunks. On real hardware this appears as visible vibration and as repeated saturation of the follower's velocity limit. We address this issue by incorporating a movement-primitive-based trajectory representation into action chunking. Specifically, a trajectory segment is represented as a linear combination of smooth basis functions, yielding smooth trajectories by construction while leaving the policy architecture, training objective, and inference procedure unchanged. The same representation also yields a closed-form, inference-time correction for the second source of jerk. We condition the predicted coefficients so that the new chunk passes through a via-point at the previous chunk's last commanded action. This correction needs no retraining and, unlike asynchronous Real-Time Chunking, applies to policies queried in one shot. We instantiate it on a one-shot (ACT) and an iterative (DiT) backbone and evaluate in simulation and on a real bimanual ALOHA platform. The representation lowers within-chunk jerk by an order of magnitude on the one-shot backbone and by 2.4 times on the iterative one, with task success statistically non-inferior. The conditioning then removes 73-84% of the boundary discontinuity, at negligible per-step cost.

AI.tldr: The paper adds a movement-primitive trajectory representation to action chunking, making chunks smooth by construction, and adds a closed-form inference-time via-point correction at the chunk boundary. It cuts within-chunk jerk and removes most of the boundary discontinuity with no retraining.
AI.motivation: Action chunks in vision-based imitation policies learn temporal structure only implicitly, so commanded trajectories are jerky within and between chunks, causing visible vibration and repeated saturation of the follower's velocity limit on real hardware.
AI.method: Each trajectory segment is represented as a linear combination of smooth basis functions, leaving the architecture, training objective and inference unchanged. The predicted coefficients are conditioned so the new chunk passes through a via-point at the previous chunk's last commanded action. The method is instantiated on a one-shot (ACT) and an iterative (DiT) backbone.
AI.result: The representation lowers within-chunk jerk by an order of magnitude on the one-shot backbone and by 2.4 times on the iterative one, with task success statistically non-inferior. The conditioning removes 73-84% of the boundary discontinuity at negligible per-step cost. Evaluation covers simulation and a real bimanual ALOHA platform.
AI.conclusion: The correction applies to policies queried in one shot, unlike asynchronous Real-Time Chunking, so it offers a low-cost way to obtain smooth action sequences.

title: Sparse Fine-Tuning for Parameter-Efficient Adversarial Training
summary: Deep neural networks achieve strong performance across many tasks but remain vulnerable to adversarial perturbations. Adversarial training (AT) is one of the most effective defenses, yet it suffers from high memory cost on large models and the persistent clean-robust accuracy trade-off. Recent work introduces parameter-efficient fine-tuning, such as LoRA, into AT, but this constraint induces a notable robustness gap relative to full-parameter AT. In this work, we revisit parameter-efficient adversarial fine-tuning from a parameter space perspective. Through gradient analysis, we find that adversarial optimization is highly concentrated on a small subset of parameters, which we call Robustness-Critical Parameters (RCPs), suggesting that robustness is encoded in a sparse subspace. Building on this observation, we propose Sparse Adversarial Fine-Tuning (SAFT), which identifies RCPs via adversarial gradient saliency and performs AT by updating only these parameters while freezing the rest. Across architectures and datasets, SAFT outperforms LoRA-based methods in both clean and robust accuracy with fewer trainable parameters, and approaches or surpasses full parameter AT in robustness while updating only about 5\% of parameters.

AI.tldr: SAFT is a sparse fine-tuning method for adversarial training that updates only Robustness-Critical Parameters, about 5% of parameters, and outperforms LoRA-based methods in clean and robust accuracy. It approaches or surpasses full-parameter adversarial training in robustness.
AI.motivation: Adversarial training is effective but memory-costly on large models and trades off clean and robust accuracy, and LoRA-based parameter-efficient adversarial fine-tuning shows a notable robustness gap relative to full-parameter training.
AI.method: Gradient analysis shows adversarial optimization concentrates on a small subset of parameters, termed Robustness-Critical Parameters (RCPs). SAFT identifies RCPs via adversarial gradient saliency and performs adversarial training by updating only these parameters while freezing the rest.
AI.result: Across architectures and datasets, SAFT outperforms LoRA-based methods in both clean and robust accuracy with fewer trainable parameters, and approaches or surpasses full-parameter adversarial training in robustness while updating only about 5% of parameters.
AI.conclusion: Robustness appears to be encoded in a sparse subspace of parameters, which makes sparse fine-tuning a parameter-efficient route to adversarial robustness.

title: Achieving Minimax-Optimal First-Order and Best-of-Both-Worlds Regret Simultaneously in Multi-Armed Bandits
summary: We study first-order and best-of-both-worlds regret guarantees in multi-armed bandits. Pogodin and Lattimore (2019) proposed an algorithm that combines minimax-optimal worst-case regret with a first-order guarantee whose loss-dependent term is $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{K L^\star}\log T)$, where $T$ denotes the horizon, $L^\star$ denotes the smallest expected cumulative loss among fixed arms, and $K$ denotes the number of arms. However, a logarithmic gap remains between this loss-dependent term and the optimal first-order scale. In this paper, we remove this logarithmic factor by proposing an efficient and parameter-free algorithm that achieves the minimax optimal first-order regret guarantee $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{K L^\star})$. Technically, our algorithm is built upon FTRL with a Tsallis entropy regularizer (Zimmert and Seldin,2021), with a learning rate adapted to the learner's cumulative loss and a sampling distribution determined by a scalar fixed point. This construction controls the combined estimation and stability cost in terms of the learner's loss. Moreover, we show that the same algorithm achieves a best-of-both-worlds guarantee, with $\mathcal{O}(\sum_{i\ne i^\star}\frac{\log T}{\Delta_i})$ regret for i.i.d. losses with a unique best arm $i^\star$, where $\Delta_i$ denotes the suboptimality gap of arm $i$.

AI.tldr: The paper gives an efficient, parameter-free algorithm for multi-armed bandits that achieves minimax-optimal first-order regret O(sqrt(K L*)) and also a best-of-both-worlds guarantee. It removes the logarithmic gap left by Pogodin and Lattimore (2019).
AI.motivation: The first-order regret bound of Pogodin and Lattimore (2019) has a logarithmic gap, O(sqrt(K L*) log T), relative to the optimal first-order scale.
AI.method: The algorithm is based on FTRL with a Tsallis entropy regularizer, with a learning rate adapted to the learner's cumulative loss and a sampling distribution determined by a scalar fixed point, which controls the combined estimation and stability cost in terms of the learner's loss.
AI.result: The algorithm achieves O(sqrt(K L*)) first-order regret. For i.i.d. losses with a unique best arm, the same algorithm achieves O(sum over i not equal to i* of log T / Delta_i) regret, which is a best-of-both-worlds guarantee.
AI.conclusion: A single parameter-free algorithm attains both minimax-optimal first-order regret and best-of-both-worlds regret, removing the logarithmic factor in the loss-dependent term.

title: CBE: A Complexity-adaptive Boundary-aware Ensemble Method for Imbalanced Data
summary: In many real-world classification tasks, datasets exhibit class imbalance, which can degrade the generalization performance of conventional learning algorithms. Data complexity has recently been recognized as a more objective indicator of learning difficulty than the imbalance ratio alone, because class overlap and complex decision boundaries often impair classifiers more severely than imbalance itself. Samples near the decision boundary are inherently difficult to classify, which has motivated many researchers to focus on such instances to improve classifier performance. However, most under-sampling approaches fail to differentiate their sampling of boundary samples across datasets of varying complexity. To overcome this limitation, we propose a complexity-adaptive boundary-aware ensemble (CBE) framework that links the sampling weight distribution to data complexity and dynamically adjusts the boundary preference of under-sampling accordingly. We also introduce an overall complexity measure that combines metrics at multiple levels and use it to divide imbalanced datasets into three categories. Extensive experiments on 24 benchmark datasets from UCI and KEEL show that the proposed method outperforms many existing methods in terms of F-measure and G-mean on Easy and Median datasets, without degrading performance on hard cases.

AI.tldr: CBE is a complexity-adaptive, boundary-aware ensemble for imbalanced classification that adjusts its boundary preference in under-sampling according to dataset complexity. It outperforms many existing methods on Easy and Median datasets without degrading performance on hard ones.
AI.motivation: Data complexity is a more objective indicator of learning difficulty than imbalance ratio alone, but most under-sampling methods do not adapt their boundary sampling across datasets of varying complexity.
AI.method: CBE links the sampling weight distribution to data complexity and dynamically adjusts the boundary preference of under-sampling. An overall complexity measure combining metrics at multiple levels divides imbalanced datasets into three categories.
AI.result: On 24 benchmark datasets from UCI and KEEL, the method outperforms many existing methods in F-measure and G-mean on Easy and Median datasets, without degrading performance on hard cases.
AI.conclusion: Adapting the boundary preference of under-sampling to data complexity can improve ensemble classification on imbalanced data across difficulty levels.

title: Topology Survives Shuffling: Robust Long-Context Memory Access Prediction for Graph Analytics
summary: Graph analytics generates irregular, topology-dependent memory-access streams via indirect traversals, limiting data prefetching. Accurate prediction enables timely prefetches that hide memory latency. However, ML predictors couple short histories with fixed horizons, fitting the training trace's node layout rather than learning transferable graph patterns. We propose LoCoMAP, a long-context representation-learning framework for memory-access prediction with independently controlled observation history and prediction horizon. We evaluate Connected Components (CC), PageRank (PR), and Single-Source Shortest Paths (SSSP) on six synthetic graph families, with Erdos-Renyi (ER) and Grid as random and deterministic controls. We test two interventions: same-family regeneration changes connectivity, while node shuffling disrupts layout but preserves connectivity. Across 18 graph-workload pairs, extending history from 8 to 128 accesses improves F1 by 7.8%, while extending prediction horizon from 8 to 512 improves F1 by 88.3%. For CC, regeneration is less disruptive than shuffling: without retraining, long context retains 95.4% of original F1 and outperforms short context in six families. Under full shuffle, long context improves CC F1 by 33.6% across ER, Barabasi-Albert, Copying Model, and Stochastic Block Model (SBM), with a 2.06x gain on SBM, but not on Watts-Strogatz or Grid, where near-zero delta mass shifts into heavy tails beyond the predictor's range. Long context outperforms short context on six real-world CC graphs. At full shuffle, long-context PR retains 57.6% of original F1 and averages 11.0% above short context. Both SSSP models retain about 30% of original F1 under full shuffle as distance updates access vertex data in a new order. Within these bounds, long-context predictors are robust across related graphs and layouts without retraining, enabling a generalizable graph prefetcher.

AI.tldr: LoCoMAP is a long-context representation-learning framework for memory-access prediction in graph analytics that controls observation history and prediction horizon independently. Long context improves prediction and stays robust across related graphs and layouts without retraining.
AI.motivation: Irregular, topology-dependent memory-access streams limit prefetching, and ML predictors couple short histories with fixed horizons, so they fit the training trace's node layout rather than transferable graph patterns.
AI.method: LoCoMAP decouples observation history from prediction horizon. The authors evaluate Connected Components, PageRank and SSSP on six synthetic graph families plus Erdos-Renyi and Grid controls, with two interventions: same-family regeneration, which changes connectivity, and node shuffling, which disrupts layout but preserves connectivity.
AI.result: Across 18 graph-workload pairs, extending history from 8 to 128 accesses improves F1 by 7.8%, and extending the horizon from 8 to 512 improves F1 by 88.3%. Under full shuffle, long context improves CC F1 by 33.6% across several families, and long-context PR retains 57.6% of original F1 and averages 11.0% above short context. Long context outperforms short context on six real-world CC graphs. Both SSSP models retain about 30% of original F1 under full shuffle.
AI.conclusion: Long-context predictors are robust across related graphs and layouts without retraining, which supports a generalizable graph prefetcher, although gains do not hold for Watts-Strogatz or Grid graphs.

title: Interpretable by Design Tabular Prediction via In-Context Local Linear Learning
summary: In-context learning (ICL) lets tabular foundation models make predictions without dataset-specific training or fine-tuning. These models achieve strong predictive accuracy, but interpreting how individual features contribute to the prediction remains difficult. In biology, for example, feature contributions can help identify biomarkers or risk genes. Post-hoc interpretability methods assign feature importance scores, but these scores do not indicate what the model actually uses and can lead to explanation errors. We introduce TICL$^3$ (Tabular In-Context Local Linear Learning), an interpretable-by-design predictor that uses a tabular foundation model to guide a simple linear prediction rule. TICL$^3$ first learns a shared linear model to capture dataset-level feature effects. Then, for each query, it retrieves similar training samples using representations from the foundation model and fits a second linear model to the residuals in that neighborhood. The shared model captures broad effects, while the local model corrects errors among similar samples. Their combined coefficients determine each feature contribution to the final query-specific linear score, so the same model makes and explains the prediction. Across 386 classification benchmark-dataset evaluations, TICL$^3$ trails TabICLv2 by 1.1 percentage points and outperforms CatBoost in 266 evaluations. It improves average support F1 over MAPLE by 4.7 points and achieves the best performance on both real-data selected-feature utility metrics.

AI.tldr: TICL3 is an interpretable-by-design tabular predictor that combines a shared linear model with a per-query local linear model fitted on retrieved neighbors, so the same model makes and explains predictions. It trails TabICLv2 by 1.1 percentage points and beats CatBoost in 266 of 386 evaluations.
AI.motivation: Tabular foundation models make accurate in-context predictions but are hard to interpret, and post-hoc importance scores do not show what the model actually uses and can lead to explanation errors.
AI.method: TICL3 first learns a shared linear model for dataset-level feature effects. For each query it retrieves similar training samples using foundation-model representations and fits a second linear model to the residuals in that neighborhood. The combined coefficients give each feature's contribution to the query-specific linear score.
AI.result: Across 386 classification benchmark-dataset evaluations, TICL3 trails TabICLv2 by 1.1 percentage points and outperforms CatBoost in 266 evaluations. It improves average support F1 over MAPLE by 4.7 points and achieves the best performance on both real-data selected-feature utility metrics.
AI.conclusion: Combining a shared linear model with local residual correction yields a predictor whose explanations are exact for the model's own predictions, at a small accuracy cost relative to the strongest foundation model.

title: Last-Iterate Convergence for Constrained MDPs: From Dual Descent to Primal-Dual
summary: We study policy optimization for infinite-horizon, discounted constrained Markov decision processes. While primal-dual ($\texttt{PD}$) methods are widely used in practice, their theoretical guarantees typically hold for an impractical mixture policy. In contrast, dual descent ($\texttt{DD}$) methods output a single policy ("last iterate") with guarantees on its performance. However, such methods require iteratively solving entropy-regularized MDPs in an inner-loop, limiting their practical effectiveness. Moreover, existing analyses rely on strong coverage assumptions that are difficult to satisfy in practice. Consequently, we first provide a new analysis of $\texttt{DD}$ methods that does not require coverage assumptions. We then employ entropy-regularized natural policy gradient and dual regularization to eliminate the inner loop, resulting in an efficient $\texttt{PD}$ algorithm. We develop a novel tracking analysis which shows that, compared to existing methods, the proposed algorithm achieves improved last-iterate convergence guarantees. Furthermore, our theoretical framework allows us to analyze a truncated bilevel method that interpolates between $\texttt{DD}$ and $\texttt{PD}$ methods. Finally, we generalize our analysis to handle linear function approximation. Compared to prior last-iterate methods, we prove stronger guarantees under less restrictive assumptions.

AI.tldr: Gives a coverage-free analysis of dual descent for constrained MDPs and an efficient primal-dual algorithm without an inner loop, with improved last-iterate convergence guarantees over prior methods. The framework also covers a truncated bilevel method that interpolates between DD and PD, and extends to linear function approximation.
AI.motivation: Primal-dual methods are widely used, but their guarantees hold only for an impractical mixture policy. Dual descent yields a single last-iterate policy with guarantees, but requires an inner loop of entropy-regularized MDP solves and relies on strong coverage assumptions that are hard to satisfy in practice.
AI.method: A new analysis of DD that needs no coverage assumptions, followed by entropy-regularized natural policy gradient with dual regularization to remove the inner loop, yielding an efficient PD algorithm analysed with a novel tracking argument. A truncated bilevel method interpolating DD and PD is analysed within the same framework, and the analysis is generalised to linear function approximation.
AI.result: The proposed PD algorithm achieves improved last-iterate convergence guarantees compared with existing methods, and the authors prove stronger guarantees under less restrictive assumptions than prior last-iterate methods. The abstract reports no numerical values.
AI.conclusion: The results make last-iterate constrained policy optimisation both theoretically stronger and more practical, since a single policy is output with guarantees and no inner loop is needed.

title: Explainable and Adaptive Machine Learning for Fraud Risk Detection in Bangladesh's Digital Banking Ecosystem
comment: 23 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables. Presented at the 11th Annual Banking Conference 2026, Bangladesh Institute of Bank Management (BIBM), Dhaka, Bangladesh, 28 October 2026
summary: The rapid expansion of digital banking and mobile financial services creates growing challenges for fraud detection, particularly under severe class imbalance and operational constraints. This study presents an explainable and adaptive machine-learning framework integrating chronological evaluation, leakage-conscious feature engineering, probability calibration, SHAP-based explainability, and adaptive risk prioritization. Experiments use the synthetic PaySim mobile-money benchmark and compare Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM. XGBoost achieved the strongest fixed-threshold performance, with PR-AUC of 0.5658, ROC-AUC of 0.9068, and F1-score of 0.5369. Platt calibration reduced the test Brier score from 0.1141 to 0.0245, improving probability reliability. SHAP analysis identified temporal, destination-account, transaction-type, and amount features as important model drivers. An adaptive top-1% policy reduced false positives from 192 to 117, but recall declined from 0.4236 to 0.2122, demonstrating a clear alert-capacity trade-off. The results provide a reproducible methodological framework rather than evidence of deployment performance in Bangladesh, since PaySim is synthetic. Validation using governed real-world financial data is therefore an important direction for future research.

AI.tldr: Builds an explainable and adaptive fraud detection framework for severely imbalanced mobile-money data, evaluated on the synthetic PaySim benchmark. XGBoost gives the best fixed-threshold performance, and Platt calibration substantially improves probability reliability.
AI.motivation: Rapid growth of digital banking and mobile financial services creates fraud detection challenges under severe class imbalance and operational constraints, calling for models that are both explainable and well calibrated.
AI.method: An integrated pipeline combining chronological evaluation, leakage-conscious feature engineering, Platt probability calibration, SHAP-based explainability and adaptive risk prioritisation. Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost and LightGBM are compared on PaySim.
AI.result: XGBoost achieves PR-AUC 0.5658, ROC-AUC 0.9068 and F1-score 0.5369. Platt calibration reduces the test Brier score from 0.1141 to 0.0245. SHAP identifies temporal, destination-account, transaction-type and amount features as key drivers. The adaptive top-1% policy reduces false positives from 192 to 117, but recall falls from 0.4236 to 0.2122.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a reproducible methodological framework that exposes a clear alert-capacity trade-off. It is not evidence of deployment performance in Bangladesh, because PaySim is synthetic, so validation on governed real-world financial data is the next step.

title: LatentWeave: Test-Time Latent Optimization for Multimodal Reasoning
summary: Recent advances in test-time optimization have shown that the multimodal reasoning performance of large multimodal language models (MLLMs) can be improved during inference without modifying backbone model parameters. However, existing approaches primarily operate at the prompt or output level, leaving the latent reasoning process largely uncontrolled and insufficient to prevent error accumulation during autoregressive generation. To address this limitation, we propose LatentWeave, a test-time framework that treats multimodal reasoning as a controllable latent trajectory. LatentWeave performs structured Latent Weaving, progressively refining intermediate hidden states segment-wise to correct emerging deviations, and further introduces Reasoning Anchors via lightweight WEAVE tokens to stabilize reasoning structure and guide answer-oriented generation. These mechanisms are designed to enable fine-grained, step-aware intervention in the latent reasoning process while keeping the main MLLM backbone parameters fixed. Extensive experiments across diverse multimodal reasoning benchmarks report improvements over the evaluated baselines; the contribution of latent optimization, anchor training, and additional test-time computation is analyzed separately in the ablation and efficiency studies. Our code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes LatentWeave, a test-time framework that refines the intermediate hidden states of a frozen multimodal LLM segment by segment, with lightweight WEAVE tokens as reasoning anchors. It reports improvements over the evaluated baselines on multimodal reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing test-time optimisation for MLLMs works at the prompt or output level, leaving the latent reasoning process uncontrolled and insufficient to prevent error accumulation during autoregressive generation.
AI.method: Latent Weaving progressively refines hidden states segment-wise to correct emerging deviations. Reasoning Anchors, implemented as lightweight WEAVE tokens, stabilise the reasoning structure and guide answer-oriented generation. The backbone parameters stay fixed throughout.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse multimodal reasoning benchmarks report improvements over the evaluated baselines. Ablation and efficiency studies analyse separately the contributions of latent optimisation, anchor training and additional test-time computation. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Fine-grained, step-aware latent intervention at inference time is presented as a way to control the reasoning trajectory of an MLLM without modifying its parameters.

title: Improving the Intrinsic Interpretability of Differentiable Decision Trees through Euclidean Feature-Concentration Regularisation
comment: 17 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Based on the author's MSc dissertation, University of Birmingham
summary: Differentiable decision trees (DDTs) support end-to-end optimisation and explicit decision paths, but dense oblique splits can obscure the role of individual input features. We propose the Euclidean-Concentrated Differentiable Decision Tree (EU-DDT), which regularises the relative absolute feature weights at each internal node using their normalised squared Euclidean distance from the uniform distribution. This encourages dominance by a small number of features while retaining probabilistic soft routing. Across five matched random seeds, EU-DDT reduces the mean effective number of features from 8.94 to 1.54 on Wine and from 45.28 to 9.06 on Digits. Mean test accuracy changes from 100.0% to 93.9% on Wine and from 92.3% to 94.6% on Digits, illustrating the dataset-dependent trade-off between concentration and predictive performance. We also use EU-DDT to parameterise a PPO actor with an MLP critic. Two random-seed runs per environment show a consistent qualitative increase in concentration while preserving effective task performance. In representative CartPole-v1 and MiniPacman runs, EU-DDT reaches 100% final evaluation success, while mean node concentration increases from 0.1272 to 0.7179 and from 0.0437 to 0.7237, respectively. These results support EU regularisation as a mechanism for reducing node-level feature complexity; the reinforcement-learning evidence remains preliminary because only two seeds are evaluated.

AI.tldr: Proposes EU-DDT, a differentiable decision tree whose regulariser concentrates node-level feature weights on a few inputs to improve interpretability. Concentration rises sharply on Wine and Digits, with a dataset-dependent accuracy trade-off, and preliminary RL results are promising.
AI.motivation: Differentiable decision trees support end-to-end optimisation and explicit decision paths, but dense oblique splits obscure the role of individual input features.
AI.method: A regulariser on the relative absolute feature weights at each internal node, measured by their normalised squared Euclidean distance from the uniform distribution, which encourages dominance by a few features while retaining probabilistic soft routing. The tree also parameterises a PPO actor paired with an MLP critic.
AI.result: Across five matched seeds, the mean effective number of features drops from 8.94 to 1.54 on Wine and from 45.28 to 9.06 on Digits. Test accuracy changes from 100.0% to 93.9% on Wine and from 92.3% to 94.6% on Digits. In RL, CartPole-v1 and MiniPacman runs reach 100% final evaluation success, while mean node concentration rises from 0.1272 to 0.7179 and from 0.0437 to 0.7237; only two seeds were evaluated.
AI.conclusion: EU regularisation is a mechanism for reducing node-level feature complexity, but the concentration-performance trade-off is dataset dependent, and the reinforcement-learning evidence remains preliminary.

title: A New AFIB Detection Method with Deep Neural Networks
summary: Early detection of atrial fibrillation (AFIB), characterized by irregular heart rhythms, can potentially save thousands of lives annually [20]. Numerous studies have attempted to address this challenge using various algorithms and methodologies. This paper introduces a novel and robust method that enhances the precision of AFIB detection. Neural Networks (NN) are widely recognized for their ability to identify complex electrocardiogram (ECG) patterns, facilitating the accurate detection of irregular heart rhythms. This study explores multiple conventional machine learning algorithms alongside neural network approaches to develop a robust AFIB detection system. To evaluate the effective- ness and robustness of the proposed method, the MIT BIH arrhythmia database (MITDB) and the Long-term Atrial Fibrillation Database (LTAFDB), both available on the Physionet site. Our approach presents a novel feature engineering technique, employing specific features such as a time series of the differences in successive heart rates (dBPM) rather than traditional inter-beat intervals. The model analyzes inputs labeled into five distinct classes, using only clean intervals identified through a new labeling method for training while treating others as outliers. This strategy ensures a more accurate and reliable AFIB detection process. The best-performing model, a Deep Neural Network (DNN), achieved an F1 score of 95.18% for binary atrial fibrillation classification on a benchmark dataset distinct from the training set. Models trained using our approach have demonstrated superior performance than previously published models.

AI.tldr: Presents a deep neural network method for atrial fibrillation detection from ECG data, using a time series of successive heart-rate differences instead of inter-beat intervals and a new labelling scheme. The best model reports an F1 score of 95.18% on a benchmark dataset distinct from the training set.
AI.motivation: Early detection of atrial fibrillation can save many lives, and numerous studies have tried various algorithms, but the authors argue that the precision of AFIB detection still needs improving.
AI.method: A feature engineering technique that uses the dBPM series, the differences in successive heart rates, in place of traditional inter-beat intervals. A labelling method trains only on clean intervals and treats the others as outliers, with inputs in five classes. Conventional machine learning and neural networks are explored on MITDB and LTAFDB.
AI.result: The best-performing model, a Deep Neural Network, achieves an F1 score of 95.18% for binary atrial fibrillation classification on a benchmark dataset distinct from the training set. The authors state that their models outperform previously published models, but the abstract gives no quantitative comparison.
AI.conclusion: The approach is claimed to make AFIB detection more accurate and reliable than earlier models, though this rests on the stated comparison rather than numbers in the abstract.

title: Event-SAMA: Language-Grounded Video Object Segmentation on Neuromorphic Event Streams
summary: Event cameras offer microsecond temporal resolution, high dynamic range and no motion blur, but referring video object segmentation (RVOS) lacks event-stream datasets and models. We introduce Event-SAMA-239K, a synthetic-event conversion of the SAMA-239K grounded video-chat corpus and all additional SAMA training data: 30,650 video clips and 392,162 images. Optical-flow, FILM or saccade upsampling followed by a linear event generator preserves all mask, referring-expression and dialogue annotations. We also introduce Event-SAMA, adapting SAMA-4B with a two-channel polarity patch embedding initialised from pretrained RGB weights and a zero-initialised event adapter. End-to-end training yields 24.37 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ on MeViS valid_u and 22.33 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ on the converted ReVOS valid subset, establishing the first event-native RVOS baseline (RGB SAMA-4B: 55.4 on MeViS). Frozen RGB SAMA-4B with pseudo-RGB renderings or E2VID reconstructions of the same events scores 13.23 and 15.94 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$. Without retraining, Event-SAMA works on real event-camera recordings when the accumulation window matches their event density. A seed-controlled ablation with a measured noise floor of 0.47 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ finds gains from diverse training sources over MeViS alone (+4.99), RGB-mean event-stem initialisation (+4.33), and a trainable SAM2 mask decoder (+2.76); the event adapter, partial ViT unfreezing and event polarity are within noise at this budget. An earlier, partially converted corpus snapshot trained with the identical recipe scores 1.38 $\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F}$ higher on MeViS and 1.12 higher on ReVOS. Both are single runs that also differ in schedule length, so we draw no conclusion about corpus scale.

AI.tldr: Introduces Event-SAMA-239K, a synthetic event-stream version of a grounded video-chat corpus, and Event-SAMA, the first event-native referring video object segmentation baseline. It reaches 24.37 J&F on MeViS valid_u, against 55.4 for the RGB model.
AI.motivation: Event cameras offer microsecond temporal resolution, high dynamic range and no motion blur, but referring video object segmentation lacks event-stream datasets and models.
AI.method: Events are synthesised from the SAMA-239K corpus and additional SAMA training data using optical-flow, FILM or saccade upsampling followed by a linear event generator, which preserves all annotations. Event-SAMA adapts SAMA-4B with a two-channel polarity patch embedding initialised from RGB weights and a zero-initialised event adapter.
AI.result: End-to-end training gives 24.37 J&F on MeViS valid_u and 22.33 J&F on the converted ReVOS valid subset, against 55.4 for RGB SAMA-4B on MeViS. Frozen RGB SAMA-4B with pseudo-RGB renderings or E2VID reconstructions scores 13.23 and 15.94 J&F. An ablation with a noise floor of 0.47 J&F finds gains from diverse training sources (+4.99), RGB-mean event-stem initialisation (+4.33) and a trainable SAM2 mask decoder (+2.76); the event adapter, partial ViT unfreezing and event polarity fall within noise.
AI.conclusion: Event-SAMA is presented as the first event-native RVOS baseline, and it works on real event-camera recordings when the accumulation window matches the event density. The authors draw no conclusion about corpus scale, since their comparisons are single runs with different schedule lengths.

title: Heterogeneous Co-Evolution Learning for Tool-Efficient Search Agents with Zero Labels
summary: Deep search agents extend language models by interleaving reasoning with external retrieval. However, effective search-agent training requires addressing two challenges beyond final-answer optimization. First, the capability frontier of agents is largely determined by training questions, whereas fixed or labeled task collections cannot adapt as agents improve. Second, outcome-only reinforcement learning treats all successful trajectories equally, even when some correct answers rely on redundant searches, creating an inherent tension between answer accuracy and tool efficiency. To address these issues, we introduce \textsc{ZEST-Search}, a zero-label and tool-efficient framework for search-agent training via heterogeneous co-evolution. Starting from unlabeled reference questions, \textsc{ZEST-Search} constructs validated search tasks online through an answer-first and evidence-path-guided generation process. A heterogeneous proposer adaptively constructs training tasks around the solver's evolving capability boundary, while the solver learns search-augmented reasoning through reinforcement learning. To jointly optimize task difficulty and search efficiency, \textsc{ZEST-Search} employs an intermediate-difficulty reward for the proposer and a task-local tool-aware reward for the solver, encouraging informative tasks and correct answers with fewer redundant searches. Experiments on seven general-domain and multi-hop question answering benchmarks demonstrate that \textsc{ZEST-Search} consistently improves search-agent performance while achieving higher tool efficiency without labeled search-training data or expert search trajectories. Further analyses show that heterogeneous generation, adaptive difficulty control, and tool-aware optimization enable more effective search-agent training.

AI.tldr: Presents ZEST-Search, a zero-label framework that trains search agents by co-evolving a task proposer and a solver with reinforcement learning. Rewards favour correct answers with fewer redundant searches, and the method improves performance on seven QA benchmarks while raising tool efficiency.
AI.motivation: Fixed or labelled question sets cannot keep pace with an improving search agent, and outcome-only reinforcement learning treats all correct trajectories equally, even those with redundant searches, creating a tension between answer accuracy and tool efficiency.
AI.method: Starting from unlabelled reference questions, validated search tasks are constructed online through answer-first and evidence-path-guided generation. A heterogeneous proposer builds tasks around the solver's evolving capability boundary, with an intermediate-difficulty reward for the proposer and a task-local tool-aware reward for the solver.
AI.result: Experiments on seven general-domain and multi-hop question answering benchmarks show consistent improvements in search-agent performance and higher tool efficiency, without labelled search data or expert search trajectories. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Heterogeneous generation, adaptive difficulty control and tool-aware optimisation together make search-agent training more effective without labelled data.

title: Smartphone Indoor Localization Enhanced by Hierarchical Multi-Sensor Context Recognition
summary: Smartphone indoor localization requires low-cost, robust positioning across scene transitions and phone-use variations. Pedestrian dead reckoning (PDR) enables infrastructure-free deployment but accumulates errors from heading drift, structural transitions, and carrying-mode changes. Existing methods often treat contextual cues as a single event stream or local correction signal, limiting their ability to address distinct localization errors. This paper presents a framework enhanced by hierarchical multi-sensor context recognition. A jointly data- and model-driven recognition model predicts environment, scene, and activity probabilities, which are converted into scene-event and action-context segments. Scene-event segments guide scene-constrained PDR correction through corridor heading constraints, landmark attraction, fixed-lag backtracking, and vertical-transition handling. Action-context segments drive action-aware RoNIN-based position compensation for carrying-mode-dependent drift. Experiments on cross-floor and multi-action trajectories against LiDAR-SLAM references show that the proposed framework outperforms PDR and representative learned inertial odometry baselines, demonstrating that hierarchical semantics provide reliable, localization-specific correction cues.

AI.tldr: Proposes a smartphone indoor localisation framework in which hierarchical multi-sensor context recognition guides corrections to pedestrian dead reckoning. It outperforms PDR and learned inertial odometry baselines on cross-floor and multi-action trajectories against LiDAR-SLAM references.
AI.motivation: Infrastructure-free PDR accumulates errors from heading drift, structural transitions and carrying-mode changes. Existing methods treat contextual cues as a single event stream or a local correction signal, which limits their ability to address these distinct errors.
AI.method: A jointly data- and model-driven recognition model predicts environment, scene and activity probabilities, which are converted into scene-event and action-context segments. Scene-event segments drive scene-constrained PDR correction through corridor heading constraints, landmark attraction, fixed-lag backtracking and vertical-transition handling. Action-context segments drive action-aware RoNIN-based position compensation for carrying-mode-dependent drift.
AI.result: Experiments on cross-floor and multi-action trajectories against LiDAR-SLAM references show that the framework outperforms PDR and representative learned inertial odometry baselines. The abstract gives no numerical values.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical semantics are shown to provide reliable, localisation-specific correction cues for smartphone indoor positioning.

title: Implicit Bias of (Stochastic) Gradient Descent on Deep Linear Diagonal Networks
summary: Modern machine learning models are often overparameterized, i.e., have more parameters than training data. This typically implies that the loss function admits multiple minimizers so that training methods (and their hyperparameter choices) have significant influence on the computed solution. We study this so-called implicit bias phenomenon in the context of training deep linear diagonal networks. Previous work has shown that the gradient flow for learning such networks converges to (almost) sparse solutions when initialized small. For an arbitrary number of layers, we extend this analysis to the practically more realistic (stochastic) gradient descent iterations. Our approach identifies (stochastic) gradient descent as a perturbed (stochastic) mirror gradient descent. This allows us to establish convergence and characterize the limiting solution, relating it to weighted $\ell_1$-minimization. Moreover, we provide sufficient conditions on the step sizes and quantify the influence of the step sizes on the implicit bias.

AI.tldr: Extends the implicit bias analysis of gradient flow in deep linear diagonal networks to (stochastic) gradient descent with any number of layers. SGD is shown to behave as a perturbed mirror descent that converges to a weighted l1-minimising solution under step-size conditions.
AI.motivation: Overparameterised models have multiple minimisers, so the training method shapes the solution found. Previous work covered gradient flow, which converges to almost sparse solutions when initialised small, but the more realistic (stochastic) gradient descent iterations had not been analysed for deep linear diagonal networks.
AI.method: Identifies (stochastic) gradient descent as a perturbed (stochastic) mirror gradient descent. This view is used to establish convergence and to characterise the limiting solution, which is related to weighted l1-minimisation.
AI.result: The analysis establishes convergence and characterises the limiting solution as a weighted l1-minimiser. Sufficient conditions on the step sizes are provided, and their influence on the implicit bias is quantified.
AI.conclusion: Step sizes affect which sparse solution is reached, so the implicit bias of practical SGD in deep linear diagonal networks can be characterised beyond gradient flow.

title: Grounding Predictive Reliability through Masked Observability
summary: An uncertainty estimate is meaningful only if its semantics can be tied to observable predictive behavior. Normal-Inverse-Gamma (NIG) evidential regression provides a structured decomposition of predictive variability into data-scale and predictive-mean components, but marginal likelihood does not identify their allocation. We address this semantic ambiguity in masked representation learning. MORSE (Masked Observability for Reliable Structured Encoding) predicts the same hidden target under controlled changes in visible context and uses normalized cross-context variation to ground predictive-mean uncertainty, while a Gaussian objective learns the conditional mean and data scale. The normalized variation plays the role of the NIG factor $1/\nu$, which the marginal leaves unidentified; this yields a policy-relative observability variance that measures dependence on visible evidence, distinct from variation induced by resampling the training set. On a Gaussian-process benchmark with a contextual reference built from analytic Bayes conditional means, MORSE has the lowest log-variance error among compared evidential, ensemble, and dropout estimators in all nine tested settings, while the estimator closest to training-set variation perturbs the model rather than its context in every setting, so the two references separate the estimators empirically. MORSE amortizes observability estimation into one forward pass per observation state. On a heteroscedastic pulse benchmark, its predictor's cross-context variance approaches a large-sample reference as training data increase. MORSE also improves low-label transfer on PTB-XL and in-distribution trajectory prediction on IMPTC.

AI.tldr: Proposes MORSE, a masked representation learning method that grounds the predictive-mean uncertainty of NIG evidential regression in how predictions change across controlled changes in visible context. On a Gaussian-process benchmark it has the lowest log-variance error among the compared estimators in all nine tested settings.
AI.motivation: NIG evidential regression decomposes predictive variability into data-scale and predictive-mean components, but marginal likelihood does not identify how variability is allocated between them, so the semantics of the uncertainty remain ambiguous.
AI.method: The same hidden target is predicted under controlled changes in visible context. The normalised cross-context variation plays the role of the NIG factor 1/nu that the marginal leaves unidentified, giving a policy-relative observability variance, while a Gaussian objective learns the conditional mean and data scale. Observability is estimated in one forward pass per observation state.
AI.result: On a Gaussian-process benchmark with a contextual reference built from analytic Bayes conditional means, MORSE has the lowest log-variance error among evidential, ensemble and dropout estimators in all nine settings. On a heteroscedastic pulse benchmark its cross-context variance approaches a large-sample reference as training data grow. MORSE also improves low-label transfer on PTB-XL and in-distribution trajectory prediction on IMPTC.
AI.conclusion: Observability variance measures dependence on visible evidence and is distinct from variation induced by resampling the training set, so the two references separate the estimators empirically.

title: Going deep, reaching further: What can Boltzmann machines efficiently represent?
comment: 34 pages of main text + 32 pages of appendices, 14 figures, 2 tables
summary: While universal approximation theorems theoretically underpin the representation capabilities of machine learning models, they have two shortcomings: They do not focus on efficient representations and they tend to be insensitive to depth and other heuristically important properties. In this work we show that these two shortcomings are intertwined. We prove that machine learning models which are deeper or have higher-order interactions can efficiently represent a larger set of functions, i.e. have larger efficient reach. It follows that deep Boltzmann machines (DBMs) have maximal efficient reach, restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs) sub-maximal, and k-body generalizations of RBMs form a hierarchy between the two, even though all are universal. More generally, (i) we provide a full characterization of machine learning models with maximal efficient reach; (ii) we derive separations between deep and shallow models for three representation tasks; and (iii) we prove that the efficient reach of shallow models constitutes an infinite hierarchy indexed by the interaction order. The proofs draw on different methodologies, namely on (i) a recent characterization of universal spin models; (ii) computational complexity bounds for spin models; and (iii) communication complexity bounds applied to shallow models. This work shows that universal machine learning models can strongly differ in their efficient representation capabilities, and provides a theoretical foundation for heuristic observations.

AI.tldr: Proves that deeper models and models with higher-order interactions can efficiently represent larger sets of functions, so deep Boltzmann machines have maximal efficient reach while restricted Boltzmann machines have sub-maximal reach. All of these models are universal, so the difference lies in efficiency.
AI.motivation: Universal approximation theorems do not focus on efficient representation and are insensitive to depth and other heuristically important properties, so the representational advantages of depth lack a rigorous efficiency-based explanation.
AI.method: Characterises the machine learning models with maximal efficient reach and derives separations between deep and shallow models for three representation tasks. The proofs use a characterisation of universal spin models, computational complexity bounds for spin models, and communication complexity bounds for shallow models.
AI.result: Deep Boltzmann machines have maximal efficient reach, restricted Boltzmann machines are sub-maximal, and k-body generalisations of RBMs form a hierarchy between the two. The efficient reach of shallow models forms an infinite hierarchy indexed by interaction order.
AI.conclusion: Universal machine learning models can differ strongly in their efficient representation capabilities, which provides a theoretical foundation for heuristic observations about depth.

title: Activation Probes Are Reliable With a Handful of Positive Examples
comment: Presented at the Mechanistic Interpretability workshop at NeurIPS 2025
summary: Efforts to monitor advanced AI for rare misalignments face a data challenge: abundant aligned examples but only a handful of misaligned ones. We test activation probes in this "few vs. thousands" regime on spam and honesty detection tasks. For our tasks, training with many negative examples is on average more positive-sample-efficient than balanced training for small numbers (1-10) of positive samples. We also find that LLM upsampling can provide a performance boost equivalent to roughly doubling the number of real positive samples, though excessive upsampling hurts performance. Finally, we show a positive scaling trend, where larger models are more positive-sample-efficient to probe. Our findings suggest we should leverage the large number of negative samples available to amplify the signal from rare but critical misalignment examples.

AI.tldr: Tests activation probes for detecting rare misalignments in a few-positives regime on spam and honesty detection. Training with many negatives is more positive-sample-efficient than balanced training for small numbers of positives, and LLM upsampling and larger models further help.
AI.motivation: Monitoring advanced AI for rare misalignments faces a data challenge: aligned examples are abundant, but only a handful of misaligned examples exist.
AI.method: Activation probes are evaluated in a "few vs. thousands" regime on spam and honesty detection tasks. Training with many negative examples is compared with balanced training, and LLM upsampling of positive examples is tested, with probing across model sizes.
AI.result: For 1-10 positive samples, training with many negatives is on average more positive-sample-efficient than balanced training. LLM upsampling gives a performance boost equivalent to roughly doubling the number of real positive samples, though excessive upsampling hurts. Larger models are more positive-sample-efficient to probe.
AI.conclusion: The large number of available negative samples should be exploited to amplify the signal from rare but critical misalignment examples.

title: Multi-output LSTM soft sensors for industrial anaerobic co-digestion using LSTM-beta-VAE generative data augmentation
summary: Anaerobic digestion (AD) requires close monitoring of key process variables, including pH, the ratio of volatile organic acids to alkaline buffer capacity and biogas production, to maintain biological stability and prevent process failure. While mechanistic frameworks such as the Anaerobic Digestion Model No. 1 are highly parameterised, computationally expensive, and difficult to calibrate for real-time applications, data-driven Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks offer a potentially more adaptable alternative. However, current data-driven approaches in AD are predominantly limited to single-output architectures that focus solely on production yields, as opposed to simultaneous prediction of vital stability indicators. Furthermore, industrial AD datasets are typically sparse and skewed toward steady-state operations. Baseline evaluations demonstrated this scarcity prevents standard algorithms (Random Forest, XGBoost) and unaugmented LSTMs from recognising the transition to unstable operations, resulting in poor estimation of stability indicators. To overcome these challenges, this study proposes a novel generative data augmentation framework using an LSTM-beta-Variational Autoencoder coupled with a multi-output LSTM (MO-LSTM) soft sensor. By synthesising physically valid sequences of these transitions to unstable operations from one year of full-scale plant data, the method safely populates sparse regions of the feature space. Trained on this augmented dataset, the MO-LSTM achieved robust simultaneous estimation across all targets. This approach mitigates data sparsity, providing a basis for hybrid mechanistic-data-driven modelling and early-warning soft sensors in industrial bioprocesses.

AI.tldr: Develops a multi-output LSTM soft sensor for industrial anaerobic co-digestion that estimates several stability indicators at once, trained on data augmented by an LSTM-beta-VAE that synthesises transitions to unstable operation. The augmentation addresses sparse, steady-state-skewed plant data.
AI.motivation: Data-driven anaerobic digestion models mostly predict only production yields. Sparse, steady-state-skewed industrial data prevents Random Forest, XGBoost and unaugmented LSTMs from recognising the transition to unstable operation, leading to poor estimates of stability indicators.
AI.method: A generative augmentation framework uses an LSTM-beta-Variational Autoencoder to synthesise physically valid sequences of transitions to unstable operation from one year of full-scale plant data. A multi-output LSTM (MO-LSTM) soft sensor is then trained on the augmented dataset.
AI.result: The MO-LSTM achieves robust simultaneous estimation across all targets when trained on the augmented dataset. The abstract gives no numerical values.
AI.conclusion: The method mitigates data sparsity and provides a basis for hybrid mechanistic-data-driven modelling and early-warning soft sensors in industrial bioprocesses.

title: Quantum-Inspired Convolutional Networks for High-Resolution Pseudo-Label Generation from Multimodal Earth Observation Data
summary: Accurate land-cover mapping from multimodal Earth observation (EO) data remains a challenge in regions where high-resolution annotations are scarce or costly to obtain. This work introduces a quantum convolutional encoder-decoder network for pseudo-label generation using Sentinel-1 SAR and Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery, guided only by coarse MODIS-derived land-cover maps. The proposed framework uses quantum-inspired convolutional blocks to enhance feature extraction and cross-sensor fusion, enabling the model to infer a fine-scale semantic structure from heterogeneous inputs. Experiments were conducted on the DFC2020 dataset, which provides a quadruple of Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 multispectral, low-resolution MODIS labels and high-resolution reference land-cover maps. The proposed training framework first learns a robust representation of multimodal inputs through the reconstruction branch before any supervision from low-resolution labels is applied. This self-supervised stage enables the model to capture a fine-scale spectral-spatial structure, which is then used to generate high-resolution pseudo-labels. These pseudo-labels are subsequently evaluated through classification metrics on the test data, demonstrating that the proposed approach produces more spatially coherent and class-consistent compared to classical baselines. The results highlight the potential of quantum-inspired deep learning to improve label generation in low-annotation remote sensing scenarios, offering a scalable path towards high-quality land-cover products for EO applications.

AI.tldr: Proposes a quantum-inspired convolutional encoder-decoder that generates high-resolution land-cover pseudo-labels from Sentinel-1 SAR and Sentinel-2 imagery, guided only by coarse MODIS-derived maps. The pseudo-labels are reported to be more spatially coherent and class-consistent than classical baselines on DFC2020.
AI.motivation: High-resolution annotations for land-cover mapping are scarce or costly, which makes accurate mapping from multimodal Earth observation data difficult in low-annotation regions.
AI.method: Quantum-inspired convolutional blocks enhance feature extraction and cross-sensor fusion. A reconstruction branch first learns a self-supervised representation of the multimodal inputs before any supervision from the low-resolution labels is applied, and this representation is then used to generate high-resolution pseudo-labels.
AI.result: The pseudo-labels are evaluated through classification metrics on the test data and are reported to be more spatially coherent and class-consistent than classical baselines. The abstract gives no numerical values.
AI.conclusion: Quantum-inspired deep learning shows potential to improve label generation in low-annotation remote sensing, offering a scalable path towards high-quality land-cover products.

title: Surface Conditioning for Zero-Shot Multivariate Correction in a Marine Biogeochemistry Emulator
summary: Bias correction in process-based models usually means iterative data assimilation with explicit covariance modelling. We propose a lightweight alternative based on a neural emulator of marine biogeochemistry (BGC), showing that the conditioning pathway of its autoencoder can serve as an observation injection point. The decoder is conditioned on surface variables via Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM), originally designed to incorporate physical boundary forcings. We extend these inputs to include surface chlorophyll-a and replace the simulated field with satellite observations at inference time. The surface substitution propagates through the water column, improving agreement with depth-resolved observations at all depths, and spreads to other output variables in a pattern consistent with expected trophic relationships.

AI.tldr: Proposes a zero-shot bias correction for a neural marine biogeochemistry emulator by injecting surface chlorophyll-a and satellite observations at inference time through the FiLM conditioning pathway of its autoencoder. The surface correction propagates through the water column and improves agreement with depth-resolved observations at all depths.
AI.motivation: Bias correction in process-based models usually relies on iterative data assimilation with explicit covariance modelling, which is heavier than a lightweight alternative.
AI.method: The decoder is conditioned on surface variables via Feature-wise Linear Modulation, originally designed for physical boundary forcings. The conditioning inputs are extended to include surface chlorophyll-a, and the simulated field is replaced by satellite observations at inference time.
AI.result: The surface substitution propagates through the water column, improving agreement with depth-resolved observations at all depths. It also spreads to other output variables in a pattern consistent with expected trophic relationships. The abstract gives no numerical values.
AI.conclusion: The conditioning pathway of the autoencoder can serve as an observation injection point, providing a lightweight route to multivariate correction without explicit covariance modelling.

title: AI at a Turning Point: From ChatGPT through Neural Networks to Neuromorphic AI
summary: The tension between the established technologies of connectionist AI and their neuromorphic challengers is attracting growing attention, above all because of the enormous energy demand of the former and the low power consumption of the latter. Developing and running large AI models consumes gigawatt- to terawatt-hours of energy, while the human brain operates on a continuous 20 watts. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) counter this energy demand with a frugal approach and bring elements of self-organization into the methodological repertoire of AI: local learning instead of global error backpropagation, event-driven computing, and time as a carrier of information. They do not replace today's AI but extend it; in hybrid systems each approach can be deployed where its strengths lie. This monograph explains the field in a generally accessible yet mathematically rigorous way. Using the text-generation module of ChatGPT as an example, the principle, elegance, and computational cost of transformer-based AI are presented and compared with the coding, learning, and network-design methods of SNNs. Throughout, relevant mechanisms of the human nervous system serve as model and reference point. Topics include spike-timing-dependent plasticity, population and temporal coding, the Neural Engineering Framework, neuromorphic hardware from Loihi 2 to commercial edge processors, and the prospects for classical and neuromorphic AI to complement and extend each other.

AI.tldr: A monograph that explains how transformer-based AI, using the text generation of ChatGPT as its example, compares with spiking neural networks, which offer local learning, event-driven computing and low energy use. It argues the two approaches can complement each other in hybrid systems.
AI.motivation: Developing and running large AI models consumes gigawatt- to terawatt-hours of energy, whereas the human brain operates on about 20 watts, which motivates neuromorphic alternatives such as spiking neural networks.
AI.method: Explains the principle and computational cost of transformer-based AI and compares them with the coding, learning and network-design methods of SNNs. Topics include spike-timing-dependent plasticity, population and temporal coding, the Neural Engineering Framework, and neuromorphic hardware from Loihi 2 to commercial edge processors.
AI.result: Not applicable: the monograph is an expository treatment, and the abstract reports no experimental findings.
AI.conclusion: Classical and neuromorphic AI are presented as complementary, with each deployed where its strengths lie in hybrid systems.

title: Optimal Contextual Pricing in Non-Stationary Environments
summary: We study contextual dynamic pricing in a non-stationary environment. In each round, a seller observes a buyer's context, posts a price, and receives only binary purchase feedback. The buyer's value is linear in the context and an unobserved feature vector that may change over time, subject to a known total variation budget $V$. We measure dynamic regret against the first-best benchmark that extracts each buyer's full value. For identical contexts, we develop a deterministic algorithm that combines binary-search exploration, lower-envelope pricing, and periodic and inconsistency-triggered restarts. It achieves regret $O((\sqrt{TV}+1)\log T)$. With heterogeneous contexts, a new geometric difficulty arises: small feature changes can leave a relaxed feasible set narrow but far from the current feature vector. We address this difficulty through a multiscale shallow-pricing algorithm that maintains relaxed feasible sets and enclosing ellipsoids at several variation scales. Larger scales provide reliable localization certificates, while the smallest active scale determines the exploitation price. The algorithm achieves dynamic regret $O((d^2+d^{3/2}\sqrt{TV})\log^2 T)$, where $d$ is the context dimension. For fixed $d$, both guarantees match the lower bound $\Omega(\sqrt{TV}+\log\log T)$ up to logarithmic factors in $T$, establishing near-optimality among deterministic algorithms for every $V\in[0,T]$, including the stationary case.

AI.tldr: Gives an algorithm for contextual dynamic pricing with binary purchase feedback when buyer values drift over time, with dynamic regret close to the lower bound. The regret is O((sqrt(TV)+1) log T) for identical contexts and O((d^2+d^{3/2} sqrt(TV)) log^2 T) for heterogeneous contexts.
AI.motivation: The buyer's value is linear in the context and an unobserved feature vector that may change within a known total variation budget. With heterogeneous contexts, small feature changes can leave a relaxed feasible set narrow but far from the current feature vector, a geometric difficulty that existing approaches do not handle.
AI.method: For identical contexts, a deterministic algorithm combines binary-search exploration, lower-envelope pricing, and periodic and inconsistency-triggered restarts. For heterogeneous contexts, a multiscale shallow-pricing algorithm maintains relaxed feasible sets and enclosing ellipsoids at several variation scales, with the smallest active scale determining the exploitation price.
AI.result: Regret is O((sqrt(TV)+1) log T) for identical contexts and O((d^2+d^{3/2} sqrt(TV)) log^2 T) for heterogeneous contexts. For fixed d, both match the lower bound Omega(sqrt(TV)+log log T) up to logarithmic factors in T.
AI.conclusion: The guarantees establish near-optimality among deterministic algorithms for every variation budget V in [0,T], including the stationary case.

title: Possibility-based Inference: A Deterministic Framework for Robust and Reliable Uncertainty Quantification in Decision-Making
summary: Decision-making under uncertainty remains a key issue in Machine Learning (ML), particularly in the deployment of safety-critical systems, where reliable quantification of system behavior is essential for evaluating behavioral impacts and strengthening confidence in ML models. This contribution, influenced by fuzzy set theory and grounded in Bayesian statistics, addresses challenges related to data precision and the performance-accuracy trade-off in Bayesian inference (BI). To this end, we introduce a possibility-based contrastive grade of prediction as an alternative quantification method to existing latent posterior-based approaches for parameter estimation (approximation) and model selection. Unlike conventional Bayesian inference, which represents uncertainty within the probabilistic framework, the proposed model adopts a possibility-based representation that allows uncertain and potentially conflicting information to be characterized more flexibly. Rather than focusing on isolated aspects of a problem, the resulting mathematical framework provides a systematic approach to data mining while mitigating overly confident, yet implausible predictions generated by highly specialized deep learning architectures.

AI.tldr: Proposes a possibility-based inference framework, influenced by fuzzy set theory, as an alternative to Bayesian posterior-based uncertainty quantification for decision-making in ML. It aims to mitigate overconfident yet implausible predictions from highly specialised deep learning architectures.
AI.motivation: Decision-making under uncertainty is key for safety-critical ML systems, but Bayesian inference faces challenges with data precision and the performance-accuracy trade-off, and it represents uncertainty only within a probabilistic framework.
AI.method: A possibility-based contrastive grade of prediction is introduced for parameter estimation and model selection, in place of latent posterior-based approaches. This allows uncertain and potentially conflicting information to be characterised more flexibly.
AI.result: The abstract reports no experimental results or quantitative comparisons. It describes the mathematical framework as a systematic approach to data mining.
AI.conclusion: The framework is presented as a more flexible way to characterise uncertain and conflicting information that mitigates overconfident implausible predictions, though the abstract gives no quantitative support for this.

title: SHPRR: An Algorithm for Pure Exploration under Constrained Regret
summary: Best Arm Identification (BAI) conventionally measures the cost of experimentation by the number of samples collected. In many operational settings, however, the cost of exploration relative to a trusted baseline already in place is equally important. We study BAI under both a fixed sampling horizon and a regret budget. Unlike generic resources considered in constrained pure exploration, regret has a distinctive structure: sampling better arms is less costly relative to the baseline. We theoretically show that the regret cost of exploration decreases across the phases of Sequential Halving, a widely used pure-exploration algorithm. This observation yields improved guarantees on the probability of identifying the best arm and motivates a more effective allocation of the regret budget. We propose Sequential Halving with Proportional Regret Rationing (SHPRR), which front-loads the regret budget to allow more exploration when many arms remain. Experiments on synthetic and real-world instances show that SHPRR improves best-arm identification performance over uniform regret allocation and existing baselines.

AI.tldr: Proposes SHPRR, a best-arm identification algorithm that allocates the regret budget across Sequential Halving phases in proportion to need, front-loading exploration while many arms remain. It improves identification performance over uniform regret allocation and existing baselines on synthetic and real-world instances.
AI.motivation: Best Arm Identification usually measures the cost of experimentation by sample count, but in operational settings the regret relative to a trusted baseline matters too. Regret has the distinctive property that sampling better arms is less costly relative to the baseline.
AI.method: Shows that the regret cost of exploration decreases across the phases of Sequential Halving, and uses Sequential Halving with Proportional Regret Rationing, which front-loads the regret budget to allow more exploration when many arms remain.
AI.result: The approach yields improved guarantees on the probability of identifying the best arm. Experiments on synthetic and real-world instances show that SHPRR improves best-arm identification performance over uniform regret allocation and existing baselines.
AI.conclusion: Front-loading the regret budget across phases is a more effective allocation of constrained exploration than uniform allocation.

title: Exploring the Potential of Symbolic Regression in Precision Livestock Farming
summary: The ability to predict farrowing time in pigs is crucial for optimal farm management and ensuring piglet survival. This study investigates the potential of explainable artificial intelligence for precision livestock farming, focusing on acceleration sensor data from sows around the time of farrowing. Accurately predicting farrowing allows farmers to balance both, piglet safety by avoiding piglet crushing events and the mother sow's welfare, by avoiding early crating. Traditional machine learning models often lack interpretability (``closed-box'' problem). Explainable artificial intelligence offers a solution by revealing the decision-making processes within the models. This work is split into two stages. First the detection of nest building behaviour and second the prediction of the remaining time to farrowing. The nest building detection was possible for 166 out of 180 sows and successful within 48 hours before farrowing for 149 sows. The nest building detection is purely based on the change of a sow's activity level and uses no machine learning techniques. Further, this study utilizes symbolic regression, an open-box modelling technique that generates interpretable mathematical formulas, to predict the remaining time until the onset of farrowing. The results are compared with closed-box models, like support vector regression and artificial neural networks, for both explainability and performance. Notably, symbolic regression achieved a mean absolute error of 9.28 hours for the time-to-farrowing prediction, outperforming the closed-box models in terms of performance and interpretability. This research demonstrates that explainable artificial intelligence, specifically symbolic regression, can offer both interpretable results and competitive performance in precision livestock farming.

AI.tldr: Uses symbolic regression to predict the remaining time to farrowing in sows from acceleration sensor data, producing interpretable formulas that match or beat closed-box models. It reaches a mean absolute error of 9.28 hours, and nest-building onset is detected from activity-level change without machine learning.
AI.motivation: Predicting farrowing supports both piglet survival, by avoiding crushing events, and sow welfare, by avoiding early crating. Traditional machine learning models are closed-box and lack interpretability.
AI.method: Two stages. Nest-building behaviour is first detected from changes in the sow's activity level without machine learning. Symbolic regression, an open-box technique that generates interpretable mathematical formulas, then predicts the remaining time to farrowing and is compared with support vector regression and artificial neural networks.
AI.result: Nest-building detection worked for 166 of 180 sows and was successful within 48 hours before farrowing for 149 sows. Symbolic regression achieved a mean absolute error of 9.28 hours for time-to-farrowing prediction, outperforming the closed-box models in performance and interpretability.
AI.conclusion: Symbolic regression can offer both interpretable results and competitive performance for precision livestock farming, demonstrating the value of explainable AI in this setting.

title: Surprise Alone Learns Lies: Evidence-Gated Continual Learning for LLMs from Streaming Claims
comment: 21 pages, 5 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Continual learning methods for large language models increasingly decide what to learn by surprise, keeping the inputs the model finds least predictable. This rule is unsafe when the stream contains lies. A planted falsehood about something the model knows has low probability under the model's belief, so it is highly surprising by construction, and a surprise-driven learner absorbs nearly every such lie, at a rate similar to random selection with the same budget. We study the problem with LoRA-adapted students (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Qwen2.5-3B and Llama-3.2-3B) that learn from a stream of true and false claims about invented people and real CounterFact facts. We report four findings. (1) A verifier key, a judge that must approve each claim, removes lies to the extent that its verifier is accurate; real LLM judges are cautious and reject unsourced truths and even source-backed updates. (2) Calibrated regression tests on unrelated knowledge slow learning down without filtering out lies. (3) The original model's own prior flags claims that contradict what it knows, without a judge. It separates lies about known facts from true new facts (AUC 0.78-0.83 across three models) but not from legitimate updates of the same kind of fact (AUC 0.53). It saves 43% of judge calls, but an attacker with access to the model can choose lies that pass it. (4) If trusted sources exist that an attacker cannot plant, routing contradicted claims to evidence recovers legitimate updates and the combined system has the lowest poison rate among learned claims; when an attacker plants matching sources for 30% of the lies, the system ends up worse than the judge alone. The acceptance signals answer different questions, and none of them decides on its own whether a claim is true.

AI.tldr: Shows that surprise-driven continual learning for LLMs absorbs planted lies about known facts, and that a verifier judge, the model's own prior, and trusted-source routing each filter lies only partially. None of these acceptance signals alone decides whether a claim is true.
