AI.motivation: Continual learning methods choose what to learn by surprise, but a planted falsehood about a known fact is improbable under the model's belief and so is surprising by construction, which makes surprise-based selection unsafe when the stream contains lies.
AI.method: LoRA-adapted students (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Qwen2.5-3B and Llama-3.2-3B) learn from streams of true and false claims about invented people and real CounterFact facts. The compared acceptance signals are a verifier judge that must approve each claim, calibrated regression tests on unrelated knowledge, the original model's own prior that flags claims contradicting its knowledge, and routing contradicted claims to trusted sources that an attacker cannot plant.
AI.result: A verifier key removes lies to the extent that its verifier is accurate, but real LLM judges are cautious and reject unsourced truths and even source-backed updates. Regression tests slow learning without filtering out lies. The model's prior separates lies about known facts from true new facts (AUC 0.78-0.83 across three models) but not from legitimate updates of the same kind of fact (AUC 0.53), saves 43% of judge calls, and can be evaded by an attacker with model access. Routing contradicted claims to trusted sources recovers legitimate updates and gives the lowest poison rate among learned claims, but when an attacker plants matching sources for 30% of the lies, the system is worse than the judge alone.
AI.conclusion: The acceptance signals answer different questions, so safe continual learning needs combined evidence rather than surprise alone, and the paper's findings show that no single signal settles the truth of a claim.

title: DWISE: Denoising Workload-Informed Scheduling Engine
summary: Unlike autoregressive large language models (AR-LLMs), diffusion LLMs (dLLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising many tokens in parallel, offering a promising path to efficient inference. Existing serving frameworks, however, schedule dLLM requests with policies designed for AR models, namely first-come-first-served (FCFS) admission and prefill priority. We find that both policies are ill-suited to dLLMs, wasting much of their speed. FCFS ignores that a dLLM request's decoding cost is highly heterogeneous and unknown at arrival, causing severe head-of-line blocking. Prefill priority, widely used in AR-LLM serving to keep time-to-first-token low, sharply cuts dLLM efficiency, as rounds that run only prompts leave most of the batch idle. We present DWISE, a Denoising Workload-Informed Scheduling Engine for efficient dLLM serving. DWISE schedules requests by their remaining work, measured in a block-level unit shared by prefill and denoising, so both phases share a round. To predict the unknown denoising workload, DWISE combines a lightweight prompt-based predictor at admission with a single refinement from the first denoising round's hidden states, which capture model-specific information absent from the prompt and require no additional model execution. Implemented in SGLang and evaluated on five models from three dLLM families under bursty workloads, DWISE reduces mean end-to-end latency over SGLang by 5.4$\times$ on average and up to 14.9$\times$ while preserving task accuracy. The code will be released publicly.

AI.tldr: DWISE is a scheduling engine for diffusion LLM serving that orders requests by their remaining denoising work, measured in a block-level unit shared by prefill and denoising. On five models from three dLLM families it reduces mean end-to-end latency over SGLang by 5.4x on average and up to 14.9x while preserving task accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing serving frameworks schedule diffusion LLM requests with autoregressive-model policies, namely first-come-first-served admission and prefill priority. FCFS ignores that each request's decoding cost is heterogeneous and unknown at arrival, causing head-of-line blocking, and prefill priority leaves most of the batch idle in rounds that run only prompts.
AI.method: DWISE measures remaining work in a block-level unit shared by prefill and denoising, so both phases share a round. It predicts the unknown denoising workload with a lightweight prompt-based predictor at admission, refined once from the first denoising round's hidden states, which capture model-specific information absent from the prompt and need no additional model execution. It is implemented in SGLang.
AI.result: Under bursty workloads on five models from three dLLM families, DWISE reduces mean end-to-end latency over SGLang by 5.4x on average and by up to 14.9x while preserving task accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Scheduling policies designed for autoregressive models waste much of the speed of diffusion LLMs, and scheduling by remaining denoising work recovers it. The authors state that the code will be released publicly.

title: Attention, Dynamic Wave and Hybrid Sequence Mixers in Language Models
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) rely on Multi-Head Attention (MHA) for sequence modeling, but scaling to long contexts is constrained by the quadratic cost of attention, motivating sub-quadratic recurrent alternatives. This paper formalizes a Dynamic Wave recurrent layer, based on input-dependent exponential damping and cosine phase modulation, and evaluates three 10.94M-parameter configurations (Pure Transformer, Pure Wave, and Hybrid Wave-Attention) on TinyStories under perplexity, latency, throughput and peak VRAM profiling up to 4096 tokens. The Hybrid configuration reaches the best perplexity, 5.95 on the full held-out split against 6.93 for the Transformer and 7.26 for Pure Wave. The efficiency picture, however, is governed by implementation rather than by architecture. Against an unfused attention baseline, Pure Wave uses 78.7% less peak VRAM at a 4096-token context (1404.3 MB vs. 6601.6 MB); against a fused scaled-dot-product attention kernel the same comparison yields no advantage at all (1404.3 MB vs. 1403.6 MB), and in training mode Pure Wave is 8.3% more expensive than the Transformer. Likewise, hoisting elementwise terms out of the recurrence loop speeds the layer up 2.53-fold with no custom kernel, reducing its latency gap to attention from 2.48-fold to 1.12-fold. A hybrid stack is found to inherit the cost of its more expensive mixer rather than the advantage of its cheaper one, its peak VRAM matching the Pure Transformer to within 0.1%. A closed-form memory model reproduces these measurements and predicts the context length beyond which attention overtakes the vocabulary projection. The findings indicate that reported efficiency gains for recurrent attention replacements must be stated relative to a named attention backend and a named implementation, and that hybridization is best justified on quality grounds.

AI.tldr: Formalizes a Dynamic Wave recurrent layer and compares it with Transformer attention on TinyStories using 10.94M-parameter models. The Hybrid Wave-Attention configuration reaches the best perplexity, but its efficiency picture is governed by implementation, so efficiency claims must be stated against a named attention backend.
AI.motivation: Scaling attention to long contexts is constrained by its quadratic cost, which motivates sub-quadratic recurrent alternatives.
AI.method: The Dynamic Wave layer is based on input-dependent exponential damping and cosine phase modulation. Three 10.94M-parameter configurations (Pure Transformer, Pure Wave and Hybrid Wave-Attention) are evaluated on TinyStories for perplexity, latency, throughput and peak VRAM up to 4096 tokens. A closed-form memory model is also given, and it reproduces these measurements.
AI.result: The Hybrid configuration reaches the best perplexity, 5.95 on the full held-out split, against 6.93 for the Transformer and 7.26 for Pure Wave. Against an unfused attention baseline, Pure Wave uses 78.7% less peak VRAM at a 4096-token context (1404.3 MB vs. 6601.6 MB), but against a fused scaled-dot-product attention kernel there is no advantage (1404.3 MB vs. 1403.6 MB), and in training mode Pure Wave is 8.3% more expensive than the Transformer. Hoisting elementwise terms out of the recurrence loop speeds the layer up 2.53-fold with no custom kernel, reducing its latency gap to attention from 2.48-fold to 1.12-fold. A hybrid stack inherits the cost of its more expensive mixer, with peak VRAM matching the Pure Transformer to within 0.1%.
AI.conclusion: Reported efficiency gains for recurrent attention replacements must be stated relative to a named attention backend and implementation, and hybridization is best justified on quality grounds. The memory model also predicts the context length beyond which attention overtakes the vocabulary projection.

title: Turing LLM Post-Training: Calibrated Distillation and Efficient Dynamic-MoE Execution
summary: We study post-training for dynamically routed mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, focusing on integrating independently optimized specialists while keeping consolidation efficient. Our approach combines calibrated multi-teacher on-policy distillation (C-MOPD), which matches each selected teacher on a local Top-$K$ support with teacher-wise loss normalization and clipping, with an execution path that uses post-capacity bounded-width dispatch, final-route replay, and asynchronous rollout--training overlap. On Turing-20B-A2B, the selected model achieves a four-domain normalized integration score of 0.9988 and retains at least 90.16\% of the measured specialist gain in every domain. At matched $K=32$, the full calibration objective scores 0.9962, compared with 0.9724 without calibration and 0.9834 without clipping. At a matched 8K response cap, the model exceeds both shared SFT and Qwen3-8B on all four reasoning-enabled mathematics and code benchmarks (unweighted mean: 85.92, versus 80.33 for Qwen3-8B and 74.21 for SFT), and improves over SFT on ten of twelve broader evaluation metrics. In a PPU-based profile, the combined execution configuration reduces consolidation step time from 398.7 to 139.3 seconds, an observed 2.86$\times$ speedup over serial execution. These results demonstrate strong specialist integration alongside more efficient consolidation, while reflecting the complete training and execution framework rather than any single component.

AI.tldr: Presents a post-training pipeline for dynamically routed mixture-of-experts models that integrates independently optimized specialists through calibrated multi-teacher on-policy distillation, with an execution path that makes consolidation more efficient. On Turing-20B-A2B the selected model reaches a four-domain normalized integration score of 0.9988.
AI.motivation: Integrating independently optimized specialists into a dynamically routed MoE model is required, and consolidation has to remain efficient while doing so.
AI.method: Calibrated multi-teacher on-policy distillation (C-MOPD) matches each selected teacher on a local Top-K support, with teacher-wise loss normalization and clipping. The execution path uses post-capacity bounded-width dispatch, final-route replay, and asynchronous rollout-training overlap.
AI.result: On Turing-20B-A2B the model achieves a four-domain normalized integration score of 0.9988 and retains at least 90.16% of the measured specialist gain in every domain. At K=32 the full calibration objective scores 0.9962, compared with 0.9724 without calibration and 0.9834 without clipping. At a matched 8K response cap the model exceeds both shared SFT and Qwen3-8B on all four reasoning-enabled mathematics and code benchmarks (unweighted mean 85.92, versus 80.33 for Qwen3-8B and 74.21 for SFT), and improves over SFT on ten of twelve broader evaluation metrics. In a PPU-based profile the combined execution configuration reduces consolidation step time from 398.7 to 139.3 seconds, an observed 2.86x speedup over serial execution.
AI.conclusion: The results show strong specialist integration alongside more efficient consolidation, and they reflect the complete training and execution framework rather than any single component.

title: TACFormer: Transformer-Based Generative Model for Target-Conditioned De Novo PROTAC Design
summary: Targeted protein degradation (TPD) represents a fundamental shift in drug discovery, moving beyond traditional target inhibition toward the event-driven removal of disease-causing proteins. A prominent strategy for TPD is the use of proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs), heterobifunctional molecules that selectively route a protein of interest (POI) to the ubiquitin-proteasome system for degradation. While PROTAC design still relies heavily on trial-and-error synthesis and experimental testing, deep generative models offer a promising means to explore PROTAC chemical space in silico and generate novel molecules. However, many existing generative methods formulate PROTAC design primarily as a linker-generation problem, with POI-binding (warhead) and E3-ligase-binding components fixed in advance. This restricts exploration of the full PROTAC chemical space and often leaves the POI implicit through the predefined warhead, rather than using protein-level information as an explicit conditioning signal during generation. To address these limitations, we propose TACFormer: a transformer-based generative model for target-aware de novo PROTAC design. The model conditions a GPT-style molecular decoder on pretrained ESM-2 representations of POI sequences, allowing POI-level information to steer full-molecule generation. Our results show that TACFormer generates highly novel and chemically diverse PROTACs while showing consistent POI-dependent shifts in generated chemical space. In particular, molecules generated under specific target conditions preferentially populate chemical neighborhoods associated with POIs in the held-out dataset, while extrapolating to novel chemotypes. By natively integrating biological context into the generative process, TACFormer moves PROTAC design toward a more biology-informed exploration of degrader chemical space.

AI.tldr: TACFormer is a transformer generative model that designs PROTAC molecules de novo, conditioned on pretrained ESM-2 representations of the protein of interest rather than on a fixed warhead. It generates novel and chemically diverse PROTACs whose chemical space shifts consistently with the target.
AI.motivation: Many generative methods treat PROTAC design as linker generation with the warhead and E3-ligase-binding components fixed in advance, which restricts exploration of PROTAC chemical space and leaves the protein of interest implicit rather than an explicit conditioning signal.
AI.method: A GPT-style molecular decoder is conditioned on pretrained ESM-2 representations of protein of interest sequences, so that protein-level information steers full-molecule generation.
AI.result: TACFormer generates highly novel and chemically diverse PROTACs with consistent POI-dependent shifts in generated chemical space. Molecules generated under specific target conditions preferentially populate chemical neighborhoods associated with POIs in the held-out dataset, while also extrapolating to novel chemotypes.
AI.conclusion: By integrating biological context into the generative process, the approach moves PROTAC design toward biology-informed exploration of degrader chemical space.

title: Data-driven Random-feature Approximation of Koopman Generators of Nonlinear Continuous-time Systems
summary: Learning continuous-time dynamical systems from data is an active area of research. The Koopman formalism is often used here, because it is a flexible approach that is informative about the system's fundamental properties. The formalism represents dynamical systems through linear operators acting on a suitable function space. A practical difficulty arising in the numerical approximation of Koopman operators is the choice of a ``dictionary'', meaning an effective finite-dimensional representation of the function space. In this paper, we focus on learning dynamical systems in continuous-time, and so we consider numerical approximations of the Koopman generator instead of the Koopman operator. Our main contribution is a data-driven random-feature method to obtain a parsimonious and effective function representation for Galerkin approximation methods such as gEDMD. The representation we construct is data-informed, which allows us to improve upon data-agnostic methods. We empirically demonstrate the suitability of our method for forecasting tasks and system analysis. The numerical experiments show that our approach is accurate, and faster than iterative optimization. Further, we prove convergence of our approximation of the vector field and the resulting trajectories. In addition to the numerical results, we also make theoretical contributions, including a general convergence criterion for the semigroup generated by the gEDMD approximation and a counterexample showing that gEDMD does not generally preserve exponential boundedness. With our contribution, we advance the frontier of efficiently learning continuous-time dynamics from data, towards interpretable and mathematically robust modelling based on the Koopman framework.

AI.tldr: Proposes a data-driven random-feature method that builds a parsimonious function representation for Galerkin approximation of the Koopman generator of continuous-time systems, with convergence proofs for the approximated vector field and resulting trajectories. The approach is accurate and faster than iterative optimization in the reported experiments.
AI.motivation: Numerical Koopman approximations depend on choosing a dictionary, an effective finite-dimensional representation of the function space, and this choice is practically difficult. Data-agnostic dictionaries do not exploit the data.
AI.method: The paper works with the Koopman generator rather than the Koopman operator, and builds a data-informed random-feature representation for Galerkin methods such as gEDMD.
AI.result: The method is accurate and faster than iterative optimization in numerical experiments on forecasting and system analysis, and the authors prove convergence of the approximated vector field and resulting trajectories. They also give a general convergence criterion for the semigroup generated by the gEDMD approximation and a counterexample showing that gEDMD does not generally preserve exponential boundedness.
AI.conclusion: The approach advances efficient learning of continuous-time dynamics from data toward interpretable and mathematically robust modelling within the Koopman framework.

title: CovFedAvg: Local Low-Loss Curves and Federated Model Selection
summary: Clients observing different parts of a prediction task may learn locally equivalent models with incompatible behavior outside their observed support. We study whether redundant models permit local low-loss paths toward a compatible shared model. CovFedAvg retains local models and curve controls on clients, fits a common endpoint through aggregated gradient contributions, and selects an actual candidate model using distributed training losses. No centralized calibration examples or client-to-client sample exchange are required. Exact selection guarantees no higher evaluated training loss than the previous model and the current-round FedAvg candidate; this is not a global-optimality, stationarity, generalization, or differential-privacy guarantee. We state conditional client-compatibility and approximate-selection bounds and retain corrected transformation identities and a separate full-gradient safeguard theorem for reference algorithms. A complementary input-support example recovers the shared absolute-value regression, while matched direct fine-tuning also solves it. Across a synthetic support task, recorded activity-recognition subjects, and participating and future gas-sensor batches, we evaluate five methods, five seeds, two network widths, and 20 rounds without calibration data. At width 16, CovFedAvg raises participating-Gas macro balanced accuracy from FedAvg's 88.88% to 89.84%; matched distributed fine-tuning reaches 91.65%. Results support feasibility and modest gains over FedAvg, but do not establish a curve-specific advantage over equally costly optimization. Exact-sum numerical experiments establish data flow; end-to-end privacy requires additional mechanisms and analysis.

AI.tldr: CovFedAvg is a federated learning method that keeps local models and curve controls on clients, fits a common endpoint from aggregated gradient contributions, and selects an actual candidate model using distributed training losses without calibration data. It gives modest gains over FedAvg but does not establish a curve-specific advantage.
AI.motivation: Clients observing different parts of a prediction task may learn locally equivalent models that behave incompatibly outside their observed support, so the question is whether redundant models permit local low-loss paths toward a compatible shared model.
AI.method: Local models and curve controls stay on clients, and a common endpoint is fitted through aggregated gradient contributions. Selection chooses an actual candidate model using distributed training losses, with no centralized calibration examples or client-to-client sample exchange.
AI.result: The exact selection guarantees no higher evaluated training loss than the previous model or the current-round FedAvg candidate, with conditional client-compatibility and approximate-selection bounds, though it is not a global-optimality, stationarity, generalization or differential-privacy guarantee. Across a synthetic support task, recorded activity-recognition subjects and gas-sensor batches, five methods were evaluated over five seeds, two network widths and 20 rounds. At width 16 CovFedAvg raises participating-Gas macro balanced accuracy from FedAvg's 88.88% to 89.84%, while matched distributed fine-tuning reaches 91.65%.
AI.conclusion: The results support feasibility and modest gains over FedAvg but do not establish a curve-specific advantage over equally costly optimization, and end-to-end privacy would require additional mechanisms and analysis.

title: Learning Calibrated Confidence for Multi-Agent Collaboration
summary: Complex information seeking on the Web often requires collecting evidence from multiple documents and reasoning across them, as in multi-hop question answering. Multi-agent systems address such tasks by dividing work among specialized agents, where upstream agents produce intermediate answers and supporting evidence that downstream agents build upon. However, upstream answers vary in correctness, and most systems provide no quantitative signal about it, leaving the downstream agent to judge whether to trust or verify what it receives based solely on the textual evidence. In this paper, we propose MASCAL. Each agent learns to produce a correctness probability for its answer by jointly optimizing task performance and confidence calibration in reinforcement learning; the upstream agent passes this probability at handoff, giving the downstream agent a quantitative basis for its decisions, and the final answer also carries a calibrated probability, quantifying the reliability of the system output. To guide the downstream agent in using this signal during training, we introduce confidence-aware weighting, which increases the learning weight at positions responsive to the upstream probability, so that the agent learns more from decisions where it actively uses the signal. Across three collaboration architectures spanning Web retrieval and reasoning tasks, MASCAL improves task accuracy and calibration quality for both agents, and generalizes to deeper collaboration chains and different model scales. Intervention analysis confirms that upstream confidence affects downstream decision behavior, and the learned final confidence supports selective answering and targeted rechecking.

AI.tldr: MASCAL trains each agent in a multi-agent web question-answering system to output a calibrated correctness probability for its answer, passes that probability downstream at handoff, and attaches a calibrated probability to the final answer. Across three collaboration architectures it improves task accuracy and calibration quality for both agents.
AI.motivation: Upstream answers in multi-agent systems vary in correctness, yet most systems give downstream agents no quantitative signal about reliability, so they must judge whether to trust or verify from the textual evidence alone.
AI.method: Each agent is trained with reinforcement learning that jointly optimizes task performance and confidence calibration. Confidence-aware weighting raises the learning weight at positions where the downstream agent responds to the upstream probability.
AI.result: Across three collaboration architectures spanning Web retrieval and reasoning tasks, MASCAL improves task accuracy and calibration quality for both agents and generalizes to deeper collaboration chains and different model scales. Intervention analysis confirms that upstream confidence affects downstream decision behavior, and the learned final confidence supports selective answering and targeted rechecking.
AI.conclusion: Passing calibrated confidence between agents gives downstream agents a quantitative basis for their decisions and makes the reliability of the system output explicit.

title: Low-Bit GDN Recurrent-State Quantization: Global Gradient-aware Allocation and Pure-Write Sliding Windows
summary: Linear attention stores historical information in a recurrent state of fixed size, providing a compact memory representation for long-context inference. Reducing state precision further lowers per-request storage requirements, but quantized writeback errors enter subsequent recurrences, degrade prediction quality on long-reasoning tasks, and can be accompanied by repetitive generation and excessively long outputs. We propose Global Gradient-aware Allocation (GGA) and the Pure-Write Sliding Window (PW) to address precision allocation and recent-information maintenance. GGA combines candidate quantization residuals with gradient sensitivity to future prediction loss to allocate head bit widths under a model-wide mixed-precision budget. PW independently maintains recent pure writes as FP8 vector pairs, propagates them through the full GDN state transition, and merges them into the low-bit historical state only after they leave the window. Across seven evaluations on Qwen3.5-4B/9B, GGA allocation alone improves over STEPQuant@4 by 19.48/29.84 percentage points. Adding PW-S8 yields seven-task macro-averages of 69.83%/78.63%, improving over STEPQuant@4 by 38.39/41.21 percentage points, respectively. Both precision reallocation and window maintenance improve task scores while mitigating excessively long outputs: at @6, GGA reduces mean generation length, averaged equally across tasks, by 10.45%/14.65% relative to STEPQuant; adding PW-S8 to GGA@4 further reduces mean generation length by 32.32%/36.77%. Comparisons at similar storage budgets further show that using additional capacity to maintain recent writes yields higher task scores and shorter mean outputs than solely increasing the bit width of the accumulated state.

AI.tldr: Proposes Global Gradient-aware Allocation (GGA) and a Pure-Write Sliding Window (PW) to quantize the recurrent state of GDN linear attention to low bit widths. Across seven evaluations on Qwen3.5-4B/9B, adding PW-S8 to GGA gives seven-task macro-averages of 69.83%/78.63%, improving over STEPQuant@4 by 38.39/41.21 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Reducing the precision of the recurrent state lowers per-request storage, but quantized writeback errors enter subsequent recurrences, degrading prediction quality on long-reasoning tasks and causing repetitive generation and excessively long outputs.
AI.method: GGA combines candidate quantization residuals with gradient sensitivity to future prediction loss to allocate head bit widths under a model-wide mixed-precision budget. PW keeps recent pure writes as FP8 vector pairs, propagates them through the full GDN state transition, and merges them into the low-bit historical state only after they leave the window.
AI.result: GGA allocation alone improves over STEPQuant@4 by 19.48/29.84 percentage points. Adding PW-S8 yields the seven-task macro-averages above. At @6, GGA reduces mean generation length, averaged equally across tasks, by 10.45%/14.65% relative to STEPQuant, and adding PW-S8 to GGA@4 further reduces it by 32.32%/36.77%. At similar storage budgets, using additional capacity to maintain recent writes yields higher task scores and shorter mean outputs than solely increasing the bit width of the accumulated state.
AI.conclusion: Both precision reallocation and window maintenance improve task scores while mitigating excessively long outputs, and spending extra capacity on recent writes can beat spending it on bit width.

title: H$^2$R: Hierarchical Hint-Based Reward for Mathematical Reasoning via Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards has shown great promise in enhancing mathematical reasoning in large language models. However, existing approaches provide limited intermediate supervision for complex, multi-step reasoning tasks. To bridge this gap, we propose \textbf{Hierarchical Hint-based Reward}, a framework that leverages the intrinsic sub-question structure of mathematical problems as structured intermediate conditioning signals during RLVR training. Unlike chain-of-thought prompting, these hierarchical hints serve as logically grounded intermediate milestones that effectively reduce the reasoning horizon toward the final answer. To validate this framework, we introduce \textbf{HiMath}, a benchmark of hierarchically structured mathematical problems. Across diverse LLMs, hierarchical hints consistently improve reasoning performance even without task-specific training. When integrated into RL training via H$^2$R, they boost Qwen2.5-Math-7B accuracy on HiMath from 30.4\% to 39.1\% using hierarchical hints, and up to 45.6\% with Oracle Hierarchical Hints. This pronounced improvement demonstrates that incorporating reliable intermediate checkpoints into reward design is essential for sustaining complex mathematical reasoning.

AI.tldr: H2R uses the sub-question structure of mathematical problems as hierarchical hints, which serve as intermediate conditioning signals during RLVR training. On HiMath, a new benchmark of hierarchically structured problems, it raises Qwen2.5-Math-7B accuracy from 30.4% to 39.1%, and up to 45.6% with Oracle Hierarchical Hints.
AI.motivation: Existing RLVR approaches provide limited intermediate supervision for complex, multi-step mathematical reasoning.
AI.method: Hierarchical Hint-based Reward (H2R) leverages the intrinsic sub-question structure of problems as logically grounded intermediate milestones during RLVR training, reducing the reasoning horizon toward the final answer. The authors also introduce HiMath, a benchmark of hierarchically structured mathematical problems.
AI.result: Hierarchical hints consistently improve reasoning performance across diverse LLMs, even without task-specific training. Integrated into RL training via H2R, they raise Qwen2.5-Math-7B accuracy on HiMath from 30.4% to 39.1%, and up to 45.6% with Oracle Hierarchical Hints.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating reliable intermediate checkpoints into reward design is essential for sustaining complex mathematical reasoning.

title: When to spend privacy: optimal allocation in private learning
summary: Privacy accounting bounds the cumulative privacy cost of Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent but does not determine how to allocate a fixed budget across iterations. We formulate the complete Gaussian noise-variance schedule as an open-loop control under a composed zero-Concentrated Differential Privacy constraint, explicitly accounting for schedule selection. For expected quadratic terminal tracking, we prove that every local minimizer exhausts the certified budget, yielding an exact-budget simplex formulation. We introduce Privacy-Budget Adjoint Mirror Descent (PB-AMD), combining pathwise adjoint gradients with entropic updates that preserve positivity, charge floors, and the prescribed budget. Under regularity and coercivity assumptions, we establish existence and budget stability of optimal schedules, design-to-training utility stability, and deterministic, stochastic, and sample-average stationarity guarantees. A linear-quadratic reduction yields an explicit square-root allocation law. Experiments demonstrate tracking improvements over several allocation rules and predictive improvements over uniform allocation in a learning-rate restart setting, where learning-rate allocation performs similarly. Comparisons at a common stationarity tolerance show lower schedule-optimization times than projected gradient descent on the tested problems. The framework connects certified privacy accounting with optimization through nonlinear training dynamics.

AI.tldr: Treats the per-iteration Gaussian noise-variance schedule of DP-SGD as an open-loop control under a composed zero-Concentrated Differential Privacy budget, and proves that every local minimizer exhausts the certified budget. The Privacy-Budget Adjoint Mirror Descent (PB-AMD) method optimizes these schedules.
AI.motivation: Privacy accounting bounds the cumulative privacy cost of DP-SGD but does not determine how to allocate a fixed budget across iterations.
AI.method: The complete Gaussian noise-variance schedule is formulated as an open-loop control under a composed zero-Concentrated Differential Privacy constraint, explicitly accounting for schedule selection. PB-AMD combines pathwise adjoint gradients with entropic updates that preserve positivity, charge floors and the prescribed budget.
AI.result: For expected quadratic terminal tracking, every local minimizer exhausts the certified budget, giving an exact-budget simplex formulation. Under regularity and coercivity assumptions the authors establish existence and budget stability of optimal schedules, design-to-training utility stability, and deterministic, stochastic and sample-average stationarity guarantees. A linear-quadratic reduction yields an explicit square-root allocation law. Experiments show tracking improvements over several allocation rules and predictive improvements over uniform allocation in a learning-rate restart setting, where learning-rate allocation performs similarly. At a common stationarity tolerance, schedule optimization is faster than projected gradient descent on the tested problems.
AI.conclusion: The framework connects certified privacy accounting with optimization through nonlinear training dynamics.

title: Observability-Aligned Evidential Masked Pretraining for Reliable VRU Motion Prediction
summary: Vulnerable road user (VRU) prediction must operate under partial observability and distribution shift, so reliable uncertainty matters alongside accuracy. Masked pretraining is attractive in this setting because it naturally exposes the model to missing content during self-supervision, but existing time-series masked autoencoding methods are typically deterministic and do not constrain how confidence should change with observability. We introduce eCoMAE, an evidential masked pretraining method for multivariate time series that explicitly aligns predictive evidence with what is observed. eCoMAE combines block-wise time-step masking with a Normal-Inverse-Gamma decoder and three observability-aware mechanisms: uncertainty-weighted mean consistency on positions visible in both a masked view and a reference pass, evidence suppression on masked positions, and representation consistency across stochastic masks. On IMPTC benchmark for VRU intention prediction under leave-one-environment-out weather shift, eCoMAE improves the strongest baseline from 0.7971 to 0.8068 in OOD accuracy and from 0.0718 to 0.0648 in OOD AURC. Additional evaluation on pedestrian trajectory forecasting across IMPTC, Waymo, nuScenes, and inD further yields the best fine-tuning MSE on all four datasets. These results show that observability-aligned evidential pretraining improves reliability under shift and remains effective beyond the primary benchmark.

AI.tldr: eCoMAE is an evidential masked pretraining method for multivariate time series that aligns predictive evidence with what is observed, for reliable vulnerable road user motion prediction under partial observability and distribution shift. It improves the strongest baseline's OOD accuracy on IMPTC from 0.7971 to 0.8068 and lowers OOD AURC from 0.0718 to 0.0648.
AI.motivation: VRU prediction must operate under partial observability and distribution shift, where reliable uncertainty matters. Existing time-series masked autoencoding methods are typically deterministic and do not constrain how confidence should change with observability.
AI.method: eCoMAE combines block-wise time-step masking with a Normal-Inverse-Gamma decoder and three observability-aware mechanisms: uncertainty-weighted mean consistency on positions visible in both a masked view and a reference pass, evidence suppression on masked positions, and representation consistency across stochastic masks.
AI.result: On the IMPTC benchmark for VRU intention prediction under leave-one-environment-out weather shift, eCoMAE improves the strongest baseline from 0.7971 to 0.8068 in OOD accuracy and from 0.0718 to 0.0648 in OOD AURC. On pedestrian trajectory forecasting across IMPTC, Waymo, nuScenes and inD it yields the best fine-tuning MSE on all four datasets.
AI.conclusion: Observability-aligned evidential pretraining improves reliability under shift and remains effective beyond the primary benchmark.

title: A physics-informed uncertainty-aware surrogate for $p$-$n$ junction diodes
summary: We develop an uncertainty-aware physics-informed surrogate for a one-dimensional $p$-$n$ junction diode, conditioned on device length, doping and bias. Using the internal state of the device as predicted by the surrogate we develop a test-suite of quantities of interest including the terminal current, depletion width, peak field and stored charge. The formalism and the quantities are can be extended to asymmetric junction and two-dimensional diodes as shown by means of benchmark analysis. For the one-dimensional symmetric junction surrogate, we obtain 0.11% median $L_1$ error on the electrostatic potential, and 1.5% and 0.61% on the electron and hole densities. Finally, we develop an uncertainty analysis which determines the validity of surrogate answer within the user-specified tolerance.

AI.tldr: Develops an uncertainty-aware physics-informed surrogate for a one-dimensional p-n junction diode, conditioned on device length, doping and bias, together with a test suite of quantities of interest. For the symmetric junction it reaches a 0.11% median L1 error on the electrostatic potential.
AI.motivation: The abstract does not state an explicit gap. It targets a surrogate of a p-n junction diode whose predictions come with uncertainty and are checked against a user-specified tolerance.
AI.method: The surrogate predicts the internal state of the device, from which quantities of interest are computed: terminal current, depletion width, peak field and stored charge. An uncertainty analysis determines whether surrogate answers are valid within the user-specified tolerance. The formalism is extended to asymmetric junctions and two-dimensional diodes through benchmark analysis.
AI.result: For the one-dimensional symmetric junction surrogate the median L1 error is 0.11% on the electrostatic potential, and 1.5% and 0.61% on the electron and hole densities.
AI.conclusion: The formalism and quantities extend to asymmetric junctions and two-dimensional diodes, and the uncertainty analysis gives a validity check on surrogate answers.

title: Enhancing Atrial Fibrillation Detection Through Hyperparameter Optimization
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables. Presented at the ICT Innovation 2025 Conference, Ohrid, North Macedonia. Accepted for publish by Springer in the Communications in Computer and Information Science Series (CCIS). In press
summary: This study explores the role of hyperparameter optimization (HPO) in enhancing the detection of Atrial Fibrillation (AF) using both machine learning and deep learning models. We evaluated a range of standard classifiers - Decision Tree, Random Forest, and XGBoost classifiers, alongside deep learning architectures including Recurrent Neural Networks, Deep Neural Networks, and Siamese Neural Networks. To fine-tune these models, we applied four HPO methods: Genetic Algorithm, Hyperband, Optuna, and SMAC3. The experiments were conducted using inter-patient and intra- patient data splits to assess model generalization and robustness in the presence of class imbalance, which is reflective of real-world AF occurrence. Our results, based on PhysioNet electrocardiogram datasets, showed that the Hyperband-optimized XGBoost model outperformed all others, achieving a peak F1 score of 96.95%. These findings highlight the critical role of suitable HPO strategies in enhancing the accuracy and robustness of AF classification outcomes in clinical settings.

AI.tldr: Compares four hyperparameter optimization methods on machine learning and deep learning models for atrial fibrillation detection using PhysioNet ECG data. The Hyperband-optimized XGBoost model performs best, with a peak F1 score of 96.95%.
AI.motivation: AF detection must generalize and remain robust under class imbalance that reflects real-world AF occurrence, and the study asks how much hyperparameter optimization contributes to this.
AI.method: Decision Tree, Random Forest and XGBoost classifiers, along with Recurrent Neural Networks, Deep Neural Networks and Siamese Neural Networks, are tuned with four HPO methods: Genetic Algorithm, Hyperband, Optuna and SMAC3. Experiments use inter-patient and intra-patient data splits.
AI.result: On PhysioNet electrocardiogram datasets the Hyperband-optimized XGBoost model outperformed all others, achieving a peak F1 score of 96.95%.
AI.conclusion: Suitable HPO strategies play a critical role in enhancing the accuracy and robustness of AF classification in clinical settings.

title: FIDE: Fiber-Informed Differentiable Experimental Design for Reference-Relative Law Dynamics
summary: Aggregate measurements generally leave an evolving population law underdetermined, so different measurement systems can be equally adequate for a scientific task while constraining different aspects of the law. We study how to resolve this residual design freedom in baseline-preserving settings, where an existing dynamical model remains the working baseline outside quantities explicitly valued by the task. \textbf{F}iber-\textbf{I}nformed \textbf{D}ifferentiable \textbf{E}xperimental Design (\textbf{FIDE}) completes each candidate's aggregate constraints by information projection relative to a common frozen reference, then ranks scientifically adequate designs by the dynamical revision required to realize the resulting completed paths. The resulting \emph{Full action} is the minimum mean-squared velocity correction needed to realize a completed path; equivalently, its square root is the sharp reference-relative expectation-rate discrepancy over a gradient-normalized Sobolev class. This defines a conditional minimum-revision principle for baseline-preserving design rather than a generic truth-recovery objective. Experiments show that this preference changes sensor selection, can help or harm withheld downstream predictions depending on baseline reliability, can be used prospectively from aggregate predictions, and remains computationally usable for a $32$-dimensional configuration law.

AI.tldr: FIDE ranks scientifically adequate experimental designs for evolving population laws by the minimum mean-squared velocity correction needed to realize their completed paths relative to a frozen reference. This preference changes sensor selection and can be used prospectively from aggregate predictions.
AI.motivation: Aggregate measurements leave an evolving population law underdetermined, so different measurement systems can be equally adequate for a task while constraining different aspects of the law. The paper resolves this residual design freedom in baseline-preserving settings, where an existing dynamical model remains the working baseline outside quantities valued by the task.
AI.method: Each candidate's aggregate constraints are completed by information projection relative to a common frozen reference, and designs are ranked by the dynamical revision needed to realize the completed paths. The Full action is the minimum mean-squared velocity correction needed to realize a completed path, and its square root is the sharp reference-relative expectation-rate discrepancy over a gradient-normalized Sobolev class.
AI.result: The preference changes sensor selection and can help or harm withheld downstream predictions depending on baseline reliability. It can be used prospectively from aggregate predictions and remains computationally usable for a 32-dimensional configuration law.
AI.conclusion: This defines a conditional minimum-revision principle for baseline-preserving design, rather than a generic truth-recovery objective.

title: One Vector or Many? Clustered Optimal-Transport Steering under Quantization
summary: Activation steering changes what a language model generates by editing its hidden states at inference time. Its most common form adds one vector, the difference of class means (DiM), to every hidden state. CHaRS (concept heterogeneity-aware representation steering) uses optimal transport instead: an entropic plan pairs the clusters of the two classes, and each hidden state moves along a mixture of the cluster displacements, weighted toward its nearest clusters. We study this family of clustered optimal-transport maps for toxicity mitigation in Gemma-2-2B and Granite-3.1-2B, and ask what the plan adds to DiM and whether that survives INT8 and NF4 quantization. We prove an identity: whatever the plan, the displacements averaged with the cluster sizes as weights equal DiM, so a clustered map can differ from DiM only for tokens whose routing weights depart from the cluster sizes. In the CHaRS protocol they stay close, and CHaRS is statistically equivalent to Mean-AcT, which adds DiM at every layer, in all eight pre-specified equivalence tests. A variant fitted on individual tokens, which routes each token mainly to its nearest clusters, leaves 37-39% less toxicity than DiM on Gemma and 51-61% less on Granite at steering strength 3 (toxic-bert), where DiM already removes 76-85% of it. Two other toxicity classifiers confirm the gain on Granite, but on Gemma only one does. At equal strength the variant has somewhat higher perplexity, but at matched toxicity it is slightly more fluent than DiM. Yet a nearly constant map from the same clusters also leaves about 30% less toxicity, so the role of treating tokens differently remains open. Under INT8 and NF4 the variant still leaves less toxicity than DiM, and transferring it from full precision to the NF4 model instead of refitting it adds no significant toxicity after correction for multiple tests.

AI.tldr: Studies clustered optimal-transport activation steering for toxicity mitigation in Gemma-2-2B and Granite-3.1-2B. The paper proves that a clustered map differs from difference-of-means (DiM) steering only through routing weights that depart from the cluster sizes, and a per-token variant leaves less toxicity than DiM, including under INT8 and NF4 quantization.
AI.motivation: Activation steering commonly adds one difference-of-class-means vector to every hidden state. The paper asks whether a clustered optimal-transport map (CHaRS) adds anything to DiM and whether that survives quantization.
AI.method: CHaRS uses an entropic optimal-transport plan that pairs the clusters of the two classes, and moves each hidden state along a mixture of cluster displacements weighted toward its nearest clusters. The paper also tests a variant fitted on individual tokens that routes each token mainly to its nearest clusters.
AI.result: The proven identity shows that displacements averaged with cluster sizes as weights equal DiM. In the CHaRS protocol CHaRS is statistically equivalent to Mean-AcT, which adds DiM at every layer, in all eight pre-specified equivalence tests. At steering strength 3 with toxic-bert, the per-token variant leaves 37-39% less toxicity than DiM on Gemma and 51-61% less on Granite, where DiM already removes 76-85%. Two other toxicity classifiers confirm the gain on Granite, but on Gemma only one does. At matched toxicity the variant is slightly more fluent than DiM, though at equal strength it has somewhat higher perplexity. A nearly constant map from the same clusters also leaves about 30% less toxicity. Under INT8 and NF4 the variant still leaves less toxicity than DiM, and transferring it to the NF4 model instead of refitting adds no significant toxicity after correction for multiple tests.
AI.conclusion: The role of treating tokens differently remains open, because a nearly constant map from the same clusters achieves a substantial part of the reduction.

title: Coupled Guidance for Flow Matching
summary: Guidance methods are essential tools for steering the generation process in diffusion models, improving the generalizability of stochastic robotic controllers and enabling high-quality controlled image synthesis. Despite strong parallels between flow-matching and diffusion, integrating guidance into flow-matching models remains quite challenging. Recent work has proposed general guidance frameworks for flow-matching, however, they are direct adaptations of diffusion guidance methods and can prove unstable. In this work, we conduct a theoretical analysis of guidance in flow-matching and show that a naive translation of diffusion-based guidance to flow-matching breaks the coupling distribution used during training, resulting in weaker control over sampling accuracy. Building on this insight, we propose Coupled Guidance, a flow-matching-specific guidance mechanism derived from a geometric perspective that leverages the coupling structure inherent to flow-matching training. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct extensive experimentation on a custom robotic collision avoidance task using ManiSkill3, four robotic dexterous manipulation tasks from the Adroit benchmark, and three image generation tasks, namely inpainting, super-resolution, and deblurring, using the ImageNet-128 and CelebA-HQ-256 datasets. Our findings show that our framework improves sample quality and guidance stability across all tasks, without imposing any additional overhead.

AI.tldr: Coupled Guidance is a flow-matching-specific guidance mechanism that preserves the coupling structure used in training, which naive translation of diffusion guidance breaks. It improves sample quality and guidance stability across robotic and image generation tasks without additional overhead.
AI.motivation: Guidance is essential for steering generation, but adapting diffusion guidance directly to flow matching can be unstable and breaks the coupling distribution used during training, weakening control over sampling accuracy.
AI.method: A theoretical analysis of guidance in flow matching motivates Coupled Guidance, which is derived from a geometric perspective and leverages the coupling structure inherent to flow-matching training.
AI.result: Experiments cover a custom robotic collision avoidance task in ManiSkill3, four dexterous manipulation tasks from the Adroit benchmark, and three image generation tasks (inpainting, super-resolution and deblurring) on ImageNet-128 and CelebA-HQ-256. Coupled Guidance improves sample quality and guidance stability across all tasks without imposing additional overhead.
AI.conclusion: Coupling-aware guidance gives a stable and low-overhead way to control flow-matching sampling in both robotics and image synthesis.

title: D-MOD: Diffusion mode estimation for accelerated MRI
summary: Diffusion models are powerful priors for accelerated MRI reconstruction, but most current methods are posterior samplers, which return a random draw from the posterior. A reproducible and high-quality reconstruction often requires averaging many samples, resulting in a high computational cost. We introduce D-MOD, a fast algorithm that instead provides a posterior mode. It uses a minorize-maximize algorithm on a lower bound of the smoothed log-posterior, which provably increases the objective. Each iteration draws S noisy samples of the current estimate at the current noise level, denoises them with a pretrained diffusion model, and combines their average with the measured k-space through a conjugate-gradient (CG) solve. We anneal the noise levels, as the distance between the bound and its target decays quadratically with noise. On fastMRI brain (T1, T2, FLAIR), a single D-MOD reconstruction exceeds, in PSNR, the 10-sample finite-MMSE estimates of DPS, DAPS and SNORE-P and stays within 0.31 dB of the strongest baselines (DiffPIR, DDS). This approach thus provides a fast deterministic reconstruction algorithm (11-73 times faster than MMSE estimates), which is useful in a clinical setting.

AI.tldr: D-MOD estimates a posterior mode for accelerated MRI reconstruction with a diffusion prior, using a minorize-maximize algorithm rather than averaging many posterior samples. A single D-MOD reconstruction exceeds the 10-sample finite-MMSE estimates of DPS, DAPS and SNORE-P in PSNR on fastMRI brain data.
AI.motivation: Most diffusion-based MRI reconstruction methods are posterior samplers that return a random draw, and a reproducible high-quality reconstruction requires averaging many samples, which is computationally costly.
AI.method: D-MOD uses a minorize-maximize algorithm on a lower bound of the smoothed log-posterior, which provably increases the objective. Each iteration draws S noisy samples of the current estimate at the current noise level, denoises them with a pretrained diffusion model, and combines their average with the measured k-space through a conjugate-gradient solve. Noise levels are annealed, since the distance between the bound and its target decays quadratically with noise.
AI.result: On fastMRI brain (T1, T2, FLAIR), a single D-MOD reconstruction exceeds the 10-sample finite-MMSE estimates of DPS, DAPS and SNORE-P in PSNR and stays within 0.31 dB of the strongest baselines, DiffPIR and DDS. It is 11-73 times faster than MMSE estimates.
AI.conclusion: D-MOD provides a fast deterministic reconstruction algorithm that is useful in a clinical setting.

title: Does System Size Matter in Uncertainty Quantification for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials?
summary: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) commonly use uncertainty estimates to flag out-of-distribution (OOD) configurations and select structures for active learning. A key question is whether the resulting structure-level uncertainty scores remain comparable across different system sizes. A common practice is to aggregate per-atom uncertainties by their mean or maximum and compare the resulting score against a fixed threshold, implicitly assuming such comparability. We test this assumption across several in-distribution (ID)/OOD pairs by characterizing both aggregations as a function of atom count. The two aggregations exhibit distinct size dependencies. Mean aggregation remains size-independent for homogeneous systems but loses sensitivity to defects in large cells. In contrast, maximum aggregation grows with system size for ID systems while remaining approximately flat for defect-containing systems, narrowing the ID-OOD gap in a manner consistent with extreme-value statistics. Although highly uncertain atoms in large structures may indicate novel local environments, retraining on these structures yields little improvement, in contrast to retraining on OOD structures constructed to lie outside the training distribution. Our results reveal a practical limitation of size-unaware uncertainty criteria and motivate size-aware calibration for more reliable OOD detection in large-scale atomistic simulations.

AI.tldr: Shows that structure-level uncertainty scores from machine-learning interatomic potentials are not comparable across system sizes under the common mean or maximum aggregation of per-atom uncertainties. Mean aggregation loses sensitivity to defects in large cells, while maximum aggregation grows with system size for in-distribution systems.
AI.motivation: Machine-learning interatomic potentials use uncertainty estimates to flag out-of-distribution configurations and select structures for active learning. Common practice compares the aggregated score against a fixed threshold, implicitly assuming that scores are comparable across sizes.
AI.method: The authors test this assumption across several in-distribution (ID) and OOD pairs by characterizing both mean and maximum aggregations as a function of atom count.
AI.result: The two aggregations show distinct size dependencies. Mean aggregation remains size-independent for homogeneous systems but loses sensitivity to defects in large cells. Maximum aggregation grows with system size for ID systems while remaining approximately flat for defect-containing systems, narrowing the ID-OOD gap in a manner consistent with extreme-value statistics. Retraining on highly uncertain atoms in large structures yields little improvement, in contrast to retraining on OOD structures constructed to lie outside the training distribution.
AI.conclusion: Size-unaware uncertainty criteria are a practical limitation, and size-aware calibration is motivated for more reliable OOD detection in large-scale atomistic simulations.

title: Escaping Path Mirages in Offline Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning
comment: 10 pages (main), 34 pages in total. Accepted to NeurIPS 2026
summary: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning remains challenging in stochastic long-horizon settings, where compounding value estimation errors hinder reliable goal reaching. While prior methods have sought to address this challenge through various approaches, a key challenge remains path mirage, where agents overcommit to spuriously successful trajectories in offline datasets induced by stochasticity, often leading to failure on difficult tasks. To address this issue, we propose Branch-aware Graph Planning (BGP), which captures stochastic branching structures by identifying high-variability points as graph nodes and designing goal-conditioned edges with segmented learning to avoid unreliable branches and reduce unnecessary stochasticity along paths. As a result, BGP enables reliable goal reaching even in highly stochastic long-horizon environments, and experiments on diverse OGBench tasks show that it substantially outperforms prior state-of-the-art offline goal-conditioned RL methods. Our implementation is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes Branch-aware Graph Planning (BGP) for offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning in stochastic long-horizon settings, targeting "path mirages" in which agents overcommit to spuriously successful trajectories. It substantially outperforms prior state-of-the-art offline goal-conditioned RL methods on diverse OGBench tasks.
AI.motivation: Compounding value estimation errors hinder reliable goal reaching in offline goal-conditioned RL, and stochasticity creates path mirages, where agents overcommit to spuriously successful trajectories in the offline dataset and often fail on difficult tasks.
AI.method: BGP captures stochastic branching structures by identifying high-variability points as graph nodes and designing goal-conditioned edges with segmented learning, which avoids unreliable branches and reduces unnecessary stochasticity along paths.
AI.result: Experiments on diverse OGBench tasks show that BGP substantially outperforms prior state-of-the-art offline goal-conditioned RL methods and enables reliable goal reaching even in highly stochastic long-horizon environments.
AI.conclusion: Modelling branching structure explicitly is a route to reliable goal reaching in stochastic long-horizon offline RL.
